Bayview Hunters Point.intro: The sunny southeast corner of the city: the Third Street commercial corridor with its murals and the 1888 Bayview Opera House, Hunters Point hill rising above it with a 70-foot sundial on top, and a working-waterfront edge that's quietly become great parkland — Heron's Head Park (a wetland peninsula literally shaped like a heron's head) and the brand-new India Basin Waterfront Park around an 1875 shipbuilder's cottage. Challenges anchor on those three zones: the corridor, the hill, and the shoreline.
Bayview Hunters Point.why_chosen: Stand on the giant Hilltop Park sundial and call exactly one minute with no clock, walk to the tip of the beak at Heron's Head Park, and guess a plant's price within 20% at Flora Grubb Gardens. A timing test, a walk, a price guess; one retryable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 45–60 minutes. (The Tuzuri Watu mural quiz, the Quesada palms and the India Basin stone skip are alternates.)

candidates.title: One Minute on the Sundial
candidates.do: Climb to Hilltop Park and its giant yellow sundial (the shadow-casting arm is 70 feet long). One teammate, the timekeeper, hands over their phone and watch and stands on the dial with eyes closed. A teammate with a phone stopwatch says "go" and starts it; the timekeeper says "stop" when they think exactly one minute has passed, counting silently in their head if they like, with no help from anyone. Within 2 seconds of 60 = complete. Off? Another teammate takes the dial and tries.
candidates.where: Hilltop Park, Whitney Young Circle at Newcomb Ave.
candidates.photo: The stopwatch showing the winning time, held up over the sundial's giant yellow arm.
candidates.why_here: A 70-foot sundial on a Bayview hilltop is the city's biggest clock — the right place to find out whether you can keep time without one.

candidates.title: Walk the Heron's Beak
candidates.do: Heron's Head Park is a peninsula that, from the air, is shaped like a heron's head. Walk the trail (~3/4 mile) all the way to the tip of the "beak" — the very end of the point, where the trail runs out into the Bay. Done when the whole team reaches the end of the trail.
candidates.where: Heron's Head Park, entrance at Cargo Way & Jennings St
candidates.place_name: Heron's Head Park - Nature Exploration Area
candidates.photo: Whole team at the trail's end at the beak's tip, Bay and skyline behind
candidates.why_here: SF's only bird-shaped park, built on an abandoned shipping terminal that turned itself into a wetland.

candidates.title: The Price Is Right at Flora Grubb
candidates.do: Flora Grubb Gardens is a jungle-like nursery that's free to wander. One teammate, the host, picks any plant and covers its price tag with a hand. The rest of the team agrees on ONE price guess together. Within 20% of the real price, over or under = complete. Off? Everyone waits five minutes (no guessing, no peeking at tags), then a new host picks a new plant and you guess again.
candidates.where: Flora Grubb Gardens, 1634 Jerrold Ave (open Sat–Sun 10am–6pm).
candidates.failable: retryable (each miss costs a five-minute wait)
candidates.photo: The host dramatically revealing the tag, guesses held up beside it.
candidates.why_here: A nursery with a car planted full of succulents and plants that cost more than a scooter — nobody's price instincts survive it.

candidates.title: Mural Memory on Third Street
candidates.do: Find the Tuzuri Watu mural ("We Are Beautiful People," 1987) at Third & Palou. Everyone studies it for 60 seconds, then the whole team turns its back. Three fixed questions, answered as a team: (1) how many human faces are painted, (2) how many of them wear something on their head, (3) what color is the largest figure's clothing. Turn around and check by counting together. Three for three = complete. Any miss = a new 60 seconds and try again.
candidates.where: Third St & Palou Ave (the Obama mural at Third & Oakdale, two blocks on, works as a second board with the same three questions).
candidates.failable: no (new study round until three for three)
candidates.photo: Backs to the wall mid-answer, then the recount with fingers on faces.
candidates.why_here: The Third Street corridor is Bayview's living room, and this is its most famous wall — dense enough to punish a lazy memory.

candidates.title: Count the Quesada Palms
candidates.do: Quesada Avenue between Third St and Newhall St has a strip of towering palm trees down its center median, wrapped by the famous Quesada community gardens. Two teammates become the counters: one walks the north sidewalk, one the south, each silently counting every palm trunk in the median. At the Newhall end they say their numbers at the same time. A match = complete. A mismatch = swap sidewalks and count again. (Team of two: you're both counters.)
candidates.where: Quesada Ave median, Third St to Newhall St
candidates.failable: no (swap sides and recount until you agree)
candidates.photo: Both counters holding up their matching number on fingers at the Newhall end, the palm boulevard behind.
candidates.why_here: A palm-boulevard-turned-neighborhood-garden that residents built themselves — Bayview's most photogenic residential block, with just enough palms to make two people disagree.

candidates.title: Skip a Stone at India Basin
candidates.do: At India Basin Waterfront Park, walk down to the shoreline (the gravel and sand edge by the old boat launch). Find flat stones and skip: the challenge is complete when any teammate gets a stone to skip THREE times on the bay — three visible touches before it sinks. Everyone throws; unlimited tries; keep the throws away from birds and people.
candidates.where: India Basin Waterfront Park shoreline, 900 Innes Ave at Griffith St
candidates.photo: The thrower mid-release with the rings on the water, the Shipwright's Cottage (1875) behind.
candidates.why_here: A $200M park opened in 2024 around SF's last shipbuilder's cottage, with the calmest patch of bay on the east side — skipping water.

candidates.title: Count the Keys
candidates.do: In front of the 1926 brick Schlage Lock office building — sole survivor of the lock factory that ran Vis Valley's economy for 70 years — every teammate secretly writes down a guess: how many keys is the WHOLE team carrying right now? No peeking in pockets. Then everyone empties their keys into a pile and you count (a fob or car key counts as one). Anyone within 2 of the true count = complete. Nobody within 2 = failed. One count, ever.
candidates.where: Schlage Lock building, Bayshore Blvd near Blanken Ave.
candidates.photo: The pile of keys on the sidewalk, the winning guess held above it, the brick building behind.
candidates.why_here: A lock factory's last building is the only proper place to count keys.

candidates.title: Silent Movie in Little Hollywood
candidates.do: Go to Little Hollywood Park in the 1920s storybook enclave named for its movie-set houses, and shoot a silent movie: one teammate, the director, generates a random number 1–10 on a phone and whispers that scene to the actor — 1 brushing teeth, 2 walking a dog, 3 making a sandwich, 4 catching a fish, 5 changing a tire, 6 parallel parking, 7 milking a cow, 8 flying a kite, 9 shoveling snow, 10 juggling (re-roll repeats). The actor performs it with no sound and no props. The rest of the team gets ONE guess. Right = new actor, new scene. Wrong = the streak restarts. Complete when the team guesses three scenes in a row.
candidates.where: Little Hollywood Park, Lathrop Ave & Tocoloma Ave (east of Bayshore Blvd)
candidates.failable: no (the streak restarts until you hit three)
candidates.photo: The actor mid-scene on the lawn, the storybook cottages behind.
candidates.why_here: Little Hollywood is Vis Valley's oddest secret — a pocket of glamour-styled cottages that was always waiting for its silent-film era.

candidates.title: One Car or Two?
candidates.do: Get to Sunnydale Station (Bayshore Blvd at Sunnydale Ave), the final stop of the T Third and the southernmost Muni Metro stop in San Francisco. Muni Metro trains run as one car or two coupled cars. Before the next arriving train is close enough to count, the team calls it out loud on video: ONE or TWO. Right = complete. Wrong = new call for the next train (every 10–12 minutes).
candidates.where: Sunnydale Muni Station platform, Bayshore Blvd & Sunnydale Ave (no boarding required)
candidates.photo: The team on the platform pointing at the verdict train, "Sunnydale" sign in frame.
candidates.why_here: Vis Valley is where SF's rail system runs out of city — the one place in the game you can call a train at the very end of the line.

Bernal Heights.intro: Bernal is a grassy dome of a neighborhood: a wild 360°-view summit ringed by a paved loop, community-built stairways and slides carved into its slopes, and the small-town main street of Cortland Avenue at its southern foot. The official analysis neighborhood runs from Cesar Chavez (north) to the I-280/Alemany interchange (south), San Jose Ave (west) to US-101 (east) — so Precita Park, Holly Park, and the Alemany markets are all in-bounds, while Balmy Alley and Mitchell's Ice Cream are not. Everything below anchors on the hill itself and the odd, community-made things Bernal bolted onto it.
Bernal Heights.why_chosen: Call where your roller stops at the bottom of the Esmeralda slides, walk a lap of the perfectly circular Holly Park in a predicted time with no clock, and a forced-perspective photo that flattens the steepest street in San Francisco. One aiming game, one pacing game, one trick shot; one retryable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 40–50 minutes.

candidates.title: Call Your Landing at the Twin Slides
candidates.do: At Esmeralda Slide Park, pick something that rolls, found or bought on the way (an orange, a can, a ball). Before each roll, one teammate marks the spot at the bottom where they say it will stop, with a shoe or a bag. Then let it go from the top of one of the twin 40-foot slides: no push, no touching it after release. Complete when it comes to rest touching the marker. Missed? Fetch it, walk back up, place a new guess and roll again — rotate guessers.
candidates.where: Esmeralda Slide Park, on the Esmeralda Ave stairway between Winfield St and Prospect Ave (community street park, open daylight hours, free).
candidates.failable: no (walk back up and roll again)
candidates.photo: Your roller at rest against the marker at the foot of the slide, the team pointing like they called it.
candidates.why_here: These are Bernal's legendary neighbor-built slides — Mayor Dianne Feinstein raced a supervisor down them at the 1979 opening; now it's your turn to call where things end up.

candidates.title: Pace the Perfect Circle
candidates.do: Holly Park sits inside Holly Circle — a street that is a complete circle, one of SF's geometric oddities, ringing one of the city's oldest parks. At the Holly Park sign, one teammate, the walker, predicts out loud how long it will take them to walk one full lap of the park's perimeter path, say "8 minutes 30". Then the walker hands over their phone and watch and walks the lap — walking, no running, no clock of any kind, and nobody gives hints — while a teammate at the sign times it. Finish within 20 seconds of the prediction = complete. Off? Another lap, another prediction, any teammate can walk it.
candidates.where: Holly Park, ringed by Holly Circle (between Highland Ave, Park St, and Murray St).
candidates.photo: The stopwatch at the finish next to the prediction written down at the start, the walker behind them catching their breath.
candidates.why_here: A park whose address is a perfect circle is pure Bernal geography — and a circle is the hardest shape to guess the length of.

candidates.title: Flatten the Steepest Street
candidates.do: Walk to the top block of Bradford Street above Tompkins Avenue — at a 41% grade, the steepest street in San Francisco (Lombard's crooked block is only 27%). Make the hill disappear in a forced-perspective photo: one teammate is the photographer (no selfies, no timers) and tilts the camera until the street runs perfectly level across the frame, while the rest of the team stands normally on the sidewalk, so in the photo they seem to lean at an impossible angle. Done when the curb runs flat, side to side, and the team looks tipped over.
candidates.where: Bradford St between Tompkins Ave and Jarboe Ave, east slope of Bernal Hill.
candidates.photo: A dead-level street with the whole team leaning like a gale is blowing — the steepest street in the city, flattened.
candidates.why_here: Tourists queue at Lombard and Filbert; Bernal quietly holds the city's actual steepest street — steep enough that tilting the camera makes gravity look broken.

candidates.title: Doves & Melted Guns
candidates.do: In Precita Park, find the peace memorial: a bench made of cedar and metal from melted-down guns, resting on a dove-shaped platform of ~900 tiles hand-painted by neighbors in the 1990s. Sit the whole team on the bench, then find and photograph 3 different painted tiles: one with a heart, one with a sun or star, and one with an animal (any 3 clearly different pictures count if those exact motifs have worn away).
candidates.where: Precita Park, Precita Ave & Folsom St, on the side across from Precita Eyes (348 Precita Ave), Bernal's famous mural studio.
candidates.photo: Team on the melted-gun bench with the dove platform visible, plus close-ups of the 3 tiles.
candidates.why_here: Guns literally turned into a park bench by Bernal neighbors, on the block where the Precita Eyes mural movement was born — it exists nowhere else.

candidates.title: Treasure Run at Alemany
candidates.do: Go to 100 Alemany Blvd, home of the Alemany Farmers' Market — founded 1943, California's first farmers' market (Saturdays 7am–2pm) — which flips into the Alemany Flea Market on Sundays (7am–3pm). Saturday: buy one fruit or vegetable for $5 or less and every teammate takes a bite. Sunday: buy one treasure for $5 or less that is older than the oldest teammate (a printed date or maker's mark proves it). Purchase made + photo taken = complete.
candidates.where: Alemany Farmers' Market / Flea Market, 100 Alemany Blvd (at the south tip of the neighborhood; note the Saturday market closes at 2pm).
candidates.photo: The team holding the purchase at the vendor's stall — mid-bite on Saturday, treasure aloft on Sunday.
candidates.why_here: The oldest farmers' market in California lives at Bernal's southern edge, and its weekend double identity (produce/flea) is a neighborhood institution.

candidates.title: I Spy From Sutrito
candidates.do: Climb to the summit of Bernal Hill (the little radio tower locals call "Sutrito," a mini Sutro Tower) and play I Spy with the whole city as the board. The spy picks anything visible from the top — a tower, a bridge, a hill, a boat, a water tank — and gives the classic clue ("I spy something red and pointy"). Teammates guess by pointing — THREE guesses each per round; the spy says yes or no. Found = the next teammate is the spy. Nobody finds it = the spy reveals, and takes another turn with a new object. Complete when every teammate has been the spy once and had their thing found.
candidates.where: Bernal Heights Park summit, off Bernal Heights Blvd (open 24/7; the Esmeralda stairway from the slides leads straight up).
candidates.photo: The team at the summit fence, everyone pointing at the last thing spied, 360° of city behind.
candidates.why_here: Bernal Hill's 466-ft bald summit is one of the only true 360° panoramas in SF — the biggest I Spy board in the city.

Castro/Upper Market.intro: The Castro/Upper Market Analysis Neighborhood is Eureka Valley plus its hilly upper flanks — Corona Heights, Kite Hill, and the stairway streets climbing toward (but not including) Twin Peaks, whose summit sits in the separate "Twin Peaks" Analysis Neighborhood. It's anchored by the Castro & Market hub: the giant Gilbert Baker pride flag at Harvey Milk Plaza, the 1922 Castro Theatre, rainbow crosswalks at 18th & Castro, the F-line's vintage-streetcar terminus, and a 1936 everything-store — with the legendary Seward Street concrete slides hidden two blocks uphill.
Castro/Upper Market.why_chosen: Play twenty questions over a $5 mystery item from a 1936 variety store, find three Rainbow Honor Walk plaques in the sidewalks, then climb Corona Heights for a team selfie on the red rock summit. A guessing game, a find, a summit climb; one retryable, zero strangers, ~$5, ≈ 40–50 minutes.

candidates.title: Twenty Questions at Cliff's
candidates.do: Cliff's Variety has sold a bit of everything since 1936. One teammate, the shopper, goes in alone and buys ONE item for $5 or less, then hides it in a bag. The rest of the team gets TWENTY yes-or-no questions to name what it is. Named within twenty = complete. Stumped = new shopper, new item, try again.
candidates.where: Cliff's Variety, 479 Castro St (between 17th & 18th).
candidates.photo: The big reveal: the item pulled from the bag, the team mid-groan or mid-cheer, Cliff's storefront behind.
candidates.why_here: A 1936 hardware-and-everything store is the perfect place to buy the most unguessable $5 object in the city.

candidates.title: Sidewalk Hall of Fame
candidates.do: Find three different bronze Rainbow Honor Walk plaques set into the sidewalks of Castro St (and Market St nearby). For each, photograph it and note from the plaque text one thing that person is famous for. Complete with three plaques photographed and three facts recorded.
candidates.where: Sidewalks along Castro St between Market and 19th St, both sides; more on Market St near Castro.
candidates.photo: A shoes-around-the-plaque shot of your favorite of the three honorees.
candidates.why_here: The Rainbow Honor Walk is the Castro's own walk of fame — 40-plus bronze portraits of LGBTQ pioneers embedded in these exact sidewalks and nowhere else on Earth.

candidates.title: Red Rock Lookout
candidates.do: Climb to the bare red-chert summit of Corona Heights Park. Done when the whole team takes a selfie at the top.
candidates.where: Corona Heights Park summit; enter from Roosevelt Way or via Museum Way off Roosevelt. Open dawn to dusk, every day.
candidates.photo: The team selfie on the red rock summit, the city spread out behind you.
candidates.why_here: Corona Heights' craggy quarried summit is the Castro/Upper Market neighborhood's own peak — the closest thing to Twin Peaks you can claim without leaving the territory.

candidates.title: Marquee Recall at the Castro Theatre
candidates.do: Stand across Castro St from the Castro Theatre's giant neon blade sign and marquee. Everyone studies the marquee for exactly 30 seconds — every title, date and showtime on it — then the whole team turns its back. One teammate at a time names ONE item from the marquee; the team keeps a written list. A repeat or anything not on the marquee ends the round. Turn around and check: complete when the list matches every line on the marquee. Short? New 30-second look, list starts over.
candidates.where: Castro Theatre, 429 Castro St (view from the opposite sidewalk).
candidates.failable: no (re-study and start the list over)
candidates.photo: The team with their backs to the marquee, the written list held up.
candidates.why_here: The 1922 movie palace is the neighborhood's crown, and its marquee changes with every program — nobody can study it before game day.

candidates.title: Walk the Rainbow
candidates.do: At 18th & Castro, the crosswalks are painted in rainbow stripes that run the length of the crossing. Each teammate picks a different color stripe. When the WALK signal comes on, everyone crosses together with both feet staying on their own color the whole way — no stepping onto a neighbor's stripe. Anyone steps off, the whole team turns around and recrosses on the next WALK signal. Complete when the team makes one clean crossing. Cross only on the signal, and keep moving with the crowd.
candidates.where: The rainbow crosswalks at 18th St & Castro St.
candidates.failable: no (recross on the next signal until it's clean)
candidates.photo: Shot from the curb: the team mid-crossing, one person per stripe, the giant rainbow flag up the block.
candidates.why_here: The Castro painted its crosswalks rainbow in 2014, and they double as the city's only balance-beam course with a WALK signal.

candidates.title: Call the Color of the Next Streetcar
candidates.do: Go to the F-line terminus at Jane Warner Plaza (17th/Castro/Market). Each vintage PCC car is painted in the livery of a different city — cream, green, orange, blue, red, two-tone. Before the next car's colors are visible coming up Market, the team calls ONE main body color out loud on video. Right = complete. Wrong = new call for the next car. Cars come every 10–15 minutes.
candidates.where: Jane Warner Plaza / F-line boarding island, Castro St at 17th & Market, under the giant pride flag.
candidates.failable: no (one call per car; keep calling)
candidates.photo: The team pointing at the arriving car, its livery filling the frame.
candidates.why_here: The Castro terminus is where SF's rolling museum of world streetcars turns around — a paint-color lottery every quarter hour.

Chinatown.intro: The oldest Chinatown in North America: ~24 dense blocks bounded by Bush, Broadway, Kearny, and Powell, entered through the Dragon Gate and threaded with hidden alleys (Ross, Spofford, Waverly "Street of Painted Balconies"). Anchors here are the Grant Avenue dragon streetlamps (installed 1925), the hand-folded cookies of the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, the Stockton Street produce markets, and the mythology-themed Willie "Woo Woo" Wong Playground. Note: Portsmouth Square closed in June 2026 for a ~2-year, $73M renovation — nothing below depends on it.
Chinatown.why_chosen: Three games up the Chinatown spine: spell SAN FRAN from torn-up fortunes in Ross Alley, hunt eight of the twelve zodiac animals across Grant Ave's shop windows and signs, and read fruit by touch on Stockton. Wordplay, a scavenger hunt, and a blind-touch test — one retryable, nothing one-shot, no strangers, everything weekend-reliable, ~$8–14 total, ≈ 40–50 minutes on foot.

candidates.title: The Ransom-Note Fortune
candidates.do: Buy one bag at the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory. Crack a cookie, tear the fortune into scraps carrying one letter each, and start assembling the phrase **SAN FRAN** ransom-note style (S, A, A, N, N, F, R — the F is the hard part; plenty of fortunes don't have one). Only letters torn from fortune slips count, each scrap used once. Keep cracking cookies from your bag until you can lay out the full phrase. If an entire bag can't produce it, buy another and reflect on your luck.
candidates.where: Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, 56 Ross Alley (between Washington & Jackson); open daily, until ~7pm weekends
candidates.cost: ~$5–8 for the bag (a small photo fee may apply inside)
candidates.failable: no (persistence — every cracked cookie is progress, and a snack)
candidates.photo: SAN FRAN assembled from torn destiny on a step in Ross Alley, the pile of sacrificed cookies alongside.
candidates.why_here: Hand-folded fortunes since 1962 in a gambling-den-era alley — and yes, locals wince at "San Fran," but spelling it out of your own fortunes absolves you.

candidates.title: Year of the Hunt
candidates.do: Find and photograph EIGHT of the twelve Chinese zodiac animals anywhere in the neighborhood — statues, murals, signs, shop goods, restaurant windows all count. One rule: no two animals may come from the same thing (a zodiac wheel or placemat showing many animals counts for only one of your eight). Complete at eight.
candidates.where: Anywhere in the neighborhood; Grant Ave shops and restaurant windows are rich hunting grounds
candidates.photo: Each find pointed at; the keeper is a teammate beside their own birth-year animal.
candidates.why_here: The zodiac is woven through every block of the oldest Chinatown in North America — and suddenly everyone remembers exactly what year they were born.

candidates.title: The Hand Knows
candidates.do: At any Stockton Street produce market, the buyer picks THREE different fruits — any fruits at all, from the everyday to the unpronounceable — hidden from one blindfolded teammate. The guesser holds each fruit for up to 30 seconds — touch only, no smelling, no tasting, no hints — and names it. All three correct = complete. Any miss = retry with three new fruits and a new guesser. Then eat your props.
candidates.where: Stockton St between Sacramento St and Broadway (market blocks)
candidates.photo: The blindfolded guesser gingerly palming a dragonfruit, market bins spilling behind — then the whole team mid-bite.
candidates.why_here: Stockton's sidewalk bins stack fruit most visitors can't name with their eyes open — naming them blind is the market's black-belt exam.

candidates.title: The Painted Balconies of Waverly Place
candidates.do: Walk the two blocks of Waverly Place, the "Street of Painted Balconies," and photograph wrought-iron or wooden balconies painted in at least 4 different colors (e.g., red, green, yellow, teal). Complete when you have 4 distinct balcony colors, each clearly on a different balcony.
candidates.where: Waverly Place, between Sacramento St and Washington St (one block west of Grant)
candidates.photo: A teammate pointing up at the 4th color's balcony (keep the other three shots in the upload).
candidates.why_here: Waverly's stacked, rainbow-painted temple and association balconies are the neighborhood's most photographed hidden street — the colors ARE the landmark.

candidates.title: The Lamplighter's Census
candidates.do: Grant Avenue's cast-iron dragon streetlamps have coiled on their posts since 1925. Stand at the Dragon Gate (Bush & Grant). BEFORE anyone takes a step up Grant, the team locks in ONE written estimate: how many dragon lampposts stand on Grant between the gate and Broadway? No research, no peeking up the street beyond what you can see from the gate. Then walk all eight blocks and count every lamp as a team. Estimate within ±15% of your count = win. You get exactly one estimate, ever.
candidates.where: Grant Ave from the Dragon Gate (at Bush) to Broadway
candidates.photo: The written estimate held up at the Dragon Gate before the walk, then the final tally beside the last lamp at Broadway.
candidates.why_here: Chinatown's mascot hides in plain sight on every block — betting on exactly how many is the neighborhood's own counting-house game.

candidates.title: Ride the Water Dragon
candidates.do: At Willie "Woo Woo" Wong Playground, find the giant carved water dragon that wraps around the two-level play tower. Every teammate goes down the tower slide once, and the team locates the phoenix sculpture bridging the tot zone. Complete when everyone has slid and the phoenix is found.
candidates.where: 830 Sacramento St, between Waverly Place and Pagoda Place
candidates.photo: A teammate mid-slide with the dragon's carved body in frame.
candidates.why_here: A $14.5M playground themed on Chinese mythology, named for Chinatown's own 5'5" USF basketball legend — the neighborhood's most joyful corner.

Excelsior.intro: The Excelsior is Mission Street's sunny southern stretch and maybe SF's most international neighborhood — fittingly, its grid is literally a map of the world: streets named for capitals (London, Paris, Naples, Moscow...) crossing avenues named for countries (Brazil, Persia, Russia, France, Italy). "Excelsior" is Latin for "ever upward," and the neighborhood delivers: two community-built mosaic stairways, a 1935 landmark bakery, and two sidewalk plaques for its most famous son, Jerry Garcia. Everything below sits on or just off the Mission corridor between Silver and Geneva — the undisputed core of the official analysis neighborhood (McLaren Park next door is its own territory; stay out of the park itself).
Excelsior.why_chosen: Find a capital meeting its own country on the Excelsior's street grid with no maps, play charades with the Last Supper mural on the Royal Baking building, and climb the rainbow mosaic stairs at the Athens Avalon Greenspace. A no-map hunt, a guessing game, a climb; one retryable, zero strangers, $0, ≈ 35–50 minutes.

candidates.title: Paris, France (No Passport Required)
candidates.do: The Excelsior's streets are named for world capitals and its avenues for countries. Phones away — no maps. Find a corner where a capital meets its OWN country (Paris St & France Ave, Naples St & Italy Ave, or Moscow St & Russia Ave) and photograph the team under the sign pair. Done with that one photo.
candidates.where: The Excelsior's capitals-and-countries grid, east of Mission St.
candidates.photo: The team under a capital-and-its-country sign pair, like PARIS / FRANCE.
candidates.why_here: The only place in SF where you can walk from London to Persia in one block.

candidates.title: Last Supper Charades
candidates.do: Go to the 1935 Art Deco Royal Baking Company building, whose facade is painted with a multi-panel "Last Supper" mural — thirteen figures, thirteen poses. Number the figures 1–13 from the left. One teammate, the performer, generates a random number on a phone (re-roll repeats) and freezes in that figure's exact pose (hands, head, lean). The team gets ONE guess at which painted figure it is — point at them. Right = the next teammate performs. Wrong = a five-minute penalty (everyone waits, no performing, no guessing), then the next teammate performs a new figure. Complete when the team has three right. Pan dulce from the legacy bakery inside is optional, and recommended.
candidates.where: Royal Bakery, 4773 Mission St (between Russia and France Aves). The mural is outdoors; the bakery's hours have changed (recently weekdays only), so don't count on going in.
candidates.failable: retryable (each wrong guess costs a five-minute wait)
candidates.photo: The performer frozen mid-pose beneath the matching painted figure, the team pointing.
candidates.why_here: A San Francisco Legacy Business baking in double-brick Dutch ovens since 1935, under the Excelsior's most famous painted facade — thirteen poses waiting to be copied.

candidates.title: Climb the Rainbow Stairs
candidates.do: At the Athens Avalon Greenspace, the stairway is mosaicked in a color gradient — cool and dark at the bottom, warm and bright at the top. Climb it from the bottom step to the top. Done when the whole team is at the top.
candidates.where: Athens Avalon Greenspace, 800 Avalon Ave at Athens St (four blocks up the hill from Mission via Avalon).
candidates.photo: The team at the top of the stairs, the mosaic gradient running down below you.
candidates.why_here: Neighbors turned a trash-strewn hillside into SF's most joyful gradient stairs — "ever upward," one toss at a time.

candidates.title: Mosaic Match in Kenny Alley
candidates.do: Find Kenny Alley — a hidden pedestrian stair alley named after a cat who lived there — whose 47 steps and walls are tiled as a waterfall pouring down the hillside. One teammate, the hider, generates a random number from 1 to 47 on a phone, walks alone to that step, and takes a close-up photo of the hand-sized patch of mosaic directly under their right foot (no landmarks in the frame — just tiles). Then the rest of the team gets the phone and has to find the exact spot. The team gets ONE claim per photo — a finger on the tiles, and the hider says yes or no. Wrong = the hider rolls a new step and shoots a new patch. Every teammate takes a turn as the hider. Complete when every patch has been found.
candidates.where: Kenny Alley, off the east side of Mission St between France Ave and Italy Ave (next to the car lot; ~4800 block of Mission).
candidates.failable: no (a wrong claim costs a new roll and a new photo)
candidates.photo: A finger on the found tiles held next to the phone showing the hider's photo, the waterfall pouring down the steps behind.
candidates.why_here: A secret stairway named for a neighborhood cat, tiled into a waterfall by local students — thousands of tiles, and only one patch matches.

candidates.title: Recite for Jerry
candidates.do: The Excelsior raised Jerry Garcia of the Grateful Dead, and the neighborhood gave him two sidewalk plaques a long block of Mission apart. Find either bronze plaque (Mission & Harrington, or Mission & Amazon). One teammate reads the plaque aloud ONCE. Then a different teammate, eyes closed, recites its text back word for word. Any slip = read it again, new reciter. Complete on a clean recital.
candidates.where: Mission St at Harrington St (~4600 block) or Mission St at Amazon Ave (~4900 block).
candidates.photo: The reciter eyes-closed mid-line, a shoe beside the plaque.
candidates.why_here: Garcia grew up at 87 Harrington St and 121 Amazon Ave; the plaques are short enough to memorize and long enough to trip on.

candidates.title: Call the Bus at "Waiting for the 52"
candidates.do: Stand at the mural "Waiting for the 52 Excelsior" (2001, Marta Ayala) — a portrait of Excelsior folks waiting for the bus — and do what it shows: wait, but with a call. Before each bus's number is readable, the team calls its line out loud on video: 52, 14, 14R, or "other." Right = complete. Wrong = new call for the next bus.
candidates.where: The mural near Mission St & Excelsior Ave, at the nearest stop.
candidates.photo: The team in front of the mural with the verdict bus and its sign readable.
candidates.why_here: A mural about waiting for a bus — the only honest way to complete it is to call the bus.

candidates.title: European Vacation, Crocker-Amazon Style
candidates.do: Collect street-blade signs for 4 different European cities WITHOUT leaving this neighborhood: photograph a teammate under 4 different street signs named for European cities, all at corners on or south of Geneva Ave and east of Mission St. Valid finds include Geneva, Naples, Munich, Prague, Cordova, Seville, and Florentine. (Geneva × Naples, Geneva × Munich, and Geneva × Prague are consecutive corners — a tidy loop via Cordova St bags all four.)
candidates.where: Crocker-Amazon residential blocks around Geneva Ave between Naples and Prague Sts; the pocket park Naples Green (Naples/Rolph/Cordova) makes a bonus backdrop.
candidates.photo: A 4-shot collage — one goofy "tourist arriving in this city" pose per sign.
candidates.why_here: Crocker-Amazon's street grid is a pocket atlas of Europe; nowhere else in SF can you "visit" Geneva, Naples, Munich, and Prague in a 15-minute walk.

Financial District/South Beach.intro: Downtown's big east wedge: the Ferry Building and the Embarcadero promenade, the skyscraper canyon, Salesforce Park floating 70 feet above the bus deck, South Park's old oval — and yes, **Union Square is inside this analysis neighborhood** (its census tract 117 is officially assigned here, verified against DataSF's tract-to-neighborhood table). Equally verified OUT: the Transamerica Pyramid and Jackson Square's 1850s block sit in tract 611.01, assigned to *Chinatown*, and Oracle Park's tract 607.01 belongs to *Mission Bay* — so I anchored nothing on them. Offices are ghosts on weekends, so every candidate leans on the waterfront, parks, monuments, and the Ferry Building, which is at its liveliest on a Saturday.
Financial District/South Beach.why_chosen: The Blindfold Market, Behind the Waterfall, and Heart Detective: a hidden-info taste deduction at the Ferry Building, a one-shot language test behind the MLK waterfall in Yerba Buena Gardens, and an observation hunt in Union Square. Two retryable with real stakes and one one-shot; none need strangers, everything runs weekend daytime, about 40–55 minutes. Mind the Doors and the Thirteen-Garden Memory Loop are the swap-ins.

candidates.title: The Blindfold Market
candidates.do: Pick a taster. The taster waits OUTSIDE the Ferry Building, eyes closed, while a teammate goes in and buys one bite-sized edible thing ($10 max) from any shop or Saturday farmers-market stall — no hints, wrapper hidden. Blindfold the taster (hands over eyes works) and feed them one bite; they don't have to say what it is. Then the blindfold comes off and the taster goes into the market alone, looks around as long as they like, comes back out, and names the shop or stall they think it came from. Right = complete. Wrong = they go back in for another look and another guess. No hints from teammates, and you may not practice.
candidates.where: Ferry Building Marketplace, foot of Market St at The Embarcadero.
candidates.failable: retryable (each wrong guess means another trip into the market)
candidates.photo: The blindfolded tasting under the clock tower, then the team at the right stall.
candidates.why_here: The 1898 ferry landmark's nave holds forty-odd food vendors and is the one downtown spot MORE alive on weekends — enough options to make taste-and-seek a real deduction.

candidates.title: Behind the Waterfall
candidates.do: Find the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial and walk the passage BEHIND its 50-foot curtain of falling water. The glass panels there carry Dr. King's words in many languages, honoring SF's sister cities — several aren't in the Latin alphabet. Phones away: no translation apps, no searching, no asking. As a team, identify FIVE of the panels' languages by name, and commit to all five in one photographed list before checking anything. Then verify (panels are captioned, or check afterward). All five right = complete. Any wrong = failed. One shot.
candidates.where: Yerba Buena Gardens, 750 Howard St side of the Great Lawn, between 3rd and 4th. Gardens open 6am–10pm daily, free.
candidates.photo: The team's written list of five languages held up in front of the panels, sheet of water blurring behind.
candidates.why_here: SF's biggest MLK memorial hides its message where you'd never look — behind a waterfall on a rooftop garden built over a convention center.

candidates.title: Heart Detective
candidates.do: Union Square keeps giant painted heart sculptures from the "Hearts in San Francisco" series stationed around the plaza, repainted by new artists each year. One teammate (the artist) slips away and photographs an extreme close-up — a palm-sized detail — of any one heart, any side. The rest of the team sees only that photo, then must find the spot: identify which heart, walk to it, and put a finger on the exact painted detail. First touch is the answer — right spot wins, wrong heart or wrong spot fails the attempt. Retry with a new close-up and a new artist. Artists may not answer questions.
candidates.where: Union Square plaza, Post/Stockton/Geary/Powell.
candidates.photo: Side-by-side keeper: the mystery close-up next to the finger-on-the-spot reveal, Dewey Monument in the background.
candidates.why_here: "I Left My Heart in San Francisco" made these hearts the square's mascot — and Union Square really is inside this neighborhood's official boundary, which nobody on the other team will believe.

candidates.title: The Thirteen-Garden Memory Loop
candidates.do: Ride up to Salesforce Park, the 5.4-acre botanical garden floating on the transit center roof (free; gondola at Mission near Fremont when running, otherwise any open stair/elevator around the block). Walk the half-mile loop ONCE as a team — no photos, no notes: the gardens are labeled with signs. Then stop and, from memory, write down the names of at least EIGHT of the thirteen gardens. Verify by re-walking with the camera out. Eight matches = complete. Short? Walk it again and re-test — memory is allowed to improve.
candidates.where: Salesforce Park, atop the block bounded by Mission/Howard and Beale/Second.
candidates.failable: no (re-walk and re-test until you pass)
candidates.photo: The handwritten list beside a garden sign, Salesforce Tower shooting straight up behind the team on the central lawn.
candidates.why_here: Thirteen labeled mini-ecosystems on a ROOF is the memory-game venue SF didn't know it built — and Ned Kahn's Bus Jet Fountain fires its 247 geysers whenever a bus rolls beneath you.

candidates.title: Parrot Patrol
candidates.do: Before entering Sue Bierman Park, the team locks in a written over/under call: will you photograph a wild red-masked parakeet within TEN minutes — yes or no? Then start the clock and hunt (listen for the squawking; that's your radar). Your call must be RIGHT to complete: photograph a parrot inside ten minutes after calling "yes", or survive the full ten minutes parrot-free after calling "no" (parrot photographed anyway = wrong call). Wrong call = wait 10 minutes, then re-call and retry.
candidates.where: Sue Bierman Park, Clay & Drumm Sts, just inland from the Ferry Building.
candidates.photo: A green parrot in frame with a teammate pointing at it — or ten smug minutes of parrotless sky if you called "no".
candidates.why_here: The legendary wild parrots of downtown really do commute to this exact park — betting on birds is older than the Financial District itself.

candidates.title: The Human Machine
candidates.do: Find the Mechanics Monument — five giant bronze workers straining to drive a punch press. ONE teammate (the foreman) studies the statue; everyone else faces away and may never look at it. Using words only — no touching, no demonstrating — the foreman must direct at least three teammates into three DIFFERENT figures' poses. When the foreman calls "done," take the photo showing posers and statue together. The other team judges it at game's end: each poser must be clearly matchable to a distinct bronze figure. One rebuild allowed if the foreman isn't confident.
candidates.where: Mechanics Monument Plaza, Market/Bush/Battery.
candidates.photo: The team mid-strain beside the bronzes, directed entirely blind — an instant album cover with a story.
candidates.why_here: Douglas Tilden's 1901 muscle-machine survived the 1906 quake and stands where the old waterfront ran before downtown was built on landfill.

candidates.title: Mind the Doors
candidates.do: The F-line's historic streetcars — each one a rescued antique from a different city and decade — stop along The Embarcadero. Go to any F-line platform. You may watch streetcars arrive for as long as you like. Then declare your attempt: the whole team lines up shoulder-to-shoulder where you believe the FRONT DOOR of the next streetcar will be when it stops, and must be in position before the streetcar is visible. No moving once it appears. If any teammate lines up with any part of the open front door, you win. Miss = wait for the next streetcar to try again (they run every ~10 minutes on weekends).
candidates.where: Any F Market & Wharves platform on The Embarcadero (Ferry Building stop is the classic).
candidates.photo: The team flattened in a line on the platform, antique streetcar door gaping open exactly at (or hilariously far from) them.
candidates.why_here: Every F car stops slightly differently because every F car IS different — a 1930s Milan tram doesn't brake like a 1950s Philadelphia PCC. Studying the fleet is the skill.

Glen Park.intro: Glen Park is a village hiding inside a big city: a two-block commercial pocket at Chenery & Diamond (indie bookstore, taqueria, market) sitting directly on top of a BART station, with a genuinely wild canyon — Glen Canyon Park, free-flowing Islais Creek, red chert outcrops, the site of America's first dynamite factory — starting three blocks away. On its Noe Valley edge, the Fairmount hillside stacks up quirky Laidley Street houses, one of SF's last wooden street-staircases (Harry Street), and the bare rock summit of Billy Goat Hill. Challenges anchor on those three worlds: canyon, village, hilltop.
Glen Park.why_chosen: One in each of Glen Park's three worlds: find Islais Creek actually running in the wild canyon and take a selfie with it, climb the hidden wooden Harry Street stairs, and mime a random BART stop (a silent minute for every wrong guess) at the village's Brutalist station. A creek hunt, a climb, a charade; one retryable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 35–45 min. (The 60-second dynamite fuse and the Bird & Beckett dig stay as alternates.)

candidates.title: Find the Running Creek
candidates.do: Islais Creek, one of the last free-flowing creeks in San Francisco, still runs through Glen Canyon Park — barely. It hides in the willows and undergrowth, and in dry spells it's down to a trickle, so you'll have to hunt for it. Walk the Gum Tree Girls Trail across the boardwalks into the canyon, find a spot where you can see the water actually moving, and take a team selfie with it. Stay on the trails and boardwalks. Done when the selfie shows running water.
candidates.where: Glen Canyon Park — follow the paved path from the rec center to its end, then right onto the Gum Tree Girls Trail and across the boardwalks toward the Islais Creek Trail.
candidates.photo: The team selfie with the creek visibly running beside you, willows all around.
candidates.why_here: A wild creek canyon in the middle of SF that exists only because three neighborhood women beat a freeway — the Gum Tree Girls — and the creek still runs, if you can find it.

candidates.title: Climb Harry Street
candidates.do: Harry Street is one of the last wooden street-staircases in San Francisco — roughly 240 steps climbing a hidden green tunnel between houses, marked only by tiny "Harry" street signs at each end. Climb it from Laidley St to the top at Beacon St. Done when the whole team reaches the top.
candidates.where: Harry Street steps, from Laidley St near Harper St up to Beacon St.
candidates.photo: The team at the top of the wooden stairs, the green tunnel dropping away below you.
candidates.why_here: A secret wooden staircase in a green tunnel that most San Franciscans have never climbed.

candidates.title: Mime a BART Stop
candidates.do: Glen Park's 1973 BART station — raw board-formed concrete and rusting Corten steel — is routinely named one of the finest Brutalist transit buildings in America. At the system map inside (outside the fare gates, no fare needed), the whole team studies the station names as long as you like. Then pick a mime: on a phone they secretly generate a random number from 1 to 50 and count that far down BART's alphabetical station list (bart.gov/stations) to get their station. They act it out: no words, no sounds, no letters, no pointing at the map. The team guesses one station at a time. Right = complete. Wrong = a one-minute penalty: everyone stands in silence, no acting and no guessing, until the minute is up; then the mime carries on with the same station. No collusion: no signals or codes agreed in advance, and no counting along the list together.
candidates.where: Glen Park BART station, Diamond St & Bosworth St
candidates.failable: retryable (each wrong guess costs a silent minute)
candidates.photo: The mime mid-act in front of the system map, the team mid-guess, concrete overhead.
candidates.why_here: A Clipper-tap territory race deserves one challenge in the architect-adored station the whole neighborhood is built around — even if the rules say you can't ride it.

candidates.title: Kaboom at the Dynamite Diamond
candidates.do: In 1868 Alfred Nobel licensed his brand-new invention to the Giant Powder Company, which built America's FIRST dynamite factory in Glen Canyon — and in 1869 it blew itself to smithereens. The ballfield sits on the factory site, and a bronze plaque (California Historical Landmark No. 1002, on a low concrete slab near the park's southern entrance by the rec center and ballfield) marks it. Find the plaque, then light the fuse: one teammate starts a stopwatch and hides the screen. Everyone else counts in their heads — no watches, no counting out loud — and the team's detonator yells "KABOOM!" when the team agrees exactly 60 seconds have passed. Within 3 seconds of 60 = complete. Off by more = new detonator, new fuse.
candidates.where: Glen Canyon Park southern entrance, by the rec center/ballfield (enter at Elk St near Chenery, or Bosworth & O'Shaughnessy)
candidates.failable: no (relight the fuse until you nail it)
candidates.photo: The stopwatch frozen somewhere between 0:57 and 1:03, held beside the dynamite plaque, team mid-"KABOOM."
candidates.why_here: The first dynamite factory in the United States exploded on this exact spot — a 60-second fuse is the least you can do.

candidates.title: Bird & Beckett, Meet Bird & Beckett
candidates.do: The village's beloved bookstore/record shop is named for jazz legend Charlie "Bird" Parker and playwright Samuel Beckett. Honor both namesakes: dig through the vinyl bins for a Charlie Parker record (any record with a bird pictured on the sleeve also counts), and find a book by Samuel Beckett on the shelves. Complete when one teammate holds the record and another holds the book in the same photo inside the shop or under its sign. Buying a cheap used paperback afterward: optional, classy.
candidates.where: Bird & Beckett Books & Records, 653 Chenery St (open Sat & Sun 12–6 pm; closed Mondays)
candidates.photo: teammates holding the Bird record and the Beckett book side by side at the shop
candidates.why_here: A bookstore that doubles as a jazz club is Glen Park's living-room — and its name is a two-part riddle you solve by crate-digging.

candidates.title: The Baby Burrito Handoff
candidates.do: La Corneta has anchored the village for 30+ years, and its cult item is the "baby burrito" — everything a super burrito has, shrunk. Buy exactly one baby burrito. Before anyone bites, photograph it lying across one teammate's open palm for scale. Then the team must finish it with every teammate taking at least one bite.
candidates.where: La Corneta Taqueria, 2834 Diamond St (Sat 10 am–10 pm, Sun 11 am–9 pm)
candidates.photo: the palm-sized baby burrito resting on an outstretched hand, hungry team crowded behind it
candidates.why_here: Splitting one tiny burrito six ways at Glen Park's 30-year taqueria institution is peak village lunch.

Golden Gate Park.intro: This neighborhood IS the park: a 3-mile-long, human-made wonderland (plus the Panhandle strip trailing east) stuffed with things that shouldn't exist in a city — a live bison herd, a 1902 Dutch windmill, a hidden garden of Shakespeare's flowers, and a 1912 menagerie carousel. The museums inside charge admission, so every candidate below anchors on the park's free (or nearly free) oddities, spread from the Koret playground in the east to the windmill by the ocean.
Golden Gate Park.why_chosen: Golden Gate Park is three miles long, so its challenges are just to get there: the Dutch Windmill at the ocean end, the hidden Shakespeare Garden by the Music Concourse (where you recite a speech), and the Bison Paddock in between. Two are just getting there, one is a recital; nothing failable, zero strangers, all $0; the travel is the challenge (the 5 Fulton runs along the north side). The carousel bet, Strawberry Hill and the Portals mind meld remain as swaps.

candidates.title: The Dutch Windmill
candidates.do: Go to the 75-foot Dutch Windmill at the park's ocean corner. Done when the whole team is standing in front of it.
candidates.where: Dutch Windmill / Queen Wilhelmina Garden, northwest corner of the park at John F. Kennedy Dr & the Great Highway
candidates.photo: The team in front of the windmill, the sails turning (or not) above you, tulips in season.
candidates.why_here: San Francisco keeps two full-size Dutch windmills by the ocean and almost nobody knows; the ocean wind that once turned them will turn yours.

candidates.title: Oberon in the Shakespeare Garden
candidates.do: Slip through the wrought-iron gate of the Shakespeare Garden, where every plant is one mentioned in Shakespeare's works. Inside, one teammate learns Oberon's flower speech from *A Midsummer Night's Dream*: "I know a bank where the wild thyme blows, / Where oxlips and the nodding violet grows, / Quite over-canopied with luscious woodbine, / With sweet musk-roses and with eglantine." Study it as long as you like, then phones away and recite all four lines word for word while the team checks. A slip? Study again and go again, or swap reciters. Done on a perfect recital.
candidates.where: Shakespeare Garden, off Martin Luther King Jr. Dr next to the California Academy of Sciences (Music Concourse area, mid-park near 9th Ave)
candidates.photo: The reciter mid-speech among the flower beds, the bronze plaques on the brick wall behind.
candidates.why_here: A hidden literary garden behind an iron gate, steps from the park's busiest plaza — most visitors walk right past it.

candidates.title: The Bison Paddock
candidates.do: Yes, there are real bison in San Francisco. Go to the Bison Paddock and find the herd — they wander and hide behind the hillocks, so you may have to walk the fence. Done when your photo shows the team with at least one bison in it.
candidates.where: Bison Paddock, along John F. Kennedy Dr just west of Spreckels Lake (west end of the park, near 39th Ave; the dirt path along the north side gets you closest)
candidates.failable: no (walk the fence until one shows)
candidates.photo: The team at the paddock fence, bison grazing behind you.
candidates.why_here: A herd of bison grazing in a city park since 1891 — the single best "wait, that exists?" in San Francisco, and they refuse to stand still for a census.

candidates.title: Menagerie Roulette
candidates.do: The Golden Gate Park Carousel (built 1912) is a *menagerie* carousel — far more than horses. Before anyone peeks at it, the team writes down three non-horse animals they bet are on it. Then buy tickets, check your guesses, and ride: challenge complete if at least TWO of your three written animals exist on the carousel AND every teammate rides (any animal). Open weekends from 10 a.m. year-round; about $2.50 a ride.
candidates.where: Koret Children's Quarter, 320 Bowling Green Dr (southeast corner of the park, near Kezar Dr)
candidates.failable: one-shot (the written guess is locked before you see the carousel; the ride happens either way)
candidates.photo: The handwritten guess list held up next to one of the matched animals, plus the team mid-ride.
candidates.why_here: A century-old menagerie carousel with frogs, roosters, and goats is the park's east-end crown jewel — and betting on which beasts it holds turns a $1 ride into a coin-flip moment.

candidates.title: Mind Meld at the Portals of the Past
candidates.do: Find the Portals of the Past: a lone marble doorway standing at the edge of Lloyd Lake — the entrance of a Nob Hill mansion that survived the 1906 earthquake and fire, moved here as a memorial. Stand in front of it in silence. No talking. Every teammate secretly writes down ONE thing they can see from where they stand that the doorway most reminds them of, or that looks most out of place beside it — one word, a real visible thing. Reveal together. Any two matching words = complete. No match = walk around to the far side of Lloyd Lake and write again from there. Three rounds, then it's failed.
candidates.where: Lloyd Lake, off John F. Kennedy Dr near Transverse Dr (mid-west park)
candidates.failable: retryable (three rounds, a lap of the lake between each)
candidates.photo: The matching words held up in the doorway, lake behind.
candidates.why_here: A doorway that survived the city's destruction, standing alone by a lake — the park's most haunting oddity, and a good test of whether your team thinks alike.

candidates.title: Summit the Island in the Lake
candidates.do: From the Stow Lake shore, cross either bridge onto Strawberry Hill — an island with a mountain on it. Climb the trail past Huntington Falls (a 110-foot artificial waterfall) to the summit, the highest point in the park. Required checkpoints, in order: (1) the red-and-green Chinese Pavilion near the base (a gift from Taipei), (2) the waterfall, (3) the summit clearing with the stone ruins of the old Sweeny Observatory. Photo at each.
candidates.where: Stow Lake / Strawberry Hill, mid-park off Stow Lake Dr (enter near 19th Ave or from the Music Concourse side)
candidates.photo: Summit shot at the ruins, plus the waterfall checkpoint with the team on the stone steps beside the falls.
candidates.why_here: A fake mountain, on an island, in a fake lake, with a fake waterfall and real earthquake ruins on top — peak Golden Gate Park absurdity, and an easy climb.

Haight Ashbury.intro: The official analysis neighborhood is bigger than the famous corner: it runs from Stanyan/Golden Gate Park east past Divisadero, and includes the Panhandle, Buena Vista Park (SF's oldest park, 1867), and Cole Valley. Anchors: the Summer of Love strip of Haight Street (giant legs, tie-dye everywhere, Amoeba Music in an old bowling alley), the rock-legend houses on the side streets, and Buena Vista Park's genuinely strange hidden history. (Tank Hill and Kezar Stadium are just OUTSIDE this neighborhood — don't use them.)
Haight Ashbury.why_chosen: A five-word, one-shot record hunt through all of Amoeba, the tombstone gutter hunt in Buena Vista Park, and a real rainbow made from sunlight in front of the 1967 Evolutionary Rainbow mural. A describe-and-find game, a hidden-history hunt, a make-it; Amoeba is the one one-shot, zero strangers, $0–5, only Amoeba depends on a venue (open 11–7 daily), ≈ 35–50 minutes. (The Grateful Dead house vote is now an alternate.)

candidates.title: Five-Word Cover at Amoeba
candidates.do: At Amoeba Music (1855 Haight St, a converted bowling alley), pick a clue-giver and a guesser; the rest of the team waits outside. The clue-giver goes in ALONE, secretly picks one record anywhere in the store, memorizes its cover, puts it back exactly where it was, and comes back out. Outside, they describe the cover to the guesser in EXACTLY five words — no artist names, no titles, no words printed on the sleeve, and nothing about where it is. Then the guesser goes in ALONE, finds the record they think it is, photographs it where it sits (don't carry it out), and comes back out. One photo, one shot: the right record = complete, anything else = failed, no retry. Reshelve everything nicely; no purchase required.
candidates.where: Amoeba Music, 1855 Haight St at Stanyan. Open daily 11am–7pm.
candidates.cost: $0 (optional: grab something from the bargain bin)
candidates.photo: The guesser's one photo of the record in its bin, next to the clue-giver's five words typed on a phone.
candidates.why_here: One of the world's great record stores, with enough covers per bin to make five words genuinely hard.

candidates.title: Tombstone Gutter Hunt
candidates.do: In Buena Vista Park, the paved path gutters are built from broken marble headstones taken from SF's demolished Gold Rush-era cemeteries in the 1930s — most were laid face-down, but some engraving still shows. Walk the paths (the stretch above the tennis courts on the Buena Vista Ave West side is the jackpot zone) and find a fragment with a complete carved WORD you can read — a whole word, every letter legible (a name, a date in words, "BELOVED"…), not just stray letters or numbers. Complete with a close-up photo of the word with a teammate's finger pointing at it.
candidates.where: Buena Vista Park; enter at Haight St & Buena Vista Ave East, or from Buena Vista Ave West near Central Ave for the tennis-court paths.
candidates.failable: no (the fragments aren't going anywhere; keep looking)
candidates.photo: A finger pointing at a whole carved word from a 100-plus-year-old tombstone, hiding in plain sight in a park gutter.
candidates.why_here: SF's oldest park recycled its dead — an Atlas Obscura-grade secret most locals walking these paths have never noticed.

candidates.title: Make Your Own Evolutionary Rainbow
candidates.do: Find *The Evolutionary Rainbow*, Yana Zegri's 1967 mural at Haight & Cole, where a rainbow evolves into animals, cities and people. Then make a REAL rainbow, out of sunlight, right there on the sidewalk in front of it. Anything you get during the game can help: spray a fine mist with the sun at your back, or stand a clear bottle or glass of water in direct sun next to something white. Painted or printed rainbows don't count, and neither do screens. No time limit. Done when the photo shows your rainbow with its colors from red to violet, the mural in the shot if you can manage it.
candidates.where: The Evolutionary Rainbow mural, 1705 Haight St at Cole St.
candidates.failable: no (keep adjusting until the light cooperates)
candidates.photo: Your homemade rainbow glowing in the mist or on white paper, the 1967 painted one behind it.
candidates.why_here: The Summer of Love's own rainbow has been on this wall since 1967 — the right place to make a new one out of light.

candidates.title: Summer of Love Record Dig
candidates.do: Inside Amoeba Music (1855 Haight St, a converted bowling alley), dig through the bins and find one album by EACH of three bands who actually lived in this neighborhood in 1967: (a) Grateful Dead, (b) Janis Joplin / Big Brother and the Holding Company, (c) Jefferson Airplane. Vinyl or CD, new or used. Complete when the team photographs all three albums held up at once inside the store (no purchase required — reshelve them nicely).
candidates.where: Amoeba Music, 1855 Haight St at Stanyan. Open daily 11am–7pm.
candidates.cost: $0 (optional: grab something from the bargain bin)
candidates.failable: no (Amoeba's stock of these three is effectively bottomless)
candidates.photo: Three psychedelic album covers fanned out in the aisles of one of the world's great record stores.
candidates.why_here: All three bands lived within a few blocks of this store during the Summer of Love — this is a pilgrimage dig, not a random one.

candidates.title: Tie-Dye Window Safari
candidates.do: Walking Haight St between Stanyan and Central, photograph FIVE different storefronts that display tie-dye visible from the sidewalk (clothing, tapestries, flags, painted signs — anything rainbow-swirled counts; five different businesses required). Complete when you have five photos, each showing the tie-dye item with enough storefront to tell the shops apart.
candidates.where: Haight St corridor, Stanyan to Central (Love on Haight at 1400 Haight is a guaranteed freebie).
candidates.failable: no (works even when shops are closed — windows never sleep)
candidates.photo: A five-shot rainbow of tie-dye storefronts.
candidates.why_here: No other street in America still sells this much tie-dye per block; it's the neighborhood's uniform.

candidates.title: Creatures of the Evolutionary Rainbow
candidates.do: Find the Evolutionary Rainbow mural at the corner of Haight & Cole — first painted by Yana Zegri in 1967 and defended by the neighborhood ever since (when an owner painted over it in 1982, protests brought it back). The rainbow contains the story of evolution. Complete with a photo (or photos) of teammates pointing at THREE different creatures painted in the mural (e.g., a fish, a dinosaur, a bird — any three distinct animals).
candidates.where: Haight St & Cole St, on the building at the corner.
candidates.photo: The team spread across a 1967 rainbow, each pointing at a different beast.
candidates.why_here: It's an original, still-surviving Summer of Love artwork — painted the same year the hippies arrived, and older than every mural around it.

candidates.title: Which House Was the Band's?
candidates.do: Somewhere on the 700 block of Ashbury St (between Waller and Frederick) is the Victorian where the Grateful Dead lived in 1966–68. Phones away, no numbers read aloud, and NO TALKING from the moment you turn onto the block. Walk it once in silence, then every teammate secretly writes down which house they think it is — by color and position ("the purple one, third from Waller on the left"). Reveal: if everyone picked the SAME house, complete, whether or not you were right. Split decision = failed — one vote only. Either way, check the number (it's 710) for bragging rights. Private homes — stay on the sidewalk, keep it quiet.
candidates.where: Ashbury St between Waller and Frederick, one block uphill from the Haight/Ashbury corner.
candidates.photo: The ballots held up in front of the house the team agreed on.
candidates.why_here: An ordinary-looking house on an ordinary block was the Grateful Dead's headquarters — does your team's instinct for "rock star house" agree?

Hayes Valley.intro: Hayes Valley is the neighborhood that killed a freeway and got cool: when the earthquake-damaged Central Freeway came down, Octavia Boulevard and Patricia's Green (with its rotating, Burning-Man-adjacent public art) grew in its place, ringed by the boutique-and-treats strip of Hayes Street. Crucially for this game, the official SF Analysis Neighborhood boundary was verified against DataSF (tracts 016200–016400, 016801/2): **Alamo Square Park and the Painted Ladies are inside Hayes Valley**, not Western Addition — so Postcard Row is ours to conquer. Anchors: the Painted Ladies, the rotating art at Patricia's Green, the alley garage where Blue Bottle began, and a Romanesque church that is now a roller disco.
Hayes Valley.why_chosen: Charades with the seven Painted Ladies (touch the right gate to win), roll something 15 yards outside the church-turned-roller-rink at Fillmore & Fell, and a window-bingo walk down Hayes St. Charades, a roll, a scavenger hunt; nothing failable, zero strangers, $0–2, ≈ 30–40 minutes.

candidates.title: Painted Lady Charades
candidates.do: At Alamo Square, face Postcard Row — the seven Painted Ladies of 710–720 Steiner. One teammate, the performer, secretly picks one of the seven at random (a random number 1–7 on a phone, counting from the left). Without words, letters or pointing, the performer acts out THAT house — its color, its trim, its windows, its shape, whatever they can mime. When a teammate thinks they've got it, they cross Steiner and touch that house's front gate or railing (sidewalk only — these are private homes, stay off the steps). Right house = complete. Wrong house = the performer draws a new number and starts over.
candidates.where: Alamo Square Park, east slope along Steiner St (between Hayes & Fulton). Open daily, dawn to midnight.
candidates.failable: no (new house, new mime, until someone touches the right one)
candidates.photo: The guesser's hand on the right gate, the performer mid-mime on the grass across the street, Postcard Row behind.
candidates.why_here: Postcard Row officially sits in Hayes Valley (verified on the city map), and everyone thinks the seven houses look alike — until they have to mime one.

candidates.title: Holy Rollers
candidates.do: Find the 1890s church at Fillmore & Fell that is now a roller rink — the Church of 8 Wheels. Out front, roll something 15 yards along the sidewalk: anything you find or buy on the way (an orange, a can, a bottle, a coin on its edge). Mark the distance first with 15 big steps. One push, then hands off: it has to roll the whole way on its own. Roll along the sidewalk, never toward the street, and stop anything that heads for the curb. Fell short or it fell over? Walk it back and roll again.
candidates.where: 554 Fillmore St at Fell St (exterior).
candidates.photo: The roller mid-release, the church-turned-rink behind, and the finish line 15 steps away.
candidates.why_here: Only Hayes Valley has a landmark church converted into a roller rink — everyone who comes here should roll something.

candidates.title: Hayes Street Window Bingo
candidates.do: Walking Hayes St between Franklin and Laguna, photograph shop windows (from the sidewalk) showing all five of: shoes, a plant, something gold, a hat, and a dog (real or pictured). One window per category.
candidates.where: Hayes St corridor, Franklin St to Laguna St.
candidates.photo: A five-shot set; the dog is usually the keeper.
candidates.why_here: Hayes Street's boutique windows are the neighborhood's whole personality.

candidates.title: A Quarter Pound, By Feel
candidates.do: At Miette, the pastel patisserie on Octavia whose back wall is jars of bulk candy sold by weight, the team fills ONE bag from the jars trying to land on exactly a quarter pound (4 oz) — no scale, no phone, just hands and arguments. Lock the bag, then let the counter weigh it. Within a quarter ounce (3.75–4.25 oz) = complete. Off? Buy it anyway (that's the evidence, and it's candy), and fill a new bag, wiser. Budget cap $10 across all attempts.
candidates.where: Miette Patisserie & Confiserie, 449 Octavia St at Linden (open daily, weekend daytime included).
candidates.failable: retryable (one weighed bag per attempt, until the $10 cap)
candidates.photo: The scale readout beside the bag, team faces either way.
candidates.why_here: Hayes Valley's sweetest storefront — a candy wall by the ounce, a block from the old freeway's footprint — is the only shop in the neighborhood with a scale that decides the game.

candidates.title: Be the Art
candidates.do: Find the current rotating installation at the center of Patricia's Green (the Arts Commission swaps it roughly yearly). One teammate, the director, studies it; everyone else keeps their backs to it. Using words only — no gestures — the director arranges the team into a human copy of the sculpture. When the director calls "done," take the photo with sculpture and copy side by side. One rebuild allowed.
candidates.where: Patricia's Green, Octavia Blvd between Hayes & Fell.
candidates.photo: The sculpture beside its blind-built human twin.
candidates.why_here: This half-block park replaced a double-deck freeway, and its ever-changing centerpiece is the neighborhood's signature.

candidates.title: The $700 Million Garage
candidates.do: Find the garage on Linden Street (315 Linden, a one-block alley off the back of Patricia's Green) where Blue Bottle Coffee began in 2005 as a wooden kiosk in a friend's garage — look for the little blue bottle. Photograph the team pointing at it.
candidates.where: Linden St between Octavia & Gough, one block south of Hayes.
candidates.photo: Team pointing at an unassuming garage in an alley — the birthplace of a coffee empire.
candidates.why_here: Third-wave coffee's origin story happened in this alley, and it still just looks like a garage.

Inner Richmond.intro: The Inner Richmond is Clement Street: San Francisco's "second Chinatown," a fog-belt main street of dumpling counters, a legendary used bookstore, a toy-store ice cream parlor, and — hiding in plain sight at Funston — a Greek temple that houses the entire internet's memory. Everything below sits on or within a block of Clement between Arguello and Park Presidio, safely inside the official analysis-neighborhood boundaries (Golden Gate Park and Lincoln Park are separate territories — nothing here touches them).
Inner Richmond.why_chosen: Find a koi, a crustacean and a fish longer than your hand at the 6th Ave Aquarium, ride the coin-operated pony with a scoop in hand at Toy Boat by Jane, and dig up a pre-1950 book at Green Apple. A creature hunt, a treat, a book dig; nothing failable, zero strangers, ~$7, ≈ 35–45 minutes, all within two blocks of Clement St.

candidates.title: Creature Checklist at the Fish Emporium
candidates.do: Browse the 6th Ave Aquarium, the cavernous fish store stacked floor to ceiling with tanks. Photograph all three of: (a) a koi, (b) a crab or lobster or shrimp, and (c) a fish longer than your hand (hand in frame next to the tank for scale). Look only — no tapping on glass. Complete when you have all three shots.
candidates.where: 6th Ave Aquarium, 425 Clement St (between 5th & 6th Ave); open weekend daytime from mid-morning
candidates.photo: The hand-for-scale shot next to the biggest fish you found.
candidates.why_here: A free walk-through aquarium disguised as a neighborhood fish shop — a classic "wait, that exists?" Clement Street oddity.

candidates.title: Pony Express
candidates.do: At Toy Boat by Jane — the toy-lined dessert cafe that's been a Clement Street landmark since 1983 — buy one scoop of ice cream, then put a teammate on the coin-operated pony in the middle of the shop and ride it. Complete when the ride has run and the scoop is in hand.
candidates.where: Toy Boat by Jane, 401 Clement St at 5th Ave; Sat opens 12pm, Sun 10am
candidates.photo: Teammate mid-ride on the mechanical pony, cone in hand, vintage toys on the shelves behind.
candidates.why_here: An ice cream parlor that's also a toy museum with an indoor pony ride exists exactly one place in San Francisco, and it's this corner.

candidates.title: The Oldest Book on Clement Street
candidates.do: Inside Green Apple Books, find a book printed before 1950 (check the copyright page). Spread out and search as long as you like, no time limit. Complete when a pre-1950 date is in hand. Reshelve everything.
candidates.where: Green Apple Books, 506 Clement St at 6th Ave; open daily
candidates.photo: The copyright page with the winning year, finger on it.
candidates.why_here: Green Apple has 70,000 books and creaky floors; somewhere in there is something older than everyone on your team put together.

candidates.title: The Chopstick Gauntlet
candidates.do: Join the line at Good Luck Dim Sum, fill out one of the famous pink order sheets, and buy at least 3 DIFFERENT dim sum items for under $10 total — cash only, so have bills ready. Then the gauntlet: on the sidewalk, every teammate must pick up one piece from the box with chopsticks and get it to their mouth — no fingers, no stabbing, no two-handed chopsticks. A drop means that teammate takes another piece and tries again. Complete when every teammate has landed one clean bite. (Chopsticks come in the bag; ask for extras.)
candidates.where: Good Luck Dim Sum, 736 Clement St (between 8th & 9th Ave); open Sat–Sun 8:00am–4:30pm
candidates.time: 15 min (the line is part of the legend)
candidates.failable: no (retry until it lands — order enough dumplings)
candidates.photo: A teammate mid-lift, dumpling wobbling in the chopsticks, pink box open, Clement Street behind.
candidates.why_here: A James Beard–recognized, cash-only Clement Street institution where a few dollars still buys a full dim sum spread — the beating heart of the "second Chinatown," and the fairest chopstick exam in the city.

candidates.title: Spell Your Colors
candidates.do: Inside Green Apple Books (est. 1967, creaky floors included), pull used books whose titles' FIRST letters spell your team's color — R-E-D or B-L-U-E — one book per letter, in order. Stack or fan the spines so the letters read top to bottom. Reshelve everything afterward. Complete when the photo clearly shows the spines spelling your color.
candidates.where: Green Apple Books, 506 Clement St at 6th Ave; open daily, weekend daytime included
candidates.time: 10–15 min (Blue teams earn their extra letter)
candidates.photo: The stacked spines spelling RED or BLUE, taken in the maze of used-book shelves.
candidates.why_here: Green Apple is the Inner Richmond's black hole of 70,000 books — people go in and don't come out; your team has to go in with a mission.

candidates.title: Blind Architect at the Internet Archive
candidates.do: Go to the Internet Archive headquarters — a white Classical Revival temple (a former Christian Science church) with giant Greek columns. One teammate, the architect, faces the building; another, the draftsman, sits with their back to it and a pen. The architect describes the facade in words only — no pointing, no photos — and the draftsman draws it. Complete when the drawing shows the right number of columns, the triangular pediment, and the steps. Wrong column count = swap roles, new drawing.
candidates.where: 300 Funston Ave at Clement St (Funston = 13th Ave)
candidates.photo: The drawing held up beside the real facade.
candidates.why_here: The Wayback Machine literally lives in this neighborhood, in a building chosen because it looks like the Archive's logo — now draw the logo blind.

Inner Sunset.intro: Fog-kissed village neighborhood between Golden Gate Park and the hills: the 9th & Irving food-and-shops hub (a worker-owned bakery, a bookstore, and SF's last magic shop) below, and the mosaic-stairway country of Golden Gate Heights above. Boundary check against the official Analysis Neighborhoods map (DataSF, point-in-polygon on the `j2bu-swwd` polygons): the 16th Avenue Tiled Steps, the Hidden Garden Steps, and Grandview Park ALL fall inside the official **Inner Sunset** polygon — not Sunset/Parkside — so the famous stairways are fair game here. Golden Gate Park itself is a separate neighborhood and is avoided.
Inner Sunset.why_chosen: Climb to the top of Turtle Hill, find a teammate's exact first name among the tiles of the 16th Avenue Tiled Steps next door, then spend five minutes in the Garden for the Environment. A summit, a name hunt, a pause; nothing failable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 35–45 minutes. (The Hidden Garden Steps, the magic trick and Arizmendi's pizza bet are alternates.)

candidates.title: Top of Turtle Hill
candidates.do: Climb the wooden stairs from 14th Ave & Moraga to the bare-sand summit of Grandview Park ("Turtle Hill"), with a 360° view down every street to the ocean and the city. Done when the whole team is at the top.
candidates.where: Grandview Park, stairs from 14th Ave & Moraga to the summit
candidates.photo: The whole team on the sandy summit, the avenues running to the ocean behind you.
candidates.why_here: Turtle Hill is one of the last remnants of the ancient dunes the whole Sunset is built on — and the best view in the neighborhood.

candidates.title: Your Name in 75,000 Pieces
candidates.do: At the 16th Avenue Tiled Steps (163 mosaic risers, "sea to stars"), find one of the 220+ handmade sponsor name tiles (animal, fish and shell shapes with donors' names baked in) that shows the EXACT first name of someone on your team: the whole name, spelled the same, not just the same first letter. Complete with a photo of that tile.
candidates.where: Moraga St between 15th & 16th Ave (stair base at 16th Ave & Moraga)
candidates.failable: no (keep looking — or try another teammate's name)
candidates.photo: The teammate pointing at the tile with their own name on it, the mosaic sweeping up the stairs behind them.
candidates.why_here: The neighborhood literally tiled its own names into its most famous landmark — you're finding the Inner Sunset's residents in the art they built.

candidates.title: Five Minutes in the Fog-Belt Farm
candidates.do: Go to the Garden for the Environment, a free half-acre teaching farm-garden open every day from dawn to dusk, and spend five minutes there as a team, wandering the beds. Phones away the whole time (one teammate can set a timer first, then pocket it too). Done after five minutes in the garden.
candidates.where: Garden for the Environment, 1590 7th Ave (at Lawton St)
candidates.photo: The team among the garden beds, the foggy avenues beyond the fence.
candidates.why_here: A working demonstration garden has been tucked into these foggy avenues since 1990 — the only garden in SF dedicated to teaching regenerative growing.

candidates.title: Orange Tiles Only
candidates.do: At the Hidden Garden Steps (148 mosaic risers), find the giant orange salamander that snakes up 26 of the steps. Every teammate climbs the salamander's stretch stepping ONLY where the orange of its body meets the step — never on the blue-and-green background tiles. Foot on the background = back to the salamander's tail. Complete when everyone has done a clean climb.
candidates.where: Hidden Garden Steps, 16th Ave between Kirkham and Lawton
candidates.failable: no (back to the tail and retry)
candidates.photo: A foot mid-step on the orange, the salamander curling up the stairs.
candidates.why_here: The second mosaic staircase of the Inner Sunset is the quieter one, and its salamander was built to be walked.
