candidates.title: First-Take Magic
candidates.do: Enter Misdirections Magic Shop — San Francisco's last brick-and-mortar magic shop — and have one teammate, the magician, buy any beginner trick for $10 or less (teammates wait outside). The magician practices out of sight as long as they like, then announces "official take" and performs it once for the team on video. Complete if the trick WORKS on that take — the coin vanishes, the card is found, the rope is restored — with no visible flub. Flubbed? More practice, and another official take.
candidates.where: Misdirections Magic Shop, 1236 9th Ave (between Lincoln & Irving); open weekend daytime.
candidates.photo: The reveal, mid-gasp, with the shop's storefront behind.
candidates.why_here: The city's last magic shop — the only place in the game where you buy a skill and have to prove it on camera.

candidates.title: Pizza of the Day Gamble
candidates.do: Arizmendi Bakery, a worker-owned co-op, bakes ONE vegetarian pizza a day and changes it daily. BEFORE anyone looks at the board or the slices, the team writes down TWO toppings they bet are on today's pizza. Then buy one slice and check. At least one of your two toppings on it = complete. Neither = failed — but you still eat the slice.
candidates.where: Arizmendi Bakery, 1331 9th Ave (between Irving & Judah).
candidates.photo: The written prediction next to the actual slice, verdict on everyone's face.
candidates.why_here: A pizza that's different every single day is a pizza begging to be bet on.

Japantown.intro: One of only three remaining Japantowns in the United States, packed into a few blocks around the Peace Pagoda: the Japan Center malls (Kinokuniya's books, Daiso, capsule-toy walls, dessert counters) hum on weekends, the Buchanan Mall pedestrian block carries Ruth Asawa's bronze origami fountains along a cobblestone "river," and a hidden brick lane of 1882 cottages (Cottage Row) survives one block north. Challenges anchor on the pagoda, the origami tradition, the mall treasure-hunt density, and that secret lane.
Japantown.why_chosen: Fold a crane talked through by teammates who found the instructions, buy and bite something with a face in the Japan Center food halls, then name three Hi-Chew flavors blind at Nijiya Market (the neighborhood's one-shot). One teammate-roles game, one snack, one blind taste; ~$10–15 total, zero strangers, ≈ 35–45 minutes.

candidates.title: Crane Landing
candidates.do: Fold a paper crane. Pick a folder: they may not look at any instructions, so the rest of the team has to find some — a printed diagram somewhere in Japantown (on a pack of origami paper, in a book in a shop), not on a phone — and talk the folder through it. Helpers may point and demonstrate with their hands, but only the folder touches the paper. Complete when it's recognizably a crane: head, tail and two wings. Torn it? Get a fresh sheet and start over.
candidates.where: Anywhere in Japantown; Paper Tree — The Origami Store (1743 Buchanan St, family-run since 1968) is the obvious first stop for paper.
candidates.failable: no (new sheet until it's a crane)
candidates.photo: The folder holding up the finished crane, the team that talked them through it crowded behind.
candidates.why_here: Japantown has had its own origami shop since 1968, steps from Ruth Asawa's bronze origami fountains — the crane is the neighborhood's own craft.

candidates.title: Eat Something With a Face
candidates.do: In the Japan Center malls' food corridors, buy one snack or dessert shaped like an animal — a taiyaki fish cone at Uji Time, a fish waffle, a panda bun, anything with a recognizable creature form — and photograph a teammate taking a bite while the animal is still clearly identifiable. Complete on purchase + photo.
candidates.where: Japan Center malls, Post St between Fillmore & Laguna (e.g. Uji Time, 22 Peace Plaza #440; malls are liveliest on weekend afternoons).
candidates.photo: Mid-chomp portrait — teammate vs. fish (or panda), face to face.
candidates.why_here: Taiyaki and animal-shaped sweets are Japan Center food-hall signatures; the malls are the neighborhood's weekend heartbeat.

candidates.title: Hi-Chew Blind Test
candidates.do: At Nijiya Market, buy Hi-Chew, the chewy Japanese fruit candy, in THREE different flavors (≤$8 total). Outside, one teammate, the taster, closes their eyes; another unwraps one piece of each and hands them over in a secret order. The taster names all three flavors. All three right = complete. Any wrong = failed, no retry.
candidates.where: Nijiya Market, 1737 Post St (Japan Center).
candidates.photo: Eyes shut, mid-chew, the three Hi-Chew wrappers fanned out beside the taster.
candidates.why_here: Japan Center's snack aisles carry flavors that exist nowhere else in the city — and the wrapper is the only answer key.

candidates.title: Call Your Capsule
candidates.do: At the Gashapon Bandai Official Shop (or any capsule-machine bank in the Japan Center malls), pick one machine. Before turning the crank, record a short video of a teammate declaring the color of the capsule shell that will come out (most machines mix 4–5 shell colors). One turn only: if the capsule matches the called color, the challenge is complete; if not, it's failed — but you keep the mystery toy either way.
candidates.where: Gashapon Bandai Official Shop, Japan Center (Kinokuniya Building, 1581 Webster St); other capsule banks throughout both malls also count.
candidates.failable: one-shot (one declared turn; win or lose, the toy is yours)
candidates.photo: The opened capsule half held next to the toy, machine wall behind — plus the declaration video.
candidates.why_here: An official Bandai gashapon shop — walls of Japanese capsule machines — is a Japantown-only phenomenon in SF.

candidates.title: Triple-Digit Treasure
candidates.do: Inside Kinokuniya Bookstore, find on the shelves a manga volume whose number is 100 or higher (English or Japanese section — One Piece alone is well past volume 110). Photograph a teammate holding it with the volume number legible, then reshelve it neatly. No purchase required.
candidates.where: Kinokuniya, 1581 Webster St, upstairs in the Kinokuniya Building of the Japan Center (open weekends 10:30am–8pm).
candidates.photo: Teammate holding a volume with a three-digit number on the spine/cover, bookstore shelves behind.
candidates.why_here: The largest Japanese bookstore in the city; only here do series run deep enough for triple digits to be findable.

candidates.title: The Six Little Cottages
candidates.do: Find Cottage Row — a brick-paved pedestrian lane hidden mid-block between Sutter and Bush (between Webster and Fillmore), a National Register historic district. Walk its full length and count the small matching 1882 cottages whose front doors open directly onto the bricks; report the count with your claim. (Referee key: six, addressed 1–6 Cottage Row.)
candidates.where: Cottage Row & the adjacent mini park; enter from Sutter St just east of Fillmore, ~3 blocks northwest of Peace Plaza.
candidates.photo: The team on the brick lane, row of cottages behind, holding up fingers for the count.
candidates.why_here: A secret Victorian lane inside the historic heart of pre-war Japantown — most San Franciscans have never heard of it.

Lakeshore.intro: San Francisco's wild southwest corner: the official Lakeshore analysis neighborhood bundles Lake Merced (a freshwater lake ringed by a 4.5-mile trail, a boathouse, and a fishing pier), Fort Funston (the city's biggest dune field, a WWII 16-inch gun battery, a hang glider launch deck, and roughly a thousand off-leash dogs), SFSU's campus, and Stonestown Galleria — which since 2024 hides SF's largest arcade in a former Nordstrom basement. Anchored on the battery-and-gliders cliffs, the lake's odd relocated conquistador statue, and Stonestown's claw machines.
Lakeshore.why_chosen: Visit the Anza statue on Lake Merced, photograph eight different dogs at Fort Funston, and keep five silent minutes at Ruth Asawa's Garden of Remembrance at SFSU. A landmark, a dog hunt, a pause; nothing failable, zero strangers, $0, ≈ 40–55 minutes (the three are spread out — Fort Funston is a ride from the lake and campus).

candidates.title: The Anza Statue
candidates.do: Find the bronze equestrian statue of Juan Bautista de Anza, the Spanish explorer who led the expedition that founded San Francisco in 1776, on Lake Merced's north shore (it stood in Justin Herman Plaza downtown until 2003). Done when the whole team is at the statue.
candidates.where: Lakeside pullout/parking area off Lake Merced Blvd at the north end of Lake Merced — the horse is visible from the road.
candidates.place_name: Equestrian Statue of Juan Bautista de Anza
candidates.photo: The team at the foot of the statue, the lake behind.
candidates.why_here: A full equestrian monument to SF's founder stands weirdly alone in a lakeside parking area — and it's the only statue in the game you're allowed to explore with your hands.

candidates.title: The Fort Funston Dog Census
candidates.do: Fort Funston is famously SF's off-leash dog paradise. Photograph 8 different dogs (from any distance; no petting required — ask the owner first if you want a close-up). 8 photos, 8 visibly different dogs = complete.
candidates.where: Fort Funston trails and parking lot — the dogs come to you.
candidates.failable: no (persistence — the supply of dogs is effectively infinite on a weekend)
candidates.photo: A grid/series of 8 distinct dogs; final shot is the team pointing at their favorite.
candidates.why_here: Fort Funston is the most famous dog spot in a famously dog-mad city; weekend dog density is a genuine local phenomenon.

candidates.title: Garden of Remembrance
candidates.do: On the SFSU campus, find Ruth Asawa's Garden of Remembrance, a waterfall garden honoring the 19 Japanese American students sent to internment camps in 1942, with one boulder for each WWII camp. Spend five minutes there in respectful silence as a team. Phones away the whole time (one teammate can set a timer first, then pocket it too). Done after the five minutes.
candidates.where: Ruth Asawa's Garden of Remembrance, SFSU campus.
candidates.photo: Afterward: the team beside the boulders and the waterfall.
candidates.why_here: A quiet, moving memorial by one of SF's greatest artists, hidden on a campus most people only drive past.

candidates.title: Dune Pictionary at the Glider Deck
candidates.do: From the Fort Funston main parking lot, walk to the wooden hang glider viewing deck at the cliff edge, then step onto the open sand beside it. Play Pictionary in the dune: one teammate, the artist, generates a random number 1–8 on a phone and draws that item from this list — 1 dog, 2 hang glider, 3 wave, 4 bunker, 5 gull, 6 surfer, 7 lighthouse, 8 crab — in the sand with a finger or stick (re-roll repeats). No letters, no numbers, no talking. The team gets three guesses. Right = the next teammate draws. Wrong = smooth the sand, new artist, streak restarts. Complete when three drawings in a row are guessed. Stay behind the fence line — the cliff is real.
candidates.where: Fort Funston, end of Fort Funston Rd off Skyline Blvd; the deck and dunes are beside the main lot.
candidates.failable: no (the streak restarts until you hit three)
candidates.photo: The winning sand drawing with the artist's finger still in it, hang gliders (if you're lucky) over the deck behind.
candidates.why_here: The only place in SF where a WWII gun battery and a hang glider launch share a dune field — and the sand is the biggest sketchpad in the city.

candidates.title: Claw Patrol
candidates.do: Descend into Round1, the giant arcade in Stonestown's former Nordstrom basement, and win any physical prize from a claw machine. Budget cap: $5 of credits. Prize in hand = complete; $5 gone with empty hands = failed.
candidates.where: Round1 Bowling & Arcade, 285 Winston Dr (lower level, Stonestown Galleria). Open weekends 10am–2am.
candidates.failable: retryable (each grab is an attempt; challenge fails when the $5 cap is spent)
candidates.photo: The winner hoisting the prize in front of the wall of claw machines.
candidates.why_here: SF's largest arcade opened here in 2024 — Stonestown's second life as the west side's indoor playground.

candidates.title: The Growing Fish Story
candidates.do: On the public fishing pier just past the Lake Merced Boathouse, tell a fish story the memory way: the first teammate says one sentence ("I caught a trout the size of a kayak."). The next repeats it and adds a sentence. Around the team it goes, each person reciting the whole story so far, word for word, then adding one line. Complete when the story reaches TEN sentences with no slips. A slip = the story restarts at sentence one.
candidates.where: Lake Merced fishing pier, behind the boathouse at 1 Harding Rd (off Skyline Blvd at Harding Park).
candidates.photo: The team on the pier mid-recital, lake and tule reeds behind.
candidates.why_here: Lake Merced is the city's only freshwater fishing lake — the natural home of the tall tale.

Lincoln Park.intro: A tiny, dramatic neighborhood that is basically one clifftop park: the Legion of Honor and its free outdoor Court of Honor (with a real Rodin *Thinker* and a mini Louvre pyramid), the Lands End Coastal Trail with shipwreck and lighthouse sightlines, the USS San Francisco Memorial built from the actual shell-torn bridge of a WWII cruiser, and a golf course laid over a forgotten 19th-century cemetery. Boundary check against the official Analysis Neighborhoods polygons: Sutro Baths, the Lands End Lookout visitor center, and Sutro Heights all fall in **Outer Richmond**, not here — so everything below anchors east of Merrie Way: the Legion, the memorial, Mile Rock overlook, Eagle's Point, and the fairways.
Lincoln Park.why_chosen: Take in the Golden Gate from Eagle's Point, hunt a lost golf ball along the public paths around Lincoln Park's cliffside course, and talk a blind walker through the stone labyrinth at Lands End Point. A view, a hunt, a guided walk; nothing failable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 40–50 minutes.

candidates.title: Eagle's Point
candidates.do: Walk to the Eagle's Point overlook at the east end of the Coastal Trail, with the Golden Gate dead ahead. Done when the whole team is at the overlook.
candidates.where: Eagle's Point overlook, Coastal Trail trailhead at 32nd Ave & El Camino del Mar (a five-minute walk from the Legion of Honor)
candidates.photo: The team at the overlook, the Golden Gate Bridge dead ahead.
candidates.why_here: The busiest stretch of water on the West Coast passes this clifftop — and nobody can look up how many boats the next ten minutes hold.

candidates.title: Lost Ball Hunt
candidates.do: Lincoln Park's golf course wraps around the Coastal Trail and the Legion of Honor, and it sheds golf balls into the rough along every public path. Walking ONLY the public trail and sidewalk edges (never onto the course), find one lost golf ball. Complete when a ball is in hand; keep it as your trophy.
candidates.where: Public paths along the course: the Coastal Trail east from Eagle's Point, Clement St, and the road up to the Legion.
candidates.photo: The found ball held up with a fairway and the bridge behind.
candidates.why_here: The only golf course in SF built on a cemetery and a cliff — and the slice count is high.

candidates.title: Walk the Vanishing Labyrinth
candidates.do: From the Eagle's Point end of the Coastal Trail, take the signed spur path down toward Lands End Point, the rocky promontory with the Golden Gate Bridge dead ahead, where a stone labyrinth is laid out on the clearing (artist Eduardo Aguilera first laid it in 2004; vandals keep scattering it and volunteers keep rebuilding it — it was back as of 2025). One teammate walks the whole spiral to the center with their eyes closed, guided only by the rest of the team's spoken directions. Step over a line = back to the entrance. Safety first: one teammate walks right beside the walker the whole way, ready to stop them, and the walker opens their eyes the moment anyone says "stop". If the labyrinth has been scattered, reaching the clearing completes it. Go slowly on the narrow spur, and skip the outermost rocks if it's wet.
candidates.where: Lands End Point spur, off the Coastal Trail about 1 km west of the Eagle's Point overlook (trail access at El Camino del Mar & 32nd Ave).
candidates.failable: no (back to the entrance and walk again)
candidates.photo: The walker at the center with eyes still closed, the team who talked them in around the spiral, the bridge beyond.
candidates.why_here: A secret, semi-mythical rock labyrinth that exists only when someone has recently rebuilt it, on the best bridge-view promontory in the city.

candidates.title: The Lighthouse That Lost Its Head
candidates.do: From the Mile Rock overlook on the Coastal Trail, spot Mile Rock Lighthouse offshore — the stubby tower whose top was sliced off in the 1960s and replaced with a helicopter pad. Get a zoomed photo clearly showing its flat helipad top, with one teammate pointing at it from the overlook railing in a second (or the same) shot. Low-tide bonus flourish: from the same stretch of trail, look down for the rusted engine blocks of the tankers *Lyman Stewart* (wrecked 1922) and *Frank H. Buck* (wrecked 1937) poking out of the surf.
candidates.where: Mile Rock overlook, Lands End Coastal Trail (the signed overlook west of the Mile Rock beach stairs, between the USS San Francisco Memorial and Eagle's Point).
candidates.photo: Zoomed shot of the decapitated, helipad-topped lighthouse; teammate pointing seaward from the overlook.
candidates.why_here: Only this clifftop gives you a lighthouse wearing a helipad and two dynamited shipwrecks in a single view — the graveyard of the Golden Gate.

candidates.title: The Cemetery Under the Fairways
candidates.do: Lincoln Park's golf course is built on top of City Cemetery (1870–1909), and exactly two monuments were left standing. Find the Kong Chow funerary altar (1893), a brick-and-stone Chinese memorial near the Hole 1 green — its inscription calls it a temporary resting place for travelers from Kong Chow before their bones returned home to China. Photograph the team beside it with the Chinese characters legible in frame. Stay on the paved cart path from the 34th Ave & Clement entrance, walk the edge, and wait for any golfers to play through before crossing near the green.
candidates.where: Lincoln Park Golf Course, near the Hole 1 green — short walk from the clubhouse entrance at 34th Ave & Clement St.
candidates.photo: Team at the 1893 altar, inscription visible, fairway rolling away behind — a graveyard hiding in plain sight.
candidates.why_here: Thousands of graves still lie beneath these fairways; this altar is one of only two markers the city forgot to remove, now SF's first archaeological landmark.

candidates.title: A Moment at the USS San Francisco
candidates.do: At the USS San Francisco Memorial stand the real bridge wings of the cruiser USS *San Francisco*, riddled with shell holes from the night Battle of Guadalcanal in November 1942, when Admiral Daniel J. Callaghan and many of the crew were lost on that bridge. Stand together at the memorial for five minutes of silence. Phones away the whole time (one teammate can set a timer first, then pocket it too). Done after the five minutes.
candidates.where: USS San Francisco Memorial overlook, 2400 El Camino del Mar (west end, by the flagpole at the Lands End parking loop above the Coastal Trail).
candidates.photo: Afterward: the team beside the shell-holed steel, the Pacific behind it.
candidates.why_here: This isn't a statue about a ship; it IS the ship — battle damage you can put your eye to, perched over the sea it sailed from.

Lone Mountain/USF.intro: A cemetery hill that became a women's college that became the Jesuit hilltop campus of the University of San Francisco. Everything here climbs: a 143-step grand staircase modeled on Rome's Spanish Steps, the 210-foot twin spires of St. Ignatius Church (in 1914 the tallest points in San Francisco, used by ship captains as a navigation landmark), and a summit with one of the city's best hidden skyline views. I anchored on the staircase, the church, and USF's surprisingly weird public art — a wolf statue, a 4,800-pound marble heart, medieval Spanish archways, and a Qing-dynasty star machine — all outdoors and open to wanderers on weekends.
Lone Mountain/USF.why_chosen: Match a teammate's climbing time up the Lone Mountain steps within five seconds, blind, stack six rocks into a tower at the heart-shaped rock garden, and name a constellation from its Chinese name beside the Emperor's star machine. A pacing duel, a balancing act, a memory test; the star names are the one one-shot, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 35–45 minutes.

candidates.title: Echo Climb on the Spanish Steps
candidates.do: Climb the Lone Mountain grand staircase from Turk Boulevard to the top terrace — walking, no running. The pacesetter goes first: start a phone stopwatch at the bottom step, climb at any pace, stop it on the top step, and announce the time. Then the echo climbs, with no watch, no phone and no counting help from anyone: start a stopwatch face-down in your pocket at the bottom, stop it at the top without looking, then check. Within 5 seconds of the pacesetter's time = complete. Off? The echo walks back down and climbs again.
candidates.where: Lone Mountain grand staircase, from Turk Blvd up to the top terrace.
candidates.failable: no (walk back down and climb again)
candidates.photo: Two stopwatch screens side by side at the top of the stairs, the city spread out below.
candidates.why_here: The Lone Mountain staircase is USF's grand ascent, long and steep enough that holding a pace up it is real work — and every miss costs you the walk back down.

candidates.title: Stack Six at the Rock Garden
candidates.do: Find the heart-shaped Rock Garden along the URBAN Trail on USF's main campus, on the path between Harney Science Center and Gleeson Library, whose posted rule is "take a rock when you need some good news… then leave a rock to pass on good news." Using rocks from the garden and the trail, stack SIX rocks one on top of another, a single tower, one rock per level. Hands off: it has to stand on its own for a count of five. Topples? Build again. Done when the video shows six rocks standing through the count. Then unstack it and put the rocks back where you found them.
candidates.where: Heart-shaped Rock Garden on the URBAN Trail, USF main campus, on the path between Harney Science Center and Gleeson Library.
candidates.photo: The six-rock tower standing on its own, the heart-shaped garden around it.
candidates.why_here: A hillside heart made of rocks people leave for good luck — the one place in the city built for stacking a few more.

candidates.title: The Emperor's Star Names
candidates.do: Near USF's Lo Schiavo Science building sits a full-size bronze replica of the armillary sphere Jesuit missionary Ferdinand Verbiest built in the 1670s for the Chinese emperor. Beside it, two teammates study these ten constellations and their Chinese names together for three minutes: (1) Orion = 猎户座 *Lièhù zuò*; (2) the Big Dipper = 北斗七星 *Běidǒu qīxīng*; (3) Cassiopeia = 仙后座 *Xiānhòu zuò*; (4) Scorpius = 天蝎座 *Tiānxiē zuò*; (5) Leo = 狮子座 *Shīzi zuò*; (6) Taurus = 金牛座 *Jīnniú zuò*; (7) Gemini = 双子座 *Shuāngzǐ zuò*; (8) Cygnus = 天鹅座 *Tiān'é zuò*; (9) Pegasus = 飞马座 *Fēimǎ zuò*; (10) Andromeda = 仙女座 *Xiānnǚ zuò*. Only then decide who speaks and who guesses (let a phone flip a coin), and the guesser puts their phone away. The speaker generates a random number from 1 to 10 on a phone, keeps it hidden, finds that constellation on the list and says ONLY its Chinese name out loud. The guesser names the constellation in English. Right = complete. Wrong = failed, no retry. Anyone who reads Chinese can help the others study but can't be the speaker or the guesser.
candidates.where: USF main campus, by the Lo Schiavo Science building.
candidates.photo: The speaker and the guesser under the sphere's bronze rings at the moment of the answer.
candidates.why_here: Verbiest's instrument mapped the sky for a Chinese emperor, where Western and Chinese astronomy met — so here you name the stars in both.

candidates.title: Walk Through the 1500s
candidates.do: USF's Kalmanovitz Hall is framed by two genuinely ancient doorways shipped from Europe: the Santa Maria de Ovila Portal (1575, from a Spanish monastery — it frames the outdoor auditorium stage) and a Romanesque portal from 12th–13th century northern Italy carved with Adam and Eve. Find both. One teammate stands framed inside the 1575 archway; at the older portal, a teammate points directly at the Adam and Eve carving. Complete when both photos are taken.
candidates.where: Kalmanovitz Hall and its outdoor terraces, USF main campus (uphill from Fulton St near Parker Ave).
candidates.photo: Teammate posed in a 450-year-old stone archway; teammate pointing at an 800-year-old Adam and Eve.
candidates.why_here: Two of the oldest built structures in San Francisco are hiding on this campus, and almost nobody knows they exist.

candidates.title: Conquer the Spanish Steps of the West
candidates.do: Climb the Lone Mountain grand staircase from Turk Boulevard to the top — every teammate, no shortcuts. Pick two counters; each silently counts the steps on the way up. At the top, both write their number down hidden and reveal together. The counts must MATCH. Mismatch = walk back down and recount on the next climb. At the mid-landing, everyone roars at the gilded lion's-head spout of the Alessandri Fountain.
candidates.where: Lone Mountain grand staircase, from Turk Blvd up to the top terrace.
candidates.photo: The two matching numbers held up at the top terrace, the city behind.
candidates.why_here: SF's own Spanish Steps — and counting them while out of breath is harder than it sounds.

Marina.intro: The Marina is 1915 World's Fair land: the Palace of Fine Arts is the fair's last ghost, the flat blocks were built on its rubble (which is why the 1989 quake hit here hardest, and why a fireboat named Phoenix is a local hero), and the waterfront is all kites, masts, and Golden Gate views from Fort Mason to the yacht harbor. Boundary note, verified: Crissy Field sits inside the Presidio's federal boundary and belongs to the **Presidio** Analysis Neighborhood, not this one — everything below stays east of Lyon Street. Anchors: the Palace, the Wave Organ jetty, Marina Green, Fort Mason's Great Meadow, and Chestnut Street.
Marina.why_chosen: Recreate a famous painting on the Palace of Fine Arts grounds and give your team one guess (the neighborhood's one-shot), record the Wave Organ actually playing, and land the Golden Gate + Alcatraz + sailboat in a single frame. An art game, a sound recording, a patience shot; one one-shot, one retryable, zero strangers, $0–10, ≈ 40–50 minutes.

candidates.title: Masterpiece, One Guess
candidates.do: The Palace of Fine Arts is an art thing — so make art. One teammate, the artist, secretly picks a famous painting (one they believe the whole team has seen). Anywhere on the Palace grounds, the artist recreates it by any means: drawn with bought supplies (up to $10), scratched in dirt, arranged from leaves and sticks, or built as a living tableau with the colonnade as backdrop. When the artist says "done," the rest of the team gets ONE collective guess at the painting's name. Right = complete. Wrong = failed. One shot.
candidates.where: Palace of Fine Arts grounds, 3601 Lyon St — lagoon lawn, colonnade, or rotunda.
candidates.photo: The recreation side by side with the artist's reveal of the real painting on their phone, rotunda behind.
candidates.why_here: A palace built for fine art deserves at least one Mona Lisa made of eucalyptus leaves.

candidates.title: Play the Bay's Pipe Organ
candidates.do: Walk the jetty at the end of Yacht Rd (past the St. Francis and Golden Gate yacht clubs) to the Wave Organ, the 1986 acoustic sculpture of 25 pipes played by the tides. Complete when the whole team is there. While you are, put an ear to a pipe: the gurgles and hums are loudest near high tide.
candidates.where: Wave Organ, end of the yacht-harbor jetty, Yacht Rd off Marina Blvd (open-air, 24/7).
candidates.photo: The whole team at the Wave Organ, pipes and stone terraces around you, the bay behind.
candidates.why_here: A wave-powered organ built out of cemetery headstones at the end of a yacht-harbor jetty exists exactly once on Earth, and it's here.

candidates.title: Bridge, Rock, and Boat
candidates.do: From anywhere along the Marina Green waterfront, capture ONE photo that contains all three: the Golden Gate Bridge, Alcatraz Island, and a sailboat with its sail up. All three must be identifiable in a single frame (no stitching).
candidates.where: Marina Green promenade, Marina Blvd between Scott and Webster.
candidates.failable: retryable (each submitted frame is an attempt; keep shooting until a sailboat crosses your composition)
candidates.photo: The trophy shot itself — bridge, prison island, and sail in one frame.
candidates.why_here: Marina Green is the only lawn in the city where those three line up across open water; on a weekend day the bay is full of sails.

candidates.title: Filibuster at Fort Mason
candidates.do: Climb to the Great Meadow at Fort Mason and find the huge bronze of Congressman Phillip Burton caught mid-speech. One teammate matches his pose exactly — right arm thrust out, left hand at the chest, mouth open like you're shouting a national park into existence — while standing beside him. Complete when the photo shows statue and human in matching poses.
candidates.where: Great Meadow, upper Fort Mason (enter from Bay St & Franklin or the stairs from Marina Blvd); open-air, 24/7.
candidates.photo: Side-by-side oratory: bronze Burton and your loudest teammate, both in full and fiery flight.
candidates.why_here: Burton wrote the law that created the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, so his statue yells forever over the parkland he made — starting with this meadow.

candidates.title: Weep With the Ladies
candidates.do: At the Palace of Fine Arts colonnade, find the giant "weeping women" sculpted atop the planter boxes — backs turned, heads bowed on their arms. Every teammate lines up and holds the exact pose directly below a row of them.
candidates.where: Palace of Fine Arts colonnade, 3601 Lyon St.
candidates.photo: The whole team in the pose with at least one stone weeping woman above.
candidates.why_here: The Palace's most famous residents, mourning for a century.

candidates.title: Lagoon Bird Bingo
candidates.do: At the Palace of Fine Arts lagoon, photograph THREE different kinds of birds (e.g., duck, gull, pigeon, coot, egret, heron, swan — any three distinct species, one clear photo each, all taken this visit). Bonus flavor: the trees here are a known roost for black-crowned night herons, hunched grumpy birds hiding in plain sight.
candidates.where: Palace of Fine Arts lagoon path, Baker St side.
candidates.failable: no (ducks, gulls, and pigeons guarantee it with persistence; a heron makes it bragging rights)
candidates.photo: A three-shot collage of your birds, lagoon and rotunda behind.
candidates.why_here: The fair's ornamental lagoon became an accidental bird sanctuary; sharp eyes can win this one single-handed.

McLaren Park.intro: This Analysis Neighborhood is essentially John McLaren Park itself — at 312 acres SF's second-largest park — plus the rec facilities tucked inside its lines (Louis Sutter Playground/McNab Lake at the northeast corner, Gleneagles Golf Course to the south). No shops, no bars, just hills: a Tiffany-blue water tower a 1956 newspaper called "a kind of high-calorie Coit Tower," America's only trail built for philosophers, an amphitheater named for hometown hero Jerry Garcia, and a log-tower playground with a 20-foot tube slide. Everything below is inside the park, free, and open weekend daytime.
McLaren Park.why_chosen: Muse for five quiet minutes at a musing station on Philosopher's Way, play name-that-tune with no voices at the Jerry Garcia Amphitheater, and take a five-minute recess at the Redwood Grove Playground. A pause, a guessing game, a recess; one retryable, zero strangers, $0, ≈ 40–55 minutes.

candidates.title: Muse on Philosopher's Way
candidates.do: Philosopher's Way is a 2.7-mile loop through McLaren Park dotted with granite "musing station" plaques. Find one, read its quote, and muse on it quietly for five minutes. Phones away the whole time (one teammate can set a timer first, then pocket it too). Then everyone shares their musing with the rest of the team. Done when everyone has shared.
candidates.where: Philosopher's Way, starting from the Overlook lot at Mansell St & Visitacion Ave.
candidates.photo: Afterward: the team gathered around the musing station's granite plaque.
candidates.why_here: A walking trail built for thinking — so think hard enough to remember.

candidates.title: Name That Tune at the Jerry Garcia Amphitheater
candidates.do: Go to the Jerry Garcia Amphitheater, the Greek-style bowl named for the Grateful Dead guitarist who grew up in the Excelsior next door. One teammate takes the stage and secretly picks a song; the rest sit up in the stands. The performer plays the song any way they like — clapping, stomping, drumming on the stage, tapping on anything — but with NO sound from their mouth: no singing, humming or whistling. The audience gets one guess. Right = complete. Wrong = everyone waits five minutes, then a new performer picks a new song. (If an actual event is underway, come back later.)
candidates.where: Jerry Garcia Amphitheater, 40 John F. Shelley Dr, mid-park.
candidates.failable: retryable (each wrong guess costs a five-minute wait)
candidates.photo: The performer mid-beat on the stage, the team in the stands mid-guess.
candidates.why_here: SF's only outdoor amphitheater, named for Jerry Garcia because 87 Harrington St is a few blocks away — the bowl is usually empty and all yours, so it's just your voice, the distance, and one chance to hear.

candidates.title: Recess at Redwood Grove
candidates.do: At the Redwood Grove Playground, with its log-and-rope tower and 16-foot stainless tube slide, have a fun time playing for five minutes — every teammate, all in. Phones away the whole time (one teammate can set a timer first, then pocket it too). Done after the five minutes.
candidates.where: Redwood Grove Playground, off John F. Shelley Dr at the group picnic area on the park's west side.
candidates.photo: Afterward: the team at the bottom of the tube slide.
candidates.why_here: McLaren's showpiece natural playground — a log tower built into the hillside redwood grove, with the best slide in the southeast of the city.

candidates.title: Pace the High-Calorie Coit Tower
candidates.do: Hike up to the La Grande Tank, the 80-foot sky-blue water tower on the park's highest ridge. From the point where the tank first comes fully into view, the team agrees on ONE guess: how many of your tallest teammate's paces to reach its base? Write it down, then that teammate walks it at a normal stride, everyone counting out loud. Within 10% = complete. Off? One more guess — the tank's circumference in paces — and pace that. Miss twice = failed.
candidates.where: La Grande Tank hilltop, off the John F. Shelley Dr loop near the Wilde Overlook (walk uphill toward the blue thing).
candidates.photo: The pacer's hand on the tank, guess and count held up side by side.
candidates.why_here: The 1956 Call-Bulletin called this tank "a kind of high-calorie Coit Tower"; painted eggshell blue to blend into the sky, it's famously hard to judge the distance to.

candidates.title: Walk the Labyrinth Without a Wobble
candidates.do: On Philosopher's Hill (along Philosopher's Way, near the reservoir), find the stone labyrinth laid into the hilltop. Each teammate must walk the winding rock-lined path from the entrance all the way to the center without stepping outside the path. Step out = that teammate returns to the entrance and starts over. Complete when every teammate has reached the center on a clean walk.
candidates.where: Hilltop stone labyrinth off Philosopher's Way near the Upper Reservoir (Philosopher's Hill).
candidates.failable: retryable (an attempt = one walk from the entrance; unlimited retries)
candidates.photo: The whole team clustered at the labyrinth's center, spiral of stones visible around your feet, bay view behind.
candidates.why_here: A hand-laid rock labyrinth on a hilltop is one of McLaren's best-kept secrets — most San Franciscans don't know it exists.

candidates.title: Animal Charades at McNab Lake
candidates.do: At McNab Lake, find the tiled mural of the San Francisco garter snake running along the retaining wall. Then play charades with what's around you: one teammate secretly picks any animal they can see right now — on the lake, in the mural, on a leash — and acts it out, no sounds, no pointing. The team gets ONE guess. Right = next actor, new animal (no repeats). Wrong = the streak restarts. Complete at three in a row.
candidates.where: McNab Lake, next to Louis Sutter Playground, near University St & Wayland St, northeast corner of the park.
candidates.photo: The actor mid-duck, the snake mural and the real ducks behind.
candidates.why_here: A community-made mosaic honoring the SF garter snake beside the duck lake locals call the park's living room — a zoo's worth of charades material.

Mission.intro: The Mission is SF's oldest neighborhood and its loudest canvas: the 1776 adobe Mission Dolores (the oldest building in the city), the mural-lined alleys of Balmy and Clarion, the 24th Street Latino Cultural District with its panaderías and taquerias, and Dolores Park with its skyline lawn and gold-painted 1906 hero hydrant. Challenges anchor on those five pillars — murals you hunt through, history you spell out with your fingers, and pan dulce you actually get to eat.
Mission.why_chosen: Name 100 famous women in front of the MaestraPeace mural on the Women's Building, collect six painted animals in Balmy Alley, and spend five phone-free minutes at Mission Dolores, the 1776 mission the neighborhood is named for. A list, a find, a pause; nothing failable, zero strangers, $0, ≈ 40–55 minutes.

candidates.title: 100 Women at MaestraPeace
candidates.do: The Women's Building on 18th Street is wrapped in *MaestraPeace* (1994), a huge mural by seven women artists celebrating women from around the world. Standing in front of it, the team writes down the names of 100 famous women: real women most people would recognize, living or historical, each famous enough to have their own Wikipedia page. No repeats, no fictional characters, and no searching — one phone or paper for the list only. Done when the list reaches 100.
candidates.where: The Women's Building, 3543 18th St (between Valencia & Guerrero).
candidates.photo: The finished list of 100 held up in front of the mural.
candidates.why_here: A building covered top to bottom in a mural honoring women — the place to see how many your team can name.

candidates.title: Balmy Alley Bestiary
candidates.do: Walk Balmy Alley and photograph SIX different animals painted in the murals. No two animals from the same mural. Complete at six.
candidates.where: Balmy Alley, between 24th St and 25th St (parallel to Treat & Harrison).
candidates.failable: no (murals rotate, but the alley always teems with creatures)
candidates.photo: Six shots, each a painted animal with a team finger pointing at it.
candidates.why_here: Balmy Alley is the birthplace of the Mission mural movement — the densest block of murals in SF.

candidates.title: Five Minutes at Mission Dolores
candidates.do: Go to Mission Dolores, the oldest building in San Francisco (founded 1776), the adobe church the whole neighborhood is named after. Spend five minutes there as a team, taking it in: the white adobe facade, the old church beside the grand basilica. Phones away the whole time (one teammate can set a timer first, then pocket it too). Done after five minutes at the mission.
candidates.where: Mission Dolores, Dolores St at 16th St.
candidates.place_name: Mission of San Francisco de Asis
candidates.photo: The team in front of the white adobe facade, a building older than the Constitution.
candidates.why_here: The neighborhood is named after this building, and it has stood here since before the United States had a constitution.

candidates.title: Concha on the Serpent's Back
candidates.do: Buy one concha at a 24th Street panadería. The carrier balances the paper bag on their head and walks it two blocks to the 24th & York Mini Park — no hands. Drop it = walk back to the bakery door and restart. Deliver it to the giant mosaic Quetzalcoatl serpent and share it astride the serpent.
candidates.where: La Reyna Bakery, 3114 24th St (or Panadería La Mejor, 3329 24th St) to the 24th & York Mini Park.
candidates.photo: Team lined up on the tiled feathered serpent, concha held seashell-side out.
candidates.why_here: Pan dulce from a decades-old panadería plus the serpent that has guarded 24th Street since 1972.

candidates.title: Pose Detective
candidates.do: In Clarion Alley, one teammate — the performer — secretly picks any human figure painted in any mural, then walks to the alley entrance and freezes in that figure's pose. The rest of the team walks the alley and must point at the right figure. Two guesses total. Right = complete. Two misses = new performer, new figure, try again.
candidates.where: Clarion Alley, between Mission St and Valencia St (parallel to 17th & 18th).
candidates.failable: retryable (new performer and figure per attempt)
candidates.photo: Performer and mural figure side by side, identical, with the team pointing.
candidates.why_here: Clarion Alley has been a free, ever-changing open-air gallery since 1992 — packed with figures practically begging for stand-ins.

candidates.title: Pirate Supply Run
candidates.do: Enter the pirate supply store at 826 Valencia and buy any one pirate item for $10 or less. While inside, find the fish theater.
candidates.where: 826 Valencia St (between 19th & 20th). Open daily 12–6pm.
candidates.photo: Freshly outfitted pirate under the 826 Valencia sign.
candidates.why_here: A functioning pirate supply shop hidden on Valencia is the Mission's best "wait, that exists?"

candidates.title: Flip at the Golden Hydrant
candidates.do: Find the golden fire hydrant at Church & 20th, the corner of Dolores Park — the hydrant that kept working after the 1906 earthquake and saved the Mission from burning. Get a plastic water bottle on the way, leave about a third of the water in it, and flip it on the sidewalk beside the hydrant: land it standing upright FIVE times in a row. Any teammate can flip, but a miss by anyone resets the streak to zero. Done when the video shows the fifth landing.
candidates.where: SW corner of Dolores Park, Church St & 20th St.
candidates.photo: The fifth bottle landing upright, the golden hydrant beside it.
candidates.why_here: One gold hydrant is the reason the Mission's Victorians survived 1906 — it gets a fresh coat of gold every April 18.

candidates.title: A Mission Burrito
candidates.do: The Mission burrito — giant, foil-wrapped, born on these blocks — is the neighborhood's gift to the world. Buy one burrito at a taqueria in the Mission (La Taqueria at Mission & 25th is the legend; it famously skips the rice) and eat it as a team, every teammate taking at least one bite. Done when it's gone.
candidates.where: La Taqueria, 2889 Mission St (at 25th St), or any taqueria in the Mission.
candidates.photo: The team mid-bite around one foil-wrapped burrito.
candidates.why_here: The Mission burrito was invented in this neighborhood's taquerias, and you can't claim the Mission without eating one.

Mission Bay.intro: The newest-built neighborhood in San Francisco — a literal bay filled in with rubble (some of it 1906 earthquake debris), now home to Chase Center's art-filled plaza, UCSF's biotech campus, and Mission Creek's improbable houseboat colony with its herons and kayakers. Boundary note, verified against the official DataSF Analysis Neighborhoods polygon: **Oracle Park IS inside Mission Bay** (the northern boundary is Townsend St, so the ballpark, Willie Mays Plaza, and the 4th & King Caltrain station all belong to this neighborhood, not Financial District/South Beach; the southern boundary is Mariposa St). Anchors: Chase Center/Thrive City, China Basin Park (opened 2024, with SF's newest beach), the Oracle Park perimeter, and Mission Creek.
Mission Bay.why_chosen: The mirror shot at Chase Center, statue charades around the ballpark (shuffle, perform, name all five in a row), and a two-birds-one-frame hunt on Mission Creek. One photo puzzle, one teammate guessing game, one patience hunt; nothing failable, zero strangers, all $0 and outdoors, ≈ 35–45 minutes.

candidates.title: Trapped in the Infinity Mirror
candidates.do: At *Seeing Spheres* — the ring of five 15.5-foot mirrored steel spheres on the Chase Center east plaza — take ONE photo in which every teammate's face is visible in a single sphere's mirror, **including the photographer** (it's a mirror shot, so the camera-holder appears too). Complete when one photo shows the whole team reflected.
candidates.where: Thrive City plaza, east entrance of Chase Center (Terry A. Francois Blvd at Warriors Way).
candidates.failable: no (rearrange and reshoot until everyone fits)
candidates.photo: The whole team inside one giant mirror, ringed by LED lights, with the other spheres reflecting to infinity behind them.
candidates.why_here: Olafur Eliasson's largest public artwork in the United States lives on this plaza, outdoors and free, 24/7.

candidates.title: Bronze Age Charades
candidates.do: Oracle Park is ringed by five Giants legends in bronze: Willie Mays (3rd & King main entrance), Orlando Cepeda and Gaylord Perry (facing each other at 2nd & King), Juan Marichal mid-leg-kick (Lefty O'Doul Plaza, by the 3rd St bridge), and Willie McCovey (China Basin Park, across the cove). Walk the statues and study their poses as long as you like. Then one teammate — the performer — secretly puts all five names in a random order (shuffle them on paper or a phone). Without words, the performer acts out each statue's pose in that order, and the rest of the team names each one. Any wrong guess = the performer reshuffles and starts over from the first statue. Complete when the team names all five in a row.
candidates.where: Oracle Park perimeter, 2nd & King to 3rd & King, plus China Basin Park; perform anywhere along the way (Willie Mays Plaza is the classic stage).
candidates.failable: no (reshuffle and start over until you get all five)
candidates.photo: The performer frozen mid-Marichal-leg-kick in front of a bronze, team pointing and shouting the answer.
candidates.why_here: No other neighborhood has a ballpark moat of Giants legends — and the official boundary puts all of them in Mission Bay.

candidates.title: Creek Patrol
candidates.do: Walk the public Mission Creek Park path on the south bank of Mission Creek (between the 4th St and 6th St bridges) and get ONE photo with at least TWO wild birds in the same frame, on or over the creek (heron, egret, cormorant, pelican, duck and gull all count — the creek is a bird highway). Complete when you have the shot.
candidates.where: Mission Creek Park path, south bank of the channel, Channel St between 4th and 6th.
candidates.failable: no (birds rotate through constantly; keep watching)
candidates.photo: Two birds sharing one frame over the last surviving sliver of the old bay.
candidates.why_here: Mission Creek is the last surviving sliver of the original bay, and it's still a bird highway through a brand-new high-rise neighborhood.

candidates.title: Round the Horn, Then Hit the Beach
candidates.do: At China Basin Park, every teammate runs the bases on the Barry Bonds Junior Giants Field — the t-ball-sized mini diamond — and touches home plate. Then the whole team walks to the park's sand beach on McCovey Cove and every member touches the sand. Complete when all teammates have done both. (If a game is using the field, wait or come back — it's a public park.)
candidates.where: China Basin Park, across McCovey Cove from Oracle Park (Terry A. Francois Blvd at Toni Stone Crossing).
candidates.photo: A teammate crossing home plate mid-sprint with Oracle Park rising across the water behind them.
candidates.why_here: A pint-size ballpark in the shadow of the real one, next to the newest beach in San Francisco — both opened in 2024 in SF's newest neighborhood.

candidates.title: Join the Knothole Gang
candidates.do: Walk the Portwalk — the free public promenade along McCovey Cove behind Oracle Park's right-field wall — and find the fenced archway where the modern "Knothole Gang" can watch real games for free, three innings at a time. Take a photo THROUGH the chain-link with the field (grass or seats) clearly visible, old-timey peeking-through-the-fence style. Complete when the through-the-fence shot exists.
candidates.where: McCovey Cove Portwalk, along the water behind right field (enter from the 3rd St / Lefty O'Doul Bridge end or from 2nd St).
candidates.photo: Faces pressed to the fence, a big-league field framed in an archway, bay at your backs.
candidates.why_here: Oracle Park deliberately revived the 1900s "knothole gang" tradition — it's one of the only MLB parks where watching baseball is free.

candidates.title: Tip Your Cap on Toni Stone Crossing
candidates.do: Find the street sign for **Toni Stone Crossing**, the street along China Basin Park named for the first woman ever to play professional big-league baseball (she broke in with the Negro Leagues' Indianapolis Clowns in 1953). Before shooting, one teammate must read her one-line story (on your phone or a park sign) aloud to the team. Photo: the whole team under the sign, every member tipping a cap (real or invisible). Complete when the sign is legible in the team cap-tip photo.
candidates.where: Toni Stone Crossing at Terry A. Francois Blvd / Bridgeview Way, Mission Rock, south edge of China Basin Park.
candidates.photo: Team mid-cap-tip beneath the Toni Stone Crossing sign, ballpark in the distance.
candidates.why_here: Mission Rock's brand-new streets honor trailblazing women — a "wait, that exists?" piece of baseball history hiding on a street sign.

Nob Hill.intro: The crest of California Street is where the Big Four railroad barons built their mansions, and everything up here still wears their names: the Stanford Court, the Mark Hopkins, the Huntington Hotel, and Grace Cathedral standing on Crocker's old block beside Huntington Park's Roman fountain. Two cable car lines cross at California & Powell under a tiny signal tower, and the neighborhood runs downhill west to the donut shops of Polk Street. Boundary check against the official Analysis Neighborhoods map: the Cable Car Museum (1201 Mason at Washington) falls just inside **Chinatown**, so it is NOT usable here — but the California/Powell crossing, the crest, and Polk to Bush all are.
Nob Hill.why_chosen: A pacing duel on the labyrinth at the crest, a water relay to the Fountain of the Tortoises in Huntington Park, then catch cable cars crossing both ways at California & Powell. A duel, a relay, a two-shot photo hunt; nothing failable, zero strangers, $0, ≈ 35–50 minutes.

candidates.title: The Clockless Labyrinth
candidates.do: Grace Cathedral's outdoor labyrinth is open 24/7. Pick two walkers and one hidden timekeeper; the walkers give up every phone and watch. Walker one walks the labyrinth entrance to center — no shortcuts, step off the line and that walk restarts — while the timekeeper secretly times it. Then walker two walks it, trying to MATCH walker one's time by feel alone (they may watch walk one; no counting out loud, no signals from anyone). Times within 20 SECONDS of each other = complete. Wider = 10-minute cooldown, then a fresh pair of walks.
candidates.where: Grace Cathedral's outdoor plaza, 1100 California St at Taylor
candidates.failable: retryable (one pair of walks per attempt, 10-min cooldown)
candidates.photo: Both walkers in the center rosette, the two secret times revealed side by side, cathedral behind.
candidates.why_here: An 800-year-old Chartres pattern turned into a pacing duel — two people trying to share one internal clock on the barons' hill.

candidates.title: Water for the Tortoises
candidates.do: The Fountain of the Tortoises sits in the center of Huntington Park (a bronze replica of Rome's famous Fontana delle Tartarughe). Give it a drink: fetch water from any public water source — a drinking fountain, a public restroom tap — carry it to the fountain any way you like (cupped hands, a cup, an emptied bottle), and pour it into the basin. Water you bought or brought doesn't count. Done when the pour is on video.
candidates.where: Huntington Park, California & Taylor (directly across from Grace Cathedral).
candidates.failable: no (spill it? go back for more)
candidates.photo: The pour: water streaming into the basin, bronze tortoises and youths above, Grace Cathedral behind.
candidates.why_here: A Roman Renaissance fountain, gifted from a Crocker family estate, splashing in the middle of the barons' old front yards — it deserves a tribute carried by hand.

candidates.title: Both Ways at the Crossing
candidates.do: Go to California & Powell, one of the few places where two cable car lines cross, under the little signal tower. Take two photos from the sidewalk: one of a California Street car crossing the intersection (running east–west), and one of a Powell Street car crossing it (running north–south). Each car has to be in the intersection itself. Done when you have both.
candidates.where: Corner of California St & Powell St, by the signal tower (stay on the sidewalk; the west corners are Nob Hill).
candidates.time: 10–20 min (cars every few minutes on each line)
candidates.photo: Two shots: a California car and a Powell car, each right in the crossing.
candidates.why_here: Two cable car lines crossing at right angles is a sight you get almost nowhere else on Earth — and it happens on top of Nob Hill.

candidates.title: The Big Four in Four Frames
candidates.do: The Big Four railroad barons all had mansions on this crest, and each is still named here. Photograph the names **STANFORD**, **HOPKINS**, and **HUNTINGTON** on three different signs (hotel signage, park sign — any sign or plaque counts, one name per photo). For the fourth baron, Crocker, take a team photo at Grace Cathedral's golden front doors — the cathedral stands on Charles Crocker's old mansion block. Done at four photos.
candidates.where: All within two blocks of California St between Powell and Taylor (Stanford Court at 905 California, Mark Hopkins at 999 California, Huntington Hotel / Huntington Park at California & Taylor, Grace Cathedral at 1100 California).
candidates.photo: Four-shot set: three baron names in signage, plus the team in front of the gilded Ghiberti "Gates of Paradise" replica doors.
candidates.why_here: The entire Gilded Age story of Nob Hill told in one two-block walk — the 1906 fire took the mansions, but the names never left.

candidates.title: Mind the Grip
candidates.do: The California Street cable car climbs right over Nob Hill. At the California & Mason stop, watch as many cars come and go as you like. Then call your shot: before the next car is in sight, the whole team lines up shoulder-to-shoulder on the sidewalk where you think the car's FRONT END will be when it stops. No moving once it appears. If anyone is level with the front of the stopped car, you win. Missed? Wait for the next car and try again.
candidates.where: California St & Mason St cable car stop (stay on the sidewalk).
candidates.failable: retryable (each try costs a wait for the next car)
candidates.photo: The team lined up on the sidewalk with the stopped cable car's front end right in front of you.
candidates.why_here: The cable cars are Nob Hill's own transit, and operators stop by feel, not at a marked line — reading where one will stop is a Nob Hill skill.

candidates.title: Duet with Tony
candidates.do: Find the statue of Tony Bennett outside the Fairmont Hotel (unveiled on his 90th birthday — he first sang "I Left My Heart in San Francisco" inside this hotel in 1961). One teammate mirrors his pose beside the statue while the rest of the team, in frame, sings the line "I left my heart in San Francisco" out loud. Done when the posed photo is taken mid-song.
candidates.where: Fairmont Hotel entrance plaza, 950 Mason St at California.
candidates.photo: Pose-match with bronze Tony, the Fairmont's grand entrance behind.
candidates.why_here: The song that IS San Francisco premiered in this exact building; the statue marks the spot.

candidates.title: The Giant Donut of Polk Street
candidates.do: Go to Bob's Donuts (moved up the street in 2025; check today's hours) and buy ONE giant donut — the dinner-plate-sized one from the case. Photograph a teammate holding it up like a porthole with their face in the hole, under the Bob's neon sign. Then the team must finish the entire donut before leaving the block. Done when it's gone.
candidates.where: Bob's Donuts, 1720 Polk St (between Clay & Washington).
candidates.photo: Face framed in the giant donut hole beneath the vintage neon sign.
candidates.why_here: A 24-hour SF institution on Nob Hill's Polk Street slope, famous for its comically oversized donuts — the cheap-treat challenge this neighborhood was built for.

Noe Valley.intro: Stroller-and-dog paradise centered on the 24th Street shopping strip, ringed by ferociously steep hills and blocks of pastel Victorians — and home to the only town square in San Francisco (plus its nationally famous $1.7M toilet saga). I anchored on 24th Street's one-of-a-kind shops, the Town Square, the 31%-grade block of 22nd Street, and a meta gift: Clipper Street — named for the Gold Rush clipper ships — runs right through the middle of the neighborhood. (Boundary check done against the official Analysis Neighborhood polygon: Billy Goat Hill and Upper Noe Rec Center are officially Glen Park, so nothing here uses them; everything below is confirmed inside Noe Valley.)
Noe Valley.why_chosen: Eat something with "baby" in its name on the Town Square, call the flyer count on the square's message board, and pick one street-sign tin at Chocolate Covered, then go stand under the real sign. A snack, a guess-then-count, a sign match; one retryable, zero strangers, ~$2–6, ≈ 30–45 minutes.

candidates.title: Snack Time in Stroller Valley
candidates.do: Noe Valley's nickname is Stroller Valley. Buy something to eat with "baby" in its name — right on the label, the package or the menu (baby carrots, a Mini Babybel, baby back ribs, a Baby Ruth…) — from any shop on the way, then eat it at the Noe Valley Town Square, every teammate taking at least one bite. Done when it's eaten.
candidates.where: Anywhere in Noe Valley to buy it; eat it at the Noe Valley Town Square, 24th St between Sanchez and Vicksburg.
candidates.photo: The team on the Town Square mid-bite, the "baby" on the label held up to the camera.
candidates.why_here: The neighborhood famous for its strollers gets a snack break with its own theme — in the only town square in San Francisco.

candidates.title: Flyer Count at the Town Square
candidates.do: At the Noe Valley Town Square — the only town square in San Francisco — find the community message board. Before anyone gets close enough to read it, the team agrees on ONE guess: how many separate flyers are pinned up right now? Write it down, then count them together. Within 3 = complete. Off? One more guess — the number of flyers with a phone number on them — and count those. Miss twice = failed.
candidates.where: Noe Valley Town Square, 24th St between Sanchez and Vicksburg
candidates.photo: The guess held up in front of the board, count written beside it.
candidates.why_here: A former parking lot turned into the neighborhood's living room — and its message board is the busiest wall in Noe.

candidates.title: Tin Hunt at Chocolate Covered
candidates.do: Inside Chocolate Covered, a tiny shop lined floor-to-ceiling with thousands of handmade tins printed with San Francisco street signs, take ONE photo of ONE tin showing a street sign. Choose well: it's your only tin photo, no retakes of a different tin. Then go find that real street sign out in the city and take a photo standing under it, with the tin photo showing on a phone held up in the frame. Done when both signs, tin and real, are in one shot.
candidates.where: Chocolate Covered, 4069 24th St (between Noe & Castro). Open daily 10:30am–6:30pm.
candidates.time: 15–30 min (depends on the street you pick)
candidates.photo: A teammate under the real street sign, holding up a phone showing the same sign on its Chocolate Covered tin.
candidates.why_here: This one-man shop has printed some 50,000 San Francisco street-sign tins — pick well, because you have to go stand under the real one.

candidates.title: Unanimous on the 31% Leg-Burner
candidates.do: Walk up the single block of 22nd Street from Church Street to Vicksburg Street — at roughly 31.5% grade it's tied for the steepest street block in San Francisco, so steep the sidewalks are staircases. Every teammate counts the sidewalk steps silently on the way up. At the Vicksburg end, everyone says their number at the same instant. All match = complete. Any disagreement = count again on the way down, then say your numbers at the bottom.
candidates.where: 22nd St between Church St and Vicksburg St
candidates.photo: Everyone holding up the matching number at the top, the staircase-sidewalk dropping away behind.
candidates.why_here: The steepest block in Noe Valley is built as stairs, and a stair is the only hill you can count.

candidates.title: Farmers Market Yardstick *(Saturday only)*
candidates.do: At the Saturday farmers market on the Town Square (8am–1pm), buy one single fruit or vegetable that is LONGER than the longest shoe on your team, for $5 or less (leeks, daikon, and monster zucchini are your friends). Complete when the produce out-measures the shoe in a side-by-side photo.
candidates.where: Noe Valley Farmers Market, Town Square, 3861 24th St — Saturdays 8am–1pm only.
candidates.failable: no (keep hunting the stalls until something measures up)
candidates.photo: The vegetable lying next to the shoe on a Town Square bench, a teammate pointing at the winner.
candidates.why_here: The Saturday market is the neighborhood's weekly heartbeat — and the measuring ceremony is peak farmers-market silliness.

candidates.title: Victorian Bingo on the Side Streets
candidates.do: On Jersey and Elizabeth Streets between Church and Castro, photograph all three: a house painted in three or more colors, a gable with a carved sunburst or fan ornament, and a pair of "twin" Victorians — two adjacent houses with matching facades.
candidates.where: Jersey St and Elizabeth St between Church and Castro.
candidates.photo: The three-shot set; the twins make the keeper.
candidates.why_here: These blocks just off 24th are some of the best-preserved Victorian streetscapes in the city.

candidates.title: Spell CLIPPER
candidates.do: Noe Valley is home to Clipper Street — the game's namesake. Walk 24th Street and photograph the letters C, L, I, P, P, E, R, IN ORDER, each from a DIFFERENT sign, storefront, or poster (one letter per sign; the two P's must come from two different signs). Finish with the team under the Clipper Street sign at Clipper & Noe.
candidates.where: 24th St between Church and Diamond, then Clipper St & Noe St.
candidates.photo: The seven letter shots as a strip, plus the team saluting under the CLIPPER street sign.
candidates.why_here: You're playing Clipper Conquest; Noe Valley has Clipper Street. Some challenges write themselves.

North Beach.intro: The official Analysis Neighborhood is far bigger than "Little Italy": it runs from the Beat-era corner of Columbus & Broadway (City Lights, Jack Kerouac Alley) through Washington Square and over Telegraph Hill — Coit Tower, the wooden Filbert Steps, the wild parrots — all the way to the waterfront, where it swallows Fisherman's Wharf, Pier 45's Musée Mécanique, and the sea lions of Pier 39. Anchors below span all three zones: piazza, hill, and pier.
North Beach.why_chosen: Square to pier to summit: catch a coin thrown across Washington Square from the Ben Franklin statue, then the one-shot K-Dock Accord at Pier 39 (two silent counters, one chance to match), then get yourselves up Telegraph Hill to Coit Tower — the trio's pure "the place is the game" entry. One throw-and-catch, one high-stakes agreement, one climb; exactly one one-shot, zero strangers, $0, ≈ 40–55 minutes.

candidates.title: Washington's Coin Toss
candidates.do: Washington Square is named for George Washington, who, legend says, once threw a silver dollar clear across a river. One teammate, the thrower, stands right next to the Benjamin Franklin statue (the 1879 bronze on a granite fountain base) and throws a coin you got during the game to a teammate standing OFF the grass, on a sidewalk or path at least 20 big steps away. The catcher has to catch it in their hands before it touches anything. Dropped it, or it fell short? Find the coin and throw again. Only throw when nobody's in the way.
candidates.where: Benjamin Franklin statue, Washington Square (Columbus Ave between Filbert & Union).
candidates.failable: no (find the coin and throw again)
candidates.photo: The catch: the coin in the catcher's hand, the lawn between you and Franklin behind.
candidates.why_here: North Beach's front lawn is named for the president of the coin-throwing legend — and Franklin, the face on the $100 bill, gets to watch.

candidates.title: The K-Dock Accord
candidates.do: At Pier 39's K-Dock, the sea lions have squatted rent-free since 1989. Pick two counters. Standing apart at the rail, each silently counts every sea lion hauled out on the floats — no talking, no pointing, no comparing, and take as long as you like. Both write their number down hidden, then reveal at the same moment. The two counts must MATCH EXACTLY. They do = complete. They don't = failed. One try, ever.
candidates.where: Pier 39, west side marina (K-Dock viewing area — free, 24/7)
candidates.photo: The simultaneous reveal — two hands, two numbers, and the raft of judges lounging behind (matching or heartbreakingly off by one).
candidates.why_here: The famous freeloaders will not hold still while you count — getting two humans to agree about them is the real negotiation.

candidates.title: Get to Coit Tower
candidates.do: Get to Coit Tower. That's it — the hill is the challenge. Any route counts: the wooden Filbert Steps through the Grace Marchant Garden (recommended, and listen for the wild parrots), the Greenwich Steps, or the road if you must. Complete when the whole team stands at the tower's base.
candidates.where: Coit Tower, 1 Telegraph Hill Blvd, atop Telegraph Hill
candidates.photo: The team at the tower's fluted base, city and bay falling away behind.
candidates.why_here: Lillie Coit's 1933 tower is the neighborhood's exclamation point, and every way up Telegraph Hill earns it — this is the "the place is the game" entry.

candidates.title: Crime Scene at Coit Tower
candidates.do: Enter Coit Tower's free ground-floor mural lobby (no elevator ticket needed — the paid ride to the top is skippable and the historic elevator is often down anyway). In Victor Arnautoff's 1934 fresco "City Life," find three painted details: (a) the robbery in progress in the lower right, (b) the car accident in the center, and (c) the newsstand with its rack of periodicals. Complete when all three are found and photographed.
candidates.where: Coit Tower lobby, 1 Telegraph Hill Blvd (lobby free, open daily from 10am)
candidates.photo: A teammate pointing at the painted holdup while making their best shocked-witness face.
candidates.why_here: Depression-era WPA frescoes wrap Coit Tower's base, and Arnautoff hid an entire crime blotter inside his street scene — a free museum most tourists ride right past.

candidates.title: Sal's Orchestra
candidates.do: The Musée Mécanique (free entry) holds 300+ antique coin-operated machines, announced by Laffing Sal, the cackling 1930s funhouse giantess. Your task: with at most $3 in quarters per attempt, get THREE machines visibly running AT THE SAME TIME, captured in one continuous video pan — teammates fan out, coins drop in sequence, timing is everything (most machines run well under a minute). Sal counts as a machine. Blow the budget with no triple = attempt over; change machine is on site, try again.
candidates.where: Musée Mécanique, Pier 45 Shed A, foot of Taylor St (weekends 10am–8pm)
candidates.photo: Frame-grab of the triple: three antique machines mid-whir in one shot, conductor's arms raised.
candidates.why_here: One of the world's largest antique arcade collections lives free on a pier — it was always begging to be played as an orchestra.

candidates.title: Old-Timey Water with Ben Franklin
candidates.do: In Washington Square, find the 1879 Benjamin Franklin statue and complete three finds: (a) the old spigot labels on its temperance-fountain base (donor Henry Cogswell thought free water would beat demon drink), (b) the inscription about the time capsule buried beneath — to be reopened in 2079, and (c) the Volunteer Firemen memorial nearby, where teammates copy the bronze firefighters' exact poses. Complete when all three are photographed with the twin spires of Saints Peter & Paul Church in at least one shot.
candidates.where: Washington Square, Columbus Ave & Filbert St/Union St
candidates.photo: Teammates frozen in firefighter poses beside the bronze crew, church spires rising behind.
candidates.why_here: North Beach's living-room lawn hides a buried time capsule, a temperance fountain, and a statue paid for by Lillie Hitchcock Coit — the firefighter superfan whose tower watches from the hill above.

candidates.title: The Language of the Birds
candidates.do: At the corner of Broadway & Columbus, twenty-three sculpted books hang frozen in flight overhead — "Language of the Birds." Your task: photograph a REAL, live bird sharing the scene — perched on or flying among the book sculptures, or sitting on the wires and fixtures immediately around them. Complete when your photo shows at least one actual bird with the books in frame.
candidates.where: Language of the Birds plaza, northwest corner of Broadway & Columbus Ave (beside City Lights); outdoors, 24/7
candidates.failable: no (patience — this corner is rarely pigeonless for long)
candidates.photo: A live bird upstaging the sculpture it inspired, flock of books overhead.
candidates.why_here: A public artwork about birds, judged complete only by an actual bird — the Beats would have approved of the collaboration.

Oceanview/Merced/Ingleside.intro: The OMI — Oceanview, Merced Heights, Ingleside — is San Francisco's sunny-name, foggy-reality southern edge: steep residential hills rising south of Ocean Avenue. Ocean Avenue's south side is its main street: Beep's Burgers has flown its neon rocket sign since 1962, Chase Luck sells buns for about a dollar, and Amos Goldbaum's purple streetcar mural faces the K Ingleside tracks down the middle of the street (the north side, City College, and Ingleside Terraces with its racetrack oval and giant sundial fall outside this map's line). Uphill, Merced Heights hides two summits most San Franciscans never find — the Lakeview & Ashton rocky outcrop, with a 360-degree view out to the Farallones, and Brooks Park's hilltop community garden — and Ocean View Park's rec center honors Minnie and Lovie Ward, the neighbors who won it back. We anchored on Ocean Avenue's streetcars and shakes and the secret hilltops.
Oceanview/Merced/Ingleside.why_chosen: Climb the hidden summit where Oceanview finally gets its ocean view, split a milkshake under Beep's 1962 neon rocket, and name the food plants on Brooks Park's secret farm hill. A summit, a shake, a garden hunt; nothing failable, zero strangers, ~$8, ≈ 35–50 minutes.

candidates.title: An Ocean View in Oceanview
candidates.do: The neighborhood is named Ocean View — go find one. Climb Lakeview & Ashton Mini Park, a half-acre knob of Franciscan sandstone also called the Orizaba Rocky Outcrop, by its short dirt trails to the summit rocks. The 360-degree view runs from Sutro Tower and Mount Davidson to San Bruno Mountain and, on a clear day, the Pacific and the Farallon Islands. Complete when the whole team is on the summit rocks in one selfie; if the Pacific is visible, get it in the frame. Stay on the trails — the native wildflowers are the point.
candidates.where: Lakeview & Ashton Mini Park (Orizaba Rocky Outcrop); enter from Orizaba Ave, Shields St or Lakeview Ave
candidates.photo: The whole team on the summit rocks, the Pacific (or the fog) behind.
candidates.why_here: A hidden sandstone summit most San Franciscans have never heard of, and the spot where Oceanview's name finally comes true.

candidates.title: Milkshake at the 1962 Burger Beacon
candidates.do: Go to Beep's Burgers, the drive-in-style burger stand feeding Ocean Avenue since 1962 under a neon rocket-ship sign (open weekend daytimes: Sat from 10am, Sun from 11am). Buy ONE milkshake (the menu lists vanilla, chocolate, strawberry, Oreo and Twinkie). Every teammate must take a sip. Complete when the shake is bought and everyone has sipped.
candidates.where: Beep's Burgers, 1051 Ocean Ave (south side, near Frida Kahlo Way / City College)
candidates.photo: the whole team crowded around one shake under Beep's neon rocket sign
candidates.why_here: A 60-plus-year-old walk-up burger stand, named for the beep of Space Age satellites, is the Ocean Avenue institution — teens line up for these shakes.

candidates.title: Summit the Secret Farm Hill
candidates.do: Climb to Brooks Park (entrance at 400 Shields St), the hilltop park on Merced Heights with an acre of community-garden plots and views to the Pacific. From the public paths, find and photograph 4 DIFFERENT food plants actually growing (vegetables, fruits, or herbs) and name each one in your claim. Finish with a team photo at the hilltop. Complete = 4 named plant photos + summit team photo.
candidates.where: Brooks Park, 400 Shields St (at Victoria Ave), Merced Heights
candidates.photo: team at the hilltop garden with the best plant find held up for the camera (not picked — pointed at!), ocean haze behind
candidates.why_here: A working farm-garden on one of SF's southwesternmost hilltops — the "Oceanview" view most San Franciscans have never seen.

candidates.title: Streetcar Meets Streetcar
candidates.do: The front of the Auto 280 repair shop at 1315 Ocean Ave is Amos Goldbaum's purple line-drawing mural "Ocean Avenue North & South" — and it has streetcars in it: a 1970s K Ingleside on the left panel, a 1930s car on the right. The real K runs down the middle of Ocean Avenue right in front. Capture ONE photo that contains a real K streetcar and at least one painted streetcar from the mural. Trains come every 10–15 minutes on weekends, so scout your angle while you wait. Shoot from the sidewalk — never from the trackway.
candidates.where: Auto 280 mural, 1315 Ocean Ave (south side, just west of Plymouth Ave)
candidates.photo: The shot itself — a real K and a painted streetcar in one frame, team optional in the foreground.
candidates.why_here: The K Ingleside rolls right past a mural of its own ancestors; only on Ocean Avenue can the two share a frame.

candidates.title: The Blind Bun
candidates.do: Chase Luck Bakery sells dim sum and Chinese buns for about a dollar apiece (listed open 7am–6pm). The taster waits outside with eyes closed. The buyer rolls a random number 1–5 on a phone and buys that bun: 1 BBQ pork, 2 egg custard, 3 red bean, 4 lotus paste, 5 taro (sold out? re-roll). Outside, the taster — eyes still closed — takes one bite and names the filling from that list. Right = complete. Wrong = wait five minutes, then the buyer rolls again and buys another bun.
candidates.where: Chase Luck Bakery, 1325 Ocean Ave (south side, just west of Plymouth Ave)
candidates.failable: retryable (wrong = a five-minute wait and another bun)
candidates.photo: The taster mid-bite, eyes shut, the filling showing, Chase Luck's storefront behind.
candidates.why_here: An Ocean Avenue dim sum counter where a bun costs about a dollar — cheap enough to guess wrong.

candidates.title: Rec Center Charades
candidates.do: Ocean View Park's rec center is named for Minnie and Lovie Ward, the neighbors who led the fight to take it back from drug dealers; today its schedule runs from pickleball to tai chi. On the park lawn, one teammate, the director, rolls a random number 1–8 on a phone and whispers that activity to the actor: 1 basketball, 2 pickleball, 3 volleyball, 4 table tennis, 5 Zumba, 6 tai chi, 7 line dancing, 8 karate (re-roll repeats). The actor mimes it — no sound, no props. The rest of the team gets ONE guess. Right = new actor, new roll. Wrong = the streak restarts. Complete when the team guesses three in a row.
candidates.where: Ocean View Park lawn, Minnie & Lovie Ward Rec Center, 650 Capitol Ave
candidates.failable: no (the streak restarts until you hit three)
candidates.photo: The actor mid-mime on the lawn, the rec center behind.
candidates.why_here: Every activity on the list is on the program of the rec center Minnie and Lovie Ward won back for Oceanview.

Outer Mission.intro: San Francisco's bottom edge: the Mission Street corridor rolling downhill to the Daly City line, with Cayuga Terrace and the Crocker-Amazon blocks around it (the official Analysis Neighborhood folds Crocker-Amazon and Mission Terrace in; note that Crocker Amazon Playground itself sits in the McLaren Park polygon, so nothing here depends on it). It's a working-class Filipino and Latino neighborhood with BART thundering overhead on elevated tracks, a hidden forest of 375+ hand-carved folk-art sculptures by park gardener Demetrio Braceros, a yard full of vintage streetcars, and the literal end of San Francisco.
Outer Mission.why_chosen: Hunt the hand-carved sculptures in Cayuga Park's secret forest, share a sweet from the bakeries at the south end of Mission St, and catch a BART train overhead in a team selfie under the viaduct. A find, a treat, a selfie; nothing failable, zero strangers, ~$5, ≈ 35–45 minutes.

candidates.title: Sculpture Safari in the Secret Forest
candidates.do: In Cayuga Park, find and photograph FIVE different hand-carved wooden sculptures by Demetrio Braceros — at least one animal and at least one person among them (he carved everyone from Adam and Eve to John Lennon).
candidates.where: Cayuga Park, Cayuga Ave at Naglee Ave.
candidates.photo: Five carving shots; the keeper is a teammate beside their favorite.
candidates.why_here: A retired gardener spent years carving a hidden forest of folk-art sculptures in a park under the BART tracks — nothing else like it exists in SF.

candidates.title: Pan Dulce at the End of the Line
candidates.do: Buy any sweet baked treat for under $5 from a bakery or donut shop on Mission St between Geneva Ave and the Daly City line (reliable weekend-daytime picks, side by side: Panadería Tikal at 5099 Mission, a Guatemalan bakery, and Western Donuts at 5101 Mission, an old-school donut counter — both open early, daily). Every teammate must take a bite. Complete = purchase made + all-bites photo evidence.
