candidates.where: Mission St, 5000–5900 blocks (Geneva Ave south to the county line).
candidates.photo: The treat held up in front of the shop sign, then the team mid-bite.
candidates.why_here: The Outer Mission's stretch of Mission St is a genuine everyday Latino/Filipino corridor — pan dulce and 5 a.m. donuts, zero tourists.

candidates.title: BART Overhead
candidates.do: Cayuga Park runs right under the elevated BART tracks. From the park's meadow or paths, take a team selfie with a BART train passing directly overhead on the viaduct. Done when the selfie shows the team and a train above you.
candidates.where: Cayuga Playground meadow/paths, Cayuga Ave & Naglee Ave, under the BART viaduct.
candidates.photo: The team selfie with a BART train roaring along the viaduct overhead.
candidates.why_here: Cayuga is the rare park built directly under BART's elevated tracks — the trains ARE the scenery, so make them the game.

candidates.title: Find the Edge of San Francisco
candidates.do: Somewhere on Mission Street south of Geneva, San Francisco ends and Daly City begins — and the sidewalk mostly doesn't tell you. Phones away. Walk south and figure out, from clues alone (street-sign styles, house-number jumps, whose trash cans line the curb, any sign you spot), exactly where the city line crosses Mission Street. When the team agrees, plant a shoe on the line and take the photo. Then — and only then — check a map: within one block of the real line = complete. Off = failed; the map has spoiled it.
candidates.where: Mission St, 5000–5900 blocks (Geneva Ave south to the county line).
candidates.photo: A shoe on the guessed line, one teammate on each "side," the map check held up beside it.
candidates.why_here: This neighborhood is where San Francisco literally ends; in a game about conquering SF territory, finding the last inch of the map by deduction is the point.

candidates.title: Streetcar Time Machine
candidates.do: From the public sidewalk at Geneva & San Jose Aves, photograph BOTH (a) a vintage streetcar (old rounded PCC-style car, not a modern Muni train) parked in Muni's Cameron Beach Yard, and (b) the 1901 brick Geneva Car Barn & Powerhouse across from the yard. One photo or two; both targets must be identifiable.
candidates.where: Geneva Ave at San Jose Ave, beside Balboa Park BART. Muni stores its historic F-line streetcars in an open shelter here, visible from the sidewalk; the Powerhouse is the arched-window brick landmark on the corner.
candidates.photo: Team pointing at a rainbow-liveried vintage streetcar through the fence, 1901 powerhouse in frame.
candidates.why_here: This corner has run streetcars since 1901 — a National Register powerhouse next to the shed where SF's antique fleet sleeps on weekends.

Outer Richmond.intro: Foggy avenues that end at the Pacific: the northern stretch of Ocean Beach, the village-y Balboa Street theater block, and the whole Point Lobos headland — Cliff House, Camera Obscura, Sutro Heights, AND the Sutro Baths ruins, all of which sit inside Outer Richmond on the official Analysis Neighborhoods map (census tract 479.04; the Lincoln Park neighborhood only begins east of Lands End, at the Legion of Honor/Eagle's Point). Anchors: a ruined Victorian mega-bathhouse, a building shaped like a camera, stone lions guarding a lost millionaire's garden, a 100-year-old movie palace, and the ghost of Playland-at-the-Beach.
Outer Richmond.why_chosen: Three stops at the edge of the city: inside the rock tunnel at the Sutro Baths ruins, on the sand of Ocean Beach, and between the stone lions at the gate of Sutro Heights Park. All three are just getting there; nothing failable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 30–40 minutes.

candidates.title: Through the Sutro Tunnel
candidates.do: Descend to the Sutro Baths ruins (stairs from the Lands End/Merrie Way lot or the trail from Point Lobos Ave) and find the rock tunnel at the north end of the ruins. Done when the whole team is inside the tunnel. Stay on the trail and in the tunnel — never on the wet rocks by the water.
candidates.where: Sutro Baths ruins, Point Lobos Ave & Merrie Way (below Lands End Lookout).
candidates.photo: Team silhouetted in the tunnel mouth with the ocean crashing behind — one of the best natural photo frames in San Francisco.
candidates.why_here: The ruins of the world's largest indoor swimming establishment are THE Outer Richmond landmark (and yes — the official map puts them in this neighborhood, not Lincoln Park).

candidates.title: Ocean Beach
candidates.do: Get down onto the sand at Ocean Beach, where the city runs out of land. Done when the whole team is on the beach. Nobody goes into the surf.
candidates.where: Ocean Beach — beach access at Balboa St & Great Highway (or anywhere along the Great Highway).
candidates.photo: The team on the sand with the Pacific behind you.
candidates.why_here: The whole Outer Richmond runs west until it hits this beach — the edge of the continent, a bus ride from downtown.

candidates.title: The Sutro Lions
candidates.do: Go to the gate of Sutro Heights Park, flanked by two stone lions (copies of Trafalgar Square's). Done when the whole team is standing between the lions.
candidates.where: Sutro Heights Park, entrance at 48th Ave & Point Lobos Ave. Free, open dawn to dusk.
candidates.photo: The team between the two stone lions at the Sutro Heights gate.
candidates.why_here: Adolph Sutro's clifftop estate is the Outer Richmond's secret garden, and its lions have guarded the gate since the 1880s.

candidates.title: Step Inside a Giant Camera
candidates.do: At the Camera Obscura — a 1946 building literally shaped like a giant camera — pay admission (~$3/person, cash) and go inside. The whole team (or at least two teammates if it's crowded) must watch the live rotating image of Seal Rocks and the surf projected onto the parabolic viewing table. Complete when you've seen the image sweep past Seal Rocks.
candidates.where: 1096 Point Lobos Ave, on the terrace behind the Cliff House building.
candidates.failable: no — but it's a weather-permitting venue (typically open daily incl. weekends 11am–5pm; call 415-750-0415). Confirm it's open before committing; if shuttered by fog/storm, pick a different challenge.
candidates.photo: Team posed in front of the camera-shaped building so the giant "CAMERA OBSCURA" lettering reads across the frame — you standing "inside a camera."
candidates.why_here: A walk-in Victorian optical instrument on a cliff is the neighborhood's weirdest survivor — one of the last pieces of the old Cliff House amusement era.

candidates.title: Marquee Scrabble at the Balboa
candidates.do: The Balboa Theatre opened in 1926 and turns 100 this year. Stand under its marquee and use ONLY the letters currently showing on it (movie titles and showtimes) — each letter as many times as it appears up there, no more — to spell one English word of at least SEVEN letters. Write it down and photograph it next to the marquee. Complete when a seven-letter word is spelled from marquee letters only.
candidates.where: Balboa Theatre, 3630 Balboa St (between 37th & 38th Ave), the heart of the Balboa Village shopping block.
candidates.photo: The word written on a phone, held up under the marquee it came from.
candidates.why_here: A neighborhood movie palace hitting exactly 100 years old in 2026 — its marquee is the block's biggest word puzzle.

candidates.title: Eat History: An It's-It Where It Was Born
candidates.do: The It's-It ice cream sandwich was invented in 1928 by George Whitney at Playland-at-the-Beach — the amusement park that ran along Ocean Beach between Balboa and Fulton until 1972 — and for 40+ years you could ONLY buy one there. Buy It's-Its (~$3 each, one to split per 2–3 players is fine) at the Safeway at 850 La Playa St, a block from the old Playland grounds, then walk to the Great Highway sidewalk between Balboa and Fulton — Playland's actual footprint — and have every teammate take a bite standing where the park stood.
candidates.where: Safeway, 850 La Playa St (at Fulton), then Great Highway between Balboa & Fulton. Grocery store: reliably open all weekend, all day.
candidates.photo: Team mid-bite, wrappers up, with the Great Highway/Ocean Beach behind — eating a 1928 invention on the spot it was invented.
candidates.why_here: Playland's rides are gone, but its dessert never left San Francisco; this is the only neighborhood where eating one is a history lesson.

Pacific Heights.intro: San Francisco's mansion district: a ridge of Gilded Age palaces, two hilltop parks with knockout bay views, and the city's most famous residential staircase, all bookended by the boutiques of upper Fillmore Street. This is where movies come to film rich-people SF — the Mrs. Doubtfire house, the What's Up, Doc? stair chase — so the challenges lean on climbing, movie lore, and gawking-from-the-sidewalk (every mansion here is a private home; everything below stays on public sidewalks and park paths). Anchors: the Lyon Street Steps, Alta Plaza and Lafayette parks, outer Broadway's "Gold Coast," and Fillmore between Jackson and California.
Pacific Heights.why_chosen: Predict the foot traffic on one step of the Lyon Street Steps (guess, count five minutes, retry until you nail it), send two counters up the *What's Up, Doc?* staircase at Alta Plaza until their numbers match, and solve today's Wordle under the witch's cap of the Haas–Lilienthal House. An estimation game, an agreement game, a word puzzle; the Wordle is the neighborhood's one one-shot, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 30–40 minutes. (The Fillmore price ladder stays the alternate.)

candidates.title: The Stair Oracle of Lyon Street
candidates.do: Pick any one step of the Lyon Street Steps and stand where you can watch it. Before you start, the team agrees on a guess: how many people will set foot on that step in the next five minutes? Write the guess down and photograph it, then start a five-minute timer and count every person (teammates don't count). Complete when your guess is within 3 of the true count (or within 10%, whichever is more generous). Missed? Pick a new number — or a new step — and run another five minutes; you know the traffic now.
candidates.where: Lyon Street Steps, Lyon St between Green St (bottom) and Broadway (top)
candidates.failable: no (retry as many five-minute rounds as you like)
candidates.photo: The guess note held up next to the final tally, the chosen step behind you, with the Palace of Fine Arts dome and the bay in the distance — bonus points (moral only) for the heart sculpture in the stairway garden if it's in residence.
candidates.why_here: SF's most manicured staircase — roughly 300 steps of hedges and bay views on the neighborhood's western edge, the local fitness pilgrimage — is also one of the city's busiest, so the count is a real game.

candidates.title: Count the Chase Steps
candidates.do: Alta Plaza Park's grand terraced staircase on the Clay Street side (at Pierce) is the one four cars famously crashed down in the 1972 *What's Up, Doc?* chase, filmed without permission. Count it: two teammates are the counters. They climb from the sidewalk to the top terrace at the same time, each counting every step silently — no talking, no fingers. At the top, both say their number at the same instant. A match = complete. A mismatch = recount together on the way down and say your numbers again at the bottom. (The chipped step edges the stunt cars left are still there — spotting one is bragging rights, not required.)
candidates.where: Alta Plaza Park, south stairs at Clay St & Pierce St
candidates.failable: no (recount up or down until the two counters agree)
candidates.photo: The two counters holding up matching numbers on the top terrace, downtown skyline behind.
candidates.why_here: The stunt that damaged these exact steps changed SF film-permitting forever — and the staircase is just long enough that two counts rarely agree the first time.

candidates.title: The Witch's Wordle
candidates.do: Find the gray 1886 Queen Anne Victorian at 2007 Franklin St — the Haas–Lilienthal House, with a corner tower topped by a pointed "witch's cap" roof. Standing under the turret, play today's Wordle (the free New York Times puzzle, on a phone) as a team: six guesses to find the five-letter word, confer all you like, no looking anything up. Get the word = complete. Six misses = failed, no retry. Nobody who has already played today's Wordle may help, so don't play it before the game.
candidates.where: 2007 Franklin St (between Washington & Jackson) — sidewalk only, no tour required
candidates.photo: The solved grid held up under the witch's cap — or the six gray rows of heartbreak.
candidates.why_here: The only intact Victorian home in SF open as a museum, wearing a witch's hat — the one place in the city where you'd go to divine a secret word.

candidates.title: Pace the Great Hedge
candidates.do: Stand at the summit of Lafayette Park (the hilltop lawn) and look across Washington St at the towering street-side hedge hiding the white Spreckels Mansion (2080 Washington St). Before anyone moves, the team agrees on ONE guess: how many of your tallest teammate's paces will it take to walk from this spot to touch the hedge? Write it down. Then that teammate walks it, normal stride, everyone counting out loud, by the park paths and the crosswalk — no shortcuts across flowerbeds. Within 10% of the guess = complete. Off? Pick a new target visible from the hedge (a lamppost, the park gate, a tree) and pace that one.
candidates.where: Lafayette Park summit (enter near Washington & Gough/Octavia), then the sidewalk at the Spreckels Mansion hedge on Washington St
candidates.failable: no (new target until a guess lands)
candidates.photo: The pacer's hand on the hedge, the guess and the real count held up side by side.
candidates.why_here: SF's most gossiped-about hedge hides its grandest mansion, directly across from the neighborhood's summit park — the perfect ruler.

candidates.title: Price Ladder on Fillmore
candidates.do: Inside any one shop on Upper Fillmore (Mollie Stone's at 2435 California St is the easy pick; a toy or gift shop works too), one teammate — the shopper — quietly gathers FIVE different items, hiding their price tags, and sets them in a row. The team must arrange them from cheapest to priciest. Lock in the order, then the shopper reveals the prices. All five in the right order = complete. Any swap = the shopper returns them and picks five new items (buy a snack on the way out if you like — not required). Be tidy and quick; put everything back where it came from.
candidates.where: Upper Fillmore St shops, roughly Jackson St to Pine St (Mollie Stone's is at California & Fillmore).
candidates.failable: no (five new items until the ladder is right)
candidates.photo: The five items in their final order, tags revealed, team behind.
candidates.why_here: Upper Fillmore is the neighborhood's main street, and its price tags are Pacific Heights' best-kept joke — guess which is the $14 candle.

candidates.title: Five-Word Mansion on the Gold Coast
candidates.do: Walk the 2800 block of Broadway (between Broderick and Baker), the heart of Billionaires' Row. One teammate, the describer, secretly picks any house on the block and describes it in EXACTLY five words — no address numbers, no colors of the front door read from the sidewalk plaque, just five words. The team points at the house on their first pick. Right = the next teammate describes. Wrong = new house, streak restarts. Complete when the team gets three in a row. Sidewalk only; every one of these is a private home.
candidates.where: Broadway, 2800 block (Broderick St to Baker St), the outer Broadway "Gold Coast"
candidates.failable: no (the streak restarts until you hit three)
candidates.photo: The describer's five words on a phone held up in front of the found house.
candidates.why_here: The most expensive block of houses in the city, and every one is trying to look different — five words should do it.

Portola.intro: SF's official Garden District: a century ago ~20 family nurseries here grew most of the city's flowers, and the last redwood-and-glass greenhouses of the "Rose Factory" still stand in ruins at 770 Woolsey. Today the neighborhood pours that heritage into art — a garden-mural trail along the San Bruno Avenue dim-sum-and-produce strip, and The Green Between, a neighbor-built greenway on old Caltrans land complete with a Gothic gate welded from garden tools and a half-buried 1969 Dodge. I anchored on the greenway, the ghost greenhouses, and the strip.
Portola.why_chosen: Walk through the gate made of garden tools on the Green Between, match painted produce on San Bruno Ave's murals to the real thing in its shops, and find the garter snake hidden in the gateway mural under the freeway. A find, a match, a hunt; nothing failable, zero strangers, $0, ≈ 30–45 minutes.

candidates.title: The Gate Made of Garden Tools
candidates.do: Enter The Green Between greenway and find artist Dana Albany's 16-foot Gothic metal gate, welded entirely from old tools and hardware. In the gate itself, locate all four of: a hammer, a faucet, a gear, and any garden tool (trowel, shears, rake...). Then walk the greenway until you find the car half-buried nose-down in the ground (a 1969 Dodge Coronet). Complete when you've photographed both.
candidates.where: The Green Between — the greenway strip between San Bruno Ave and the 101 sound wall; enter at the Burrows St end (Burrows St just east of San Bruno Ave).
candidates.photo: Team posed with the half-buried Dodge, plus one shot of a teammate's finger on each of the four objects found in the gate (a 4-tile collage counts).
candidates.why_here: A cathedral gate built from the Garden District's own tools, on a park the neighbors built themselves — it exists nowhere else in SF.

candidates.title: Painted to Real
candidates.do: San Bruno Ave wears its garden history on its walls: "Portola Gardens" is painted on San Bruno Market (2480 San Bruno) and "Portola Blossoms" on the Hawaiian Drive-Inn (2600 San Bruno). Pick any fruit, vegetable or flower painted in either mural, then find the REAL thing for sale inside a shop on the same street and photograph the two side by side (painted on one phone, real in hand). Complete with two matches from two different murals. Buying is optional.
candidates.where: 2444–2600 San Bruno Ave (about 3 blocks).
candidates.photo: A painted tomato beside a real one.
candidates.why_here: These murals were painted to tell Portola's nursery history; the produce markets on the same block still sell the subject matter.

candidates.title: Snake at the Gateway
candidates.do: Hidden somewhere in the mural on the freeway-gateway art island is the endangered San Francisco garter snake — often called the most beautiful snake in North America — tucked into the painted grass among flowers and butterflies. Find it and photograph a teammate pointing right at it. No hints from anyone who's already seen it.
candidates.where: The Portola's freeway-gateway art island: the painted support pillar where San Bruno Ave meets Alemany Blvd under US-101 (the northeast entrance to the Portola).
candidates.photo: A finger on the painted snake, butterflies all around it.
candidates.why_here: An endangered local snake hiding in a mural at the neighborhood's front door — a real-life "Where's Waldo."

candidates.title: Garden District Blind Touch
candidates.do: At any market on San Bruno Ave (San Bruno Market, 2480 San Bruno, is the classic), one teammate — the shopper — goes in alone, counts along the produce display, and buys whatever sits in the 3rd, 8th and 13th bins (skip a repeat or anything over $2; take the next bin), $5 total max, keeping them hidden in the bag. Outside, a teammate closes their eyes and is handed the items one at a time: they may touch, squeeze and smell, but not look or taste. Name all three correctly = complete. Any miss = the shopper reshuffles and a new teammate takes the test — one attempt per teammate. When everyone has missed, the shopper buys three new items and the round starts over. Eat the evidence afterward.
candidates.where: San Bruno Ave commercial strip (2400–2600 blocks).
candidates.failable: no (one attempt per teammate per bag; a new bag costs money)
candidates.photo: An eyes-closed teammate mid-squeeze of a mystery vegetable; bonus style if the "Welcome to the Portola — Garden District" sign (San Bruno & Silliman) is behind.
candidates.why_here: The Portola literally fed and flowered SF — identifying its produce blind is the neighborhood's own quiz.

candidates.title: Bottle Flip Under the Marquee
candidates.do: Stand beneath the restored neon marquee of the 1927 Art Deco Avenue Theater — the neighborhood's old movie palace, whose sign (99 pieces of glass) neighbors fought years to relight. Flip a partly-filled water bottle (any size, about a third full) and land it standing upright on the sidewalk. Every teammate must land one. A miss = flip again; unlimited tries.
candidates.where: Avenue Theater, 2650 San Bruno Ave (sidewalk).
candidates.photo: The bottle standing, "AVENUE" glowing above it.
candidates.why_here: The Avenue is San Bruno Ave's Art Deco crown jewel — landed under lights, like a premiere.

candidates.title: Birds on the Ghost Greenhouses
candidates.do: San Francisco's last surviving commercial greenhouses — the 1922 Garibaldi family "Rose Factory" — stand as beautiful ruins behind a fence on Woolsey St. From the sidewalk, before anyone studies the frames, the team agrees on ONE guess: how many birds will land on or fly through the greenhouse frames in the next FIVE minutes? Write it down, start the clock, and count together (do not enter the fenced site). Within 2 = complete. Off? Call the next five minutes.
candidates.where: 770 Woolsey St (the full block around Woolsey at Bowdoin St, University Mound); pick the sidewalk with the clearest sightline through the fence.
candidates.photo: The guess and tally with the redwood-and-glass frames behind the fence.
candidates.why_here: This one block IS why Portola is the Garden District; the ruins are its most astonishing "wait, that exists?" sight, and the birds have moved in.

Potrero Hill.intro: Sunny, village-y hill where nearly every north–south street is named for a US state, goats once grazed the slopes (hence "Goat Hill"), and the north face drops straight toward the downtown skyline. Anchored on: the Vermont Street switchbacks at McKinley Square (the "other Lombard" — verified inside the official Analysis Neighborhood boundary: the 101 freeway line crosses Vermont only at the very bottom near 22nd, so the curves themselves are in-bounds), the 18th Street commercial strip, and the postcard skyline views from the hilltop parks.
Potrero Hill.why_chosen: Walk down Vermont Street's hairpins, find six state-named street signs with no map, and call how many people walk through Farley's door in three minutes. A walk, a no-phone hunt, a called shot; nothing failable, zero strangers, ~$5, ≈ 30–40 minutes. (The "Hill" book hunt at Christopher's and Four Bases in a Row are alternates.)

candidates.title: Crookeder Than Lombard?
candidates.do: Start at the top of Vermont Street's curves at McKinley Square (20th & Vermont, where the "trucks not advised" sign marks the drop) and walk down alongside the switchbacks as a team, on the sidewalk, never in the roadway. Done when the whole team reaches the last curve (don't continue to 22nd St under the freeway — that sliver is out of the neighborhood). Fun fact to argue on the way down: the Travel Channel measured Vermont's sinuosity at 1.56 vs Lombard's 1.2 — locals say this WPA 1930s street is the real crookedest street in San Francisco.
candidates.where: Vermont St between 20th St (McKinley Square) and the bottom of the curves, west edge of Potrero Hill
candidates.photo: The team mid-switchback, the serpentine curves and tree canopy snaking downhill behind you.
candidates.why_here: Potrero Hill's proudest claim: its crooked street out-crookeds the famous one — without a single tourist bus.

candidates.title: State Street Sweep
candidates.do: Potrero Hill's north–south streets are almost all named for US states. Phones away — no maps. Photograph your team under SIX different state-named street signs (Texas, Missouri, Connecticut, Arkansas, Wisconsin, Carolina, Rhode Island, Kansas, Vermont, Utah, Mississippi, Pennsylvania...). De Haro and San Bruno don't count.
candidates.where: Along or just off the 18th Street strip.
candidates.photo: Six state-sign shots; the keeper is the team pointing up at one of them.
candidates.why_here: A whole hill of streets named for the states — half of them within a few blocks of each other.

candidates.title: Door Count at Farley's
candidates.do: At Farley's (1315 18th St, "Serving Coffee & Community" since 1989), buy any drink — hot chocolate or steamed milk counts (~$5) — and take a seat with a view of the door. Before the clock starts, the team agrees on ONE guess: how many people will walk in through that door in the next THREE minutes? Count together. Within 2 = complete. Off? Call the next three.
candidates.where: Farley's, 1315 18th St (between Missouri & Texas).
candidates.photo: The tally sheet beside the drink, the door in the background.
candidates.why_here: Potrero's 1989 coffeehouse is the hill's living room, and nobody knows how full it gets on a Saturday until they sit and count.

candidates.title: Blind Slice at Goat Hill
candidates.do: Go to Goat Hill Pizza at 18th & Connecticut (open daily from 11am) — named for Potrero Hill's original nickname, from the goats that grazed here. Buy two slices with clearly different toppings (≤$10 total). Outside, a teammate closes their eyes and is handed one bite of each in a secret order; they must say which slice is which. Right = complete. Wrong = new taster, re-shuffle — one attempt per teammate, and when the slices run out, so do the attempts: buy two more or mark it failed.
candidates.where: Goat Hill Pizza, 300 Connecticut St at 18th St.
candidates.failable: retryable (one attempt per teammate per pair of slices)
candidates.photo: Eyes shut, mid-bite, the Goat Hill sign behind.
candidates.why_here: The hill's namesake pizzeria, and the tastiest sense test in the game.

candidates.title: Hill Hunt at Christopher's Books
candidates.do: Inside Christopher's Books, the tiny corner bookshop at 18th & Missouri, find a book with the word "Hill" in its title. No phones, no asking the staff — shelf logic only.
candidates.where: Christopher's Books, 1400 18th St at Missouri (open Sat 10–8, Sun 10–6).
candidates.photo: The book held up at the shop's corner entrance.
candidates.why_here: A one-room neighborhood treasure on the hill — browse politely.

candidates.title: Four Bases in a Row
candidates.do: At the Potrero Hill Recreation Center ballfield (Arkansas & 22nd), with the downtown skyline behind the outfield, play catch the Little League way: one teammate stands on the pitcher's mound and must throw a ball (bring one, or buy a cheap one on 18th St) to a teammate standing on first, then second, then third, then home — four clean catches in a row. Any drop = start again from first. Team of two: the catcher runs to the next base between throws.
candidates.where: Potrero Hill Rec Center, 801 Arkansas St (public field; wait out any game in progress).
candidates.photo: The throw to home, Salesforce Tower standing behind the backstop.
candidates.why_here: The ballfield with the best skyline backdrop in the city.

Presidio.intro: The Presidio is the only neighborhood on the board that's an entire national park: a 218-year-old Army post turned playground, with a Lucasfilm campus, giant Andy Goldsworthy sculptures growing out of the forest, a working Civil War fort under the Golden Gate Bridge, and a soldier-built pet cemetery under a freeway viaduct. Note: Crissy Field is inside this neighborhood — the Marina Analysis Neighborhood ends at Lyon Street, and everything west of it (Letterman, Tunnel Tops, Crissy Field, Fort Point) is Presidio turf. The park is huge, so all six candidates cluster along the walkable Letterman–Main Post–Crissy corridor (plus one at Fort Point on the west end).
Presidio.why_chosen: Stand under the Golden Gate Bridge at Fort Point, send one teammate twenty logs along Goldsworthy's Wood Line, and fly a paper plane 20 yards over the Army's old Crissy Field airstrip. A landmark, a balance walk, a flight with five throws; zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 40–50 minutes. (Yoda, the egg toss and the pet cemetery are alternates.)

candidates.title: Under the Bridge (Literally)
candidates.do: Go to Fort Point, the 1861 brick fort at the very foot of the Golden Gate Bridge, and stand with the bridge directly overhead. Done when the whole team is there under the span.
candidates.where: Fort Point National Historic Site, end of Marine Drive, directly beneath the bridge's south anchorage. Open Friday–Sunday, 10 AM–5 PM year-round — a safe bet for a weekend game, but check it's not a holiday closure day.
candidates.photo: The team pointing straight up, the underside of the Golden Gate Bridge filling the sky above you.
candidates.why_here: Fort Point is the only place in the world where you can stand on an 1861 brick fortress while the Golden Gate Bridge arches directly over your head.

candidates.title: Walk the (Wood) Line
candidates.do: Find Andy Goldsworthy's *Wood Line*, a 1,200-foot serpentine line of eucalyptus logs snaking through the cypress grove. One teammate must walk TWENTY consecutive logs without stepping off (arms out for balance — no holding hands). Step off = start the twenty over, and anyone can take the next try. Complete with one clean twenty.
candidates.where: Off Lovers' Lane near Presidio Blvd & W Pacific Ave.
candidates.photo: The walker balanced on the curving line, arms out like a tightrope walker, the team counting logs behind.
candidates.why_here: A land-art sculpture you're allowed to balance on — Goldsworthy's line was always meant to be walked.

candidates.title: Crissy Field Flight School
candidates.do: Crissy Field was the Army's 1920s airfield — time for your team's first flight. Fold one paper airplane from paper you get during the game (a flyer, a map, a receipt), then launch it from the Crissy Field grass airstrip or East Beach lawn. Success = a single throw that flies at least 20 yards (about 20 big steps; pace it off from launch spot to landing spot). You get 5 throws total, any teammates, any folds; tip — throw with the wind. Mark complete on a qualifying flight, failed after 5 unsuccessful throws.
candidates.where: Crissy Field East Beach / airfield lawn, off Mason Street (inside the Presidio — Marina territory doesn't start until Lyon Street).
candidates.failable: retryable (each throw is an attempt; 5 attempts max)
candidates.photo: The paper airplane mid-flight (or triumphantly at its landing spot) with the Golden Gate Bridge in the background, pilot mid-follow-through.
candidates.why_here: Crissy Field hosted historic first flights as a 1920s Army airfield; the restored grass airstrip is still right there under the bridge.

candidates.title: Yoda Paparazzi Count
candidates.do: Find the Yoda Fountain outside Lucasfilm's headquarters. Before you're close enough to see who's around it, the team agrees on ONE guess: how many people (not counting your team) will take a photo of Yoda in the next TEN minutes? Write it down, then sit on the low wall and count — a phone or camera pointed at the statue counts, each person once. Within 2 of the true count = complete. Off? Call the next ten.
candidates.where: Yoda Fountain, One Letterman Drive (Letterman Digital Arts Center, just inside the Lombard Gate at Lombard & Lyon). The fountain is outdoors and accessible anytime — don't count on the lobby, which is weekdays-only.
candidates.photo: The tally sheet held up beside the bronze Yoda, a stranger's camera raised behind.
candidates.why_here: Lucasfilm's world headquarters is in the Presidio, and Yoda has presided over its fountain since 2005 — the most photographed small statue in San Francisco, and nobody knows the rate.

candidates.title: Egg Toss at the Outpost
candidates.do: At the Outpost nature playground at Presidio Tunnel Tops, find the giant wooden bird's nest. Stand ten paces back. Each teammate tosses an "egg" — a tennis ball, a pinecone, a rolled sock — into the nest. Complete when every teammate has landed one inside (unlimited tries). Wait your turn if others are playing in it, and collect every egg after.
candidates.where: The Outpost at Presidio Tunnel Tops, near the Main Post/Crissy Field overlook. Free; open daily 9:30 AM to 5 PM (6 PM April–October).
candidates.photo: The egg mid-air over the nest, Tunnel Tops parkland behind.
candidates.why_here: Tunnel Tops is SF's newest park (2022), built on top of the highway tunnels, and its nature playground was built from the Presidio's own fallen trees.

candidates.title: Good Dogs, Brave Cats, and One Weird Pet
candidates.do: At the Presidio Pet Cemetery (open daily, free — stay on the wood-chip path and be gentle with the graves), find and photograph headstones for THREE different kinds of animal, and at least one must be something that is neither a dog nor a cat (the 424 handmade markers include birds, fish, hamsters, and reptiles). The animal type must be readable from the headstone itself. Complete with all three photos.
candidates.where: McDowell Ave at Crissy Field Ave, tucked under the Highway 101 viaduct — look for the little white picket fence.
candidates.photo: Three headstone close-ups — ideally including a beloved Army goldfish or parakeet — with the freeway soaring overhead.
candidates.why_here: Since the 1950s, Army families buried their pets here with hand-painted headstones; it's one of SF's strangest and sweetest hidden landmarks.

Presidio Heights.intro: The quietest of the northside mansion neighborhoods: an early-1900s grid of architect-designed houses (Maybeck, Julia Morgan) between the Presidio Wall and California Street, whose north–south streets are named for trees (Cherry, Maple, Spruce, Locust, Laurel, Walnut) and whose main street is Sacramento Street's boutique row. South of California, Laurel Heights and the Laurel Village shops sit on the old Laurel Hill Cemetery, emptied of some 35,000 graves around 1940. Anchored on the 150-foot Byzantine dome of Temple Emanu-El looming across Arguello, the boutique windows, and the vanished cemetery.
Presidio Heights.why_chosen: Have two generals under Temple Emanu-El's Byzantine dome call out words, one round a minute, until they say the same one, spend ten quiet minutes reading at Books Inc. in Laurel Village, and refight Senator Broderick's 1859 duel with oranges on the old Laurel Hill Cemetery ground (this time both duelists have to survive). A mind meld, a pause, a throw-and-catch duel; nothing failable, zero strangers, ~$2, ≈ 40–50 minutes.

candidates.title: The Byzantine Generals
candidates.do: Temple Emanu-El's dome is modeled on Byzantium's Hagia Sophia, so this is your Byzantium, and like the generals in the famous puzzle, two of you have to arrive at the same answer. Stand on the east sidewalk of Arguello facing the dome and pick two generals. Round 1: when the phone clock ticks over to a new minute, count "3, 2, 1" and both generals say any word out loud at the same moment. Same word = complete. Different? No talking; wait for the next minute, then both say a word that links the two words just said ("dome" and "orange" might both lead to "round"). Keep going, one round a minute, until you say the same word together. Plurals count as the same word; a word already said can't be used again.
candidates.where: East sidewalk of Arguello Blvd between Sacramento St and Clay St, facing Temple Emanu-El (2 Lake St) across the boulevard
candidates.failable: no (keep playing rounds until the words match)
candidates.photo: The two generals mid-shout on the same word, the dome looming across Arguello.
candidates.why_here: Arthur Brown Jr. modeled the 1926 temple's 150-foot dome on Hagia Sophia, the great domed church of Byzantine Constantinople, which makes this the one corner in the game to replay the Byzantine Generals problem of agreeing by message alone.

candidates.title: Ten Quiet Minutes at Books Inc.
candidates.do: Go into Books Inc. in Laurel Village, the West's oldest independent bookseller, and spend ten minutes there as a team reading: each teammate picks any book off the shelves and reads it, phones away the whole time (one teammate can set a timer first, then pocket it too). Done after ten minutes of reading. Reshelve everything the way you found it; no purchase required.
candidates.where: Books Inc., 3515 California St (Laurel Village); open daily into the evening
candidates.photo: The team reading in the aisles, each with a different book.
candidates.why_here: Books Inc. traces its roots to an 1851 Gold Rush bookshop and bills itself as the West's oldest independent bookseller; its Laurel Village store sits on ground that was a Gold Rush–era cemetery.

candidates.title: Ten Paces on Laurel Hill
candidates.do: In 1859 Senator David Broderick was shot in a duel and buried in Lone Mountain Cemetery (renamed Laurel Hill in 1867), which covered what's now Laurel Heights until some 35,000 graves were moved to Colma around 1940. Refight it, gently. Buy two oranges at Cal-Mart in Laurel Village and walk three blocks to Laurel Hill Playground. On the ball field (or any open patch well away from the play area and other people), two duelists stand back to back, one orange each. The team counts ten paces out loud as the duelists walk apart; on "Turn!" they turn, and on "Fire!" both toss their orange underhand to the other at the same moment. Both oranges must be caught in the hands. Touching the ground or getting trapped against a body = a misfire: pick them up, walk back to the middle and duel again. Complete when both duelists catch in the same volley. Unlike Broderick, everyone survives.
candidates.where: Oranges from Cal-Mart, 3585 California St (Laurel Village; open daily until 6:30–7pm); duel at Laurel Hill Playground, Euclid Ave at Collins St
candidates.failable: no (misfire? walk back and duel again)
candidates.photo: Video of the winning volley: two oranges crossing in mid-air and both caught.
candidates.why_here: Laurel Heights stands on the old Laurel Hill Cemetery (bounded by California, Presidio, Geary and Parker), whose most famous grave was Broderick's, the senator killed in the Broderick–Terry duel, and its playground still carries the Laurel Hill name.

candidates.title: Where's the Scout?
candidates.do: Start on the east corner of Arguello & Sacramento. One teammate, the scout, sets off while everyone else keeps their eyes on Temple Emanu-El's dome (no watching which way the scout goes). Within 5 minutes the scout must reach a public sidewalk spot inside Presidio Heights, at or east of Maple St, from which some of the dome shows over the rooftops or trees. Pick a street corner or the edge of a shop or park, not someone's front steps. The scout texts ONE photo of the view with the dome in it (no street signs, house numbers or shop names in frame), then stays put: no moving, waving, calling or location sharing. The team hunts for the spot by reading the dome's size and angle in the photo. Done when a teammate taps the scout on the shoulder.
candidates.where: Start at Arguello Blvd & Sacramento St (east corner); the scout hides anywhere in Presidio Heights at or east of Maple St
candidates.failable: no (keep hunting until you find the scout)
candidates.photo: Side by side: the scout's clue photo, then the whole team with the scout on the spot, the dome in the distance.
candidates.why_here: The temple's 150-foot dome is visible for blocks around, the one landmark rising above the neighborhood's rooftops and trees, so the angle you see it from tells you where you're standing.

candidates.title: The Tree Street Census
candidates.do: Presidio Heights' north–south streets are a row of trees: Cherry, Maple, Spruce, Locust, Laurel and Walnut. Pick one block of any of them, corner to corner. Before stepping onto it, the team writes down ONE guess: how many trees grow along both sidewalks of this block? Count only trees rooted in the sidewalk or the curbside planting strip; skip anything growing in a yard or behind a fence, wall or hedge. Then walk the block and count together. Within 2 of the guess = complete. Missed? Pick a block on a different tree street and call a new number. You know the local density now.
candidates.where: Any one block of Cherry, Maple, Spruce, Locust, Laurel or Walnut St, north of California St
candidates.failable: no (a new block for each new guess)
candidates.photo: The written guess and the final count held up under the tree street's sign.
candidates.why_here: The neighborhood's grid is named for trees, six of them in a row between Arguello Blvd and Presidio Ave, so a census puts the neighborhood's own naming to the test.

candidates.title: The Sacramento Street Shopping List
candidates.do: Walk the boutique row on Sacramento St from Presidio Ave toward Spruce St, playing the memory-chain game on the shop windows. At the first window, a teammate names one specific thing visible in it ("a brass lamp", not "stuff"). At the next window, the next teammate recites the list so far in order, then adds one thing from this window. Keep rotating: one new item per window. Each time an item is added, a different teammate photographs it. That photo roll is the answer key, and nobody looks at it mid-game. No notes, no prompting. A wrong item, wrong order, skipped item or 5-second freeze wipes the list, and the next teammate starts a new one at the next window. Run out of street? Cross over and work back along the other side. Done when a teammate recites a perfect ten-item list and adds the eleventh.
candidates.where: Sacramento St between Presidio Ave and Spruce St (the 3300–3600 blocks); sidewalk only, works even when shops are closed
candidates.failable: no (a slip just restarts the chain)
candidates.photo: The photo roll of the winning list in order, ending with a video of the final recital at the eleventh window.
candidates.why_here: Sacramento Street's row of furniture, tableware and fashion boutiques, galleries and cafés is Presidio Heights' whole main street, and window-shopping it is how the neighborhood spends an afternoon.

Russian Hill.intro: Russian Hill (roughly Van Ness to Columbus, Broadway/Pacific up to Bay Street) is the city's vertical playground: the eight-switchback "crookedest" block of Lombard, the 31.5% Filbert Street wall — among the steepest street blocks in SF — and a secret network of stairway gardens like Macondray Lane and Ina Coolbrith Park, all threaded by the Powell–Hyde cable car. I anchored on the hill's three superpowers: absurd slopes, hidden pedestrian lanes, and postcard views — plus the 1948 birthplace of Swensen's.
Russian Hill.why_chosen: Walk down the crookedest block in the world (the trio's "the place is the game" entry), land the cable car + Alcatraz timing shot on Hyde, and build a freestanding tower that stands truly vertical on the 31.5% Filbert Street slope. One icon, one timing shot, one engineering puzzle; nothing failable, zero strangers, $0–10, ≈ 40–55 minutes.

candidates.title: Walk the Crookedest Street
candidates.do: Walk the famous crooked block of Lombard Street from top (Hyde) to bottom (Leavenworth) on the sidewalk stairs. That's it — the street is the challenge.
candidates.where: Lombard St, 1000 block, between Hyde St and Leavenworth St.
candidates.photo: The team at the bottom with the brick switchbacks and hydrangeas rising behind.
candidates.why_here: The "crookedest street in the world" is Russian Hill's global calling card.

candidates.title: Postcard Ambush
candidates.do: Recreate SF's most famous postcard, live: ONE photo containing a moving Powell–Hyde cable car, the Bay with Alcatraz behind it, and at least one teammate. Stake out your angle and time the shot; if a car passes and you miss, wait for the next one (roughly every 10 minutes on weekends).
candidates.where: Hyde St between Lombard and Bay (Hyde & Greenwich or Hyde & Lombard crests give the Alcatraz backdrop).
candidates.photo: The proof IS the challenge: cable car + Alcatraz + teammate in one frame.
candidates.why_here: The Hyde Street line cresting Russian Hill with Alcatraz behind is the most reproduced image of San Francisco — now with you in it.

candidates.title: Stand Up Straight on the 31.5%
candidates.do: Filbert Street between Leavenworth and Hyde is one of the steepest blocks in San Francisco. On a SLOPED part of the sidewalk (not a flat stair tread), build something at least ONE FOOT tall that stands truly upright — plumb to gravity, not tilted with the hill. Use anything you're carrying, find, or buy nearby (up to $10). It must stand on its own for a count of ten with no hands touching it, and a phone level app held against it must read within 5° of vertical. Falls or leans too far? Rebuild and try again.
candidates.where: Filbert St between Leavenworth St and Hyde St (sidewalk only; keep everything off the roadway). Shops for supplies along Hyde St a block or two south and on Polk St a few blocks west.
candidates.photo: The tower standing dead vertical against the plunging street, level app reading shown, team hands in the air.
candidates.why_here: On a 31.5% grade "straight up" is the hard part — everything wants to lean with the hill, and you have to out-engineer it.

candidates.title: Find Barbary Lane
candidates.do: Locate the hidden pedestrian lane that inspired "28 Barbary Lane" in Tales of the City and traverse it end to end: enter at Jones & Union area (Macondray Lane runs between Green and Union) and walk east until you descend the wooden plank stairway that drops you out onto Taylor Street. Everyone must touch the Taylor Street sidewalk at the bottom.
candidates.where: Macondray Lane, between Jones St and Taylor St (parallel to and between Green and Union); the wooden stairs are the Taylor St end.
candidates.photo: Team on the rickety-charming wooden stairway under the tree canopy, with a "Macondray Lane" street sign or the Taylor St exit in frame.
candidates.why_here: A cobbled, gardens-and-cottages footpath with no roadway and a secret wooden staircase — a National Register historic district most visitors never find.

candidates.title: Couplet for the Poet
candidates.do: Climb the stair-garden of Ina Coolbrith Park (named for California's first poet laureate) to an upper terrace with a Bay view. Pick a poet. The rest of the team hands the poet ONE word to end the first line with; the poet must immediately write a two-line poem about the other team whose second line ends in a rhyme for that word. Real rhyme = complete. No rhyme within a minute = the team picks a new word and the poet tries again.
candidates.where: Ina Coolbrith Park, Vallejo St at Taylor St (stairs continue up the Vallejo Street steps).
candidates.photo: The poet holding the handwritten couplet, Bay Bridge panorama behind.
candidates.why_here: A hidden hillside park honoring SF's bohemian poet laureate — the only place in the city where writing bad poetry is basically mandatory.

candidates.title: First Scoop on Earth
candidates.do: Buy one scoop (any flavor) at the original Swensen's — the 1948 corner shop where the worldwide chain began — and finish it before leaving the corner of Union & Hyde. Completion = empty cone/cup shown at the corner.
candidates.where: Swensen's Ice Cream, 1999 Hyde St (at Union St). Note: typically opens around noon on weekends — schedule this for afternoon passes.
candidates.photo: Teammate mid-lick under the vintage neon SWENSEN'S sign, cable car tracks on Hyde in view.
candidates.why_here: Earle Swensen opened this exact corner shop in 1948; every Swensen's on the planet descends from this one.

Seacliff.intro: Seacliff is one of the smallest of the 41 official neighborhoods: a 1913 master-planned "residence park" (landscape architect Mark Daniels) of pastel stucco mansions — Willis Polk and Julia Morgan both built here — draped over the bluffs between the Presidio and Lincoln Park. Its treasure is China Beach, a pocket cove named for the Chinese fishermen who anchored their junks and camped there from Gold Rush times (mid-century maps called it Phelan Beach before the old name won out). Everything below is outdoors, free, and inside the official boundary — Baker Beach belongs to the Presidio and Lands End to Lincoln Park, so we stay off both. Note: swimming at China Beach is unsafe and never part of any challenge — sand only.
Seacliff.why_chosen: Build a beach-found junk that stands on its own at China Beach, draw one of the four characters of the Fishermen's Stone from memory for your team to identify, and read a page each out loud at San Francisco's first Little Free Library. A build, a memory game, a story time; nothing failable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 35–45 minutes. (The China Beach stairway wager stays the alternate one-shot.)

candidates.title: Junk Boat Shipyard
candidates.do: On the sand at China Beach, build a model junk (Chinese sailing boat) at least 12 inches long from found beach materials only (driftwood, kelp, stones, feathers — nothing brought with you). It must have a hull and at least one standing "sail." Complete when the finished boat stands on its own on the sand.
candidates.where: China Beach, down the stairway/drive at the seaward end of Sea Cliff Avenue
candidates.photo: The finished junk on the sand with the Golden Gate Bridge in the background
candidates.why_here: This cove is named for the Chinese fishermen whose junks anchored right here — you're relaunching the fleet.

candidates.title: The Fishermen's Stone, From Memory
candidates.do: Find the 1981 memorial stone at the top of the China Beach access drive honoring the Chinese fishermen who camped in the cove since Gold Rush times. It's carved with four Chinese characters; number them 1–4 in reading order. One teammate, the drawer, studies all four as long as they like — no photos — then walks twenty paces away and turns their back. On a phone they secretly generate a random number from 1 to 4 and draw that character from memory, on paper you got during the game or on the phone. The rest of the team, looking at the stone, points at ONE character they think it is. Right = complete. Wrong = a new drawer and a new number.
candidates.where: Seaward end of Sea Cliff Avenue, beside the China Beach entrance/parking
candidates.photo: The drawing held up beside the stone, the team pointing at the matching character.
candidates.why_here: The stone is the neighborhood's origin story in granite — the only monument in Seacliff, and the hardest four characters your memory will meet today.

candidates.title: Story Time at SF's First Little Free Library
candidates.do: Find the Little Free Library at 25th Avenue & Lake Street — the very first one in San Francisco, and still running. Pick any book from it and take turns: each teammate reads one full page out loud to the others. Done when everyone has read a page. Put the book back when you're done (or leave one of your own in its place).
candidates.where: Little Free Library at 25th Ave & Lake St
candidates.photo: A teammate mid-page, the rest of the team listening beside the little library box.
candidates.why_here: San Francisco's Little Free Library movement started on this corner, and it still runs on neighbors trading books.

candidates.title: How Far to the Tower?
candidates.do: At the little seaward overlook with the pair of backless memorial benches on Sea Cliff Avenue, the whole team looks at the Golden Gate Bridge's south tower and agrees on ONE guess: how far away is it, in miles, as the crow flies? Write it down, then check with the phone map's distance-measuring tool. Within 20% = complete. Off? Guess the distance to Point Bonita Lighthouse across the strait and check that.
candidates.where: North-side overlook on Sea Cliff Avenue, about a block east of the China Beach gate (near 29th Ave)
candidates.failable: no (second target if the first misses)
candidates.photo: The guess held up with the bridge behind, map check beside it.
candidates.why_here: Seacliff's street-end bridge views are its calling card — and nobody guesses the distance right the first time.

candidates.title: The Only Avenue With a Compass
candidates.do: Phones away, no maps. Somewhere within three blocks of the China Beach gate is the only numbered avenue in San Francisco whose name carries a compass direction. Find its street sign by walking and reading signs — no asking. Complete when the whole team is under the sign and someone reads it aloud on video.
candidates.where: Sea Cliff, within three blocks of Sea Cliff Ave & 28th Ave (the answer is on the map; the challenge is finding it without one)
candidates.photo: The team under the sign that gives it away.
candidates.why_here: A one-of-a-kind street name inside a 1913 gated residence park — geography trivia you can only solve on foot.

candidates.title: The Beach Wager
candidates.do: At the top of the China Beach stairway, before anyone can see the sand, every teammate secretly writes down a guess: how many people will be on the beach when you reach the bottom? Then walk down together and count everyone on the sand (not in the water, not on the stairs). If at least one teammate's guess is within 3 of the count, you win. One attempt only — no peeking over the rail before guesses are locked.
candidates.where: China Beach stairway, from the parking area at the end of Sea Cliff Avenue down to the beach
candidates.failable: one-shot (guesses lock before the first step)
candidates.photo: The winning guess held up on the sand, the cove behind.
candidates.why_here: The long stair-and-ramp plunge to the cove is the neighborhood's signature descent — and the beach below is never the same size twice.

South of Market.intro: SoMa is the big-shouldered grid south of Market Street — the official Analysis Neighborhood runs from Market down to Division/13th, and does NOT include the waterfront (South Beach, Oracle Park, and the Embarcadero fall in Financial District/South Beach; Mission Bay is its own neighborhood). Offices are dead on weekends, so everything below anchors on the weekend-alive core: Yerba Buena Gardens (open daily 6am–10pm, free), the Old Mint at 5th, and the SOMA Pilipinas cultural district's hero-named streets between 3rd and 4th.
South of Market.why_chosen: Ride the 1906 carousel (the trio's pure-joy entry), call five coin flips in a row at the Mint that struck them, then bowl a homemade frame outside the bowling alley on the Yerba Buena rooftop. One ride, one streak of nerve, one roll; nothing failable, zero strangers, ~$6–10 total, ≈ 30–45 minutes.

candidates.title: Ride the 1906 Survivor
candidates.do: Buy carousel tickets ($3/rider) and ride a full cycle of the LeRoy King Carousel — the hand-carved 1906 Charles Looff carousel that once spun at Playland at the Beach. At least two teammates must ride (riders under 42" need a paying companion). Complete when the ride ends.
candidates.where: Children's Creativity Museum carousel pavilion, 221 4th St at Howard (Yerba Buena Gardens). Weekends 10am–4pm — no museum admission needed for the carousel.
candidates.photo: Teammates mid-spin on their carved animals, organ pipes and painted menagerie in frame.
candidates.why_here: A 120-year-old carousel that outlived Playland itself, parked in the middle of SoMa under a Douglas Hollis "Whirligig" wind sculpture.

candidates.title: Call It at the Mint
candidates.do: Stand on the 5th Street steps (or Mint Plaza side) of the Old Mint — the 1874 "Granite Lady" that survived the 1906 earthquake and fire while holding roughly a third of the nation's gold reserve. Flip a coin and call it in the air; complete the challenge by calling it correctly 5 times IN A ROW. A miss resets the streak — keep flipping until you hit it. The coin has to be a real one you get during the game, however you manage it (change from something you buy is the easy way); coins you brought from home don't count.
candidates.where: Old San Francisco Mint, 88 5th St at Mission; Mint Plaza is the quieter flank.
candidates.cost: ~$1–3 (whatever you buy to get the coin)
candidates.failable: no (persistence — the streak resets, the challenge doesn't)
candidates.photo: The winning flip: your hard-won coin on a palm, granite columns of the Mint rising behind.
candidates.why_here: Calling coins at the very building that struck them — SoMa's homage to Jet Lag's Royal Australian Mint coin flip.

candidates.title: Street Bowling at Yerba Buena
candidates.do: Above Moscone, the Yerba Buena rooftop has a real bowling alley (the Ice Skating & Bowling Center, 750 Folsom). Bowl your own frame outside it: set up "pins" from anything you find or buy on the way (cans, bottles, cups), then step back a full bowling lane — 60 feet, about 20 big steps — and roll anything (an orange, a can, a ball) at them. Rolled, not thrown, and it has to stay on the ground. Knock over at least one pin = complete. Missed? Fetch it and roll again. Use the open pavement, out of everyone's way, and pick up after yourselves.
candidates.where: Outside the Yerba Buena Ice Skating & Bowling Center, 750 Folsom St (the Yerba Buena rooftop, south of Howard).
candidates.place_name: Yerba Buena Ice Skating & Bowling Center
candidates.photo: The video of your roll and the pins going down, the rooftop gardens around you.
candidates.why_here: Downtown San Francisco hides a bowling alley on top of a convention center — here you bowl a frame outside it with whatever you can find.

candidates.title: Hero Streets, No Maps
candidates.do: The little streets between 3rd, 4th, Folsom, and Harrison are named for Philippine national heroes. Stand at Folsom & 4th and read this list aloud once: **Lapu Lapu, Rizal, Mabini, Bonifacio, Tandang Sora.** Then all phones become cameras ONLY — no maps, no searching, no asking. You have 15 minutes to find and photograph the team under THREE of the five hero street signs by pure wandering and street-sense. Clock expires = 10-minute cooldown, then restart (prior photos void — but what you learned is yours to keep).
candidates.where: SOMA Pilipinas hero streets, inside 3rd/4th/Folsom/Harrison
candidates.photo: The team pointing up at a blade reading LAPU LAPU, timer screenshot in the corner of the upload.
candidates.why_here: The only street grid in America that doubles as a roll call of Philippine heroes — and it's just small enough to find blind, if you're sharp.

candidates.title: Gold-Medal Form
candidates.do: Go to Victoria Manalo Draves Park, named for the SoMa-born diver who won BOTH springboard and platform gold at the 1948 London Olympics — the first Asian American woman to win Olympic gold. On the lawn or playground (feet-on-the-ground or a small hop only), every teammate strikes a mid-air "perfect dive" pose — arms in a point overhead, toes together. Complete when you've captured the whole team in dive form in one frame, park sign or playground visible.
candidates.where: Victoria Manalo Draves Park, Folsom St at Sherman (between 6th & 7th), next to Bessie Carmichael School.
candidates.photo: The team lined up in synchronized-diving poses (jumping counts as mid-air), park sign in frame — a podium shot 78 years in the making.
candidates.why_here: A SoMa-born diver out-dove the world in 1948; her park is one of the only true green squares in western SoMa.

Sunset/Parkside.intro: SF's foggiest quarter: a giant pastel grid of Doelger-built rowhouses running downhill into the longest stretch of Ocean Beach, with beloved food strips on Irving, Noriega, and Taraval, the brand-new car-free Sunset Dunes park on the old Great Highway, and Stern Grove's hidden eucalyptus canyon at the southern edge. (Boundary check against the official Analysis Neighborhoods map: the 16th Avenue Tiled Steps and Grandview Park fall in Inner Sunset, and the Doggie Diner head falls in Lakeshore — so none of those are used here.)
Sunset/Parkside.why_chosen: Spin Polly Ann's flavor wheel and eat whatever it lands on, find a run of five rowhouses in five different colors, and get down into Stern Grove to the 1892 Trocadero Clubhouse. A gamble, a hunt, a hidden place; nothing failable, zero strangers, ~$5, ≈ 40–55 minutes.

candidates.title: Spin the Wheel of Fortune at Polly Ann
candidates.do: At Polly Ann Ice Cream (scooping on Noriega since 1955), ask the counter to spin their famous flavor Wheel of Fortune. One player buys a single scoop of whatever flavor the wheel lands on — durian included — and takes at least three bites. Complete when the wheel's flavor is bought and bitten.
candidates.where: Polly Ann Ice Cream, 3138 Noriega St at 39th Ave (open daily from late morning)
candidates.failable: no (the wheel decides the flavor, but eating it is always possible — that's the fun)
candidates.photo: The spinner mid-lick of the mystery flavor, pointing at the wheel behind the counter
candidates.why_here: Polly Ann's spin-the-wheel-and-eat-what-you-get ritual is a one-of-a-kind Sunset institution — roulette you can taste.

candidates.title: The Doelger Rainbow
candidates.do: The Sunset is the world's biggest showcase of identical pastel stucco rowhouses. Find one block face where FIVE consecutive attached houses are each painted a clearly different color. Complete when the photo shows five adjacent, five-colored facades.
candidates.where: Anywhere in the avenues — the blocks between Irving and Vicente from ~30th to 47th Ave are prime hunting ground
candidates.failable: no (keep walking blocks until you find a run of five)
candidates.photo: Five adjacent rowhouses in five different colors, in one shot.
candidates.why_here: Henry Doelger's "white cliffs" of the Sunset are the neighborhood's defining look — this turns the famous sameness into a color scavenger hunt.

candidates.title: Roadhouse in the Woods
candidates.do: Enter Stern Grove and descend into the eucalyptus canyon to find the Trocadero Clubhouse, the white-and-green 1892 Victorian roadhouse hiding at the bottom. Complete when your whole team is standing on its front porch/steps.
candidates.where: Stern Grove — enter at 19th Ave & Sloat Blvd and follow the main path down; the Trocadero is near the west end of the concert meadow
candidates.photo: Full team posed like an old-timey band on the gingerbread porch of the Victorian
candidates.why_here: A gold-rush-era roadhouse at the bottom of a fog-forest canyon in the middle of the avenues — most San Franciscans don't know it exists.

candidates.title: Bigger Than Your Biggest Teammate
candidates.do: On the sand at Ocean Beach (between Lincoln Way and Sloat Blvd), write your team name — or team color, if the name is long — in letters drawn in the sand, each letter TALLER than your tallest teammate. To prove scale, that teammate lies down in the sand next to one letter. Complete when the photo shows every letter plus the human yardstick.
candidates.where: Ocean Beach, easiest access from the Judah, Noriega, or Taraval stairwells off the old Great Highway
candidates.failable: no (smooth the sand and redraw until it's right)
candidates.photo: Shot from the seawall/dune above: giant sand letters with a teammate lying beside one for scale, ocean behind
candidates.why_here: This is SF's longest, widest run of open beach — the only neighborhood with enough sand for person-sized typography.

candidates.title: The Plover Stand
candidates.do: Walk out onto Sunset Dunes (the car-free former Great Highway) and find any posted Snowy Plover protection sign along the dune fencing. Then every teammate holds a one-legged "plover stand" next to it for a fully counted 30 seconds. If anyone's second foot touches down, the attempt fails; you get 3 attempts total.
candidates.where: Sunset Dunes park, between Lincoln Way and Sloat Blvd (dune-fence signs are posted along the beach side)
candidates.failable: retryable (an attempt = one 30-second team hold; max 3 attempts)
candidates.photo: The whole team frozen on one leg beside the plover sign, dunes and ocean behind
candidates.why_here: Ocean Beach's dunes are the protected wintering ground of the snowy plover — the tiny shorebird this stretch of coast is famous for guarding (and that a local coffee drink is named after).

candidates.title: Beignet o'Clock on Noriega
candidates.do: Join the line at Devil's Teeth Baking Company and buy one of their weekend-only beignets (any pastry under $5 counts if beignets are sold out). Complete when the purchase is in hand outside the shop.
candidates.where: Devil's Teeth Baking Company, 3876 Noriega St near 45th Ave (weekends roughly 7am–3pm; beignets go until they sell out — a late-afternoon game breaks this one, so schedule accordingly)
candidates.time: 10–20 min (the line is part of the legend)
candidates.failable: no (the fallback pastry keeps it completable any time the shop is open)
candidates.photo: Powdered-sugar-dusted grin holding the beignet in front of the teal storefront
candidates.why_here: Devil's Teeth is the Outer Sunset's surf-town breakfast institution; its weekend beignet line is a neighborhood ritual.

Tenderloin.intro: Downtown's most storied thirty-odd blocks: a National Register historic district where 400-plus early-1900s residential hotels stack bay windows, fire escapes, and vintage blade signs, Little Saigon's banh mi counters line Larkin Street, and the Market Street edge glitters with 1920s theater-palace marquees. Boundary verified against the official Analysis Neighborhoods dataset: Market Street north to roughly Post/Sutter, Powell west to Van Ness — so UN Plaza, the Golden Gate Theatre, the Warfield, and the Orpheum are all in-bounds, while Union Square plaza itself belongs to a neighbor. Everything below sticks to the neighborhood's busy, daytime-comfortable corridors: Larkin, O'Farrell/Geary, the Market edge, and UN Plaza.
Tenderloin.why_chosen: Banh mi in Little Saigon first (the trio's simple pleasure — around $6 of the city's best cheap lunch, fuel for what follows), then work the Blade Sign Alphabet east through the historic district, and finish inside the Main Library — officially Tenderloin turf — hunting down *Tales of the City* with no phones, no catalog, no staff. One taste, one alphabet hunt, one shelf-logic quest; nothing failable, zero strangers, all on the neighborhood's busiest daytime corridors, ≈ 40–55 minutes. Memorize the Nations is the swap-in if the library is closed.

candidates.title: The Six-Dollar Legend
candidates.do: Buy one banh mi at Saigon Sandwich (560 Larkin St at Eddy) — or, if the line is out the door, at any other banh mi counter on Larkin between Turk and O'Farrell. Every teammate takes at least one bite. Complete when the sandwich is bought and everyone has bitten.
candidates.where: Larkin St, Eddy to O'Farrell (officially designated Little Saigon); Saigon Sandwich is open daily, weekends from 7am
candidates.photo: The whole team mid-bite on the Larkin sidewalk, Vietnamese storefront signage behind.
candidates.why_here: Larkin between Turk and O'Farrell is San Francisco's official Little Saigon, and this closet-sized counter has sold arguably the city's best cheap lunch for decades — around $6, wrapped in paper.

candidates.title: Blade Sign Alphabet
candidates.do: The Uptown Tenderloin Historic District keeps the West's densest collection of century-old hotel signs. Photograph five vintage hotel signs — neon blades or painted ghost signs, five different buildings — whose hotel names begin with FIVE DIFFERENT letters. No phone research or maps; eyes up, feet moving. Complete at the fifth letter.
candidates.where: Richest hunting along Geary, O'Farrell, and Eddy between Larkin and Taylor; the Cadillac Hotel (398 Eddy) is a classic opener
candidates.photo: Sign #5 with a teammate pointing up, plus the full five-letter set in the upload.
candidates.why_here: The neighborhood's skyline is spelled in hundred-year-old neon — working the alphabet through it is the Tenderloin's own crossword.

candidates.title: The Catalog Is You
candidates.do: Enter the Main Library (free, everyone welcome). From the door: all phones away, no catalog computers, no asking staff. Find a physical copy of Armistead Maupin's *Tales of the City* on the open shelves — any edition, and any volume of the series counts — using nothing but floor directories, shelf signage, and your own logic. Complete when a teammate is holding the book. (No copy on the shelf after an honest search of the right section? Any book by Maupin counts.)
candidates.where: SF Main Library, 100 Larkin St at Grove — one block from UN Plaza (weekends roughly 10–6 Sat, 12–6 Sun; check hours)
candidates.failable: no (the book is in there somewhere)
candidates.photo: The book held aloft under the library's 75-foot atrium skylight.
candidates.why_here: The city's flagship library is officially IN the Tenderloin — six floors of it — and the most San Francisco novel ever written is hiding inside on a knowable shelf. Our homage to Jet Lag's Dewey Decimal challenge.

candidates.title: Double Feature
candidates.do: Strike a full-team showbiz pose (jazz hands, red-carpet wave, or dramatic bow) under the Golden Gate Theatre's corner marquee at Golden Gate Ave/Taylor/Market, then walk one block east on Market and repeat a DIFFERENT pose under the Warfield's marquee at 982 Market. Complete when you have both photos, each showing the marquee or vertical blade sign plus the pose.
candidates.where: Market St's theater edge: Golden Gate Theatre (1 Taylor St) and the Warfield (982 Market St), one block apart
candidates.photo: A two-frame set: jazz hands under "GOLDEN GATE," second pose under the Warfield sign.
candidates.why_here: Two rival 1922 vaudeville palaces a block apart — the Tenderloin's Market Street edge was the West Coast's Broadway, and the marquees still blaze.

candidates.title: Memorize the Nations
candidates.do: UN Plaza's light-standard columns carry the names of all UN member nations (the Charter was signed in SF in 1945). Pick one reciter and one verifier. The reciter chooses any single column and any run of SEVEN CONSECUTIVE country names on it, studies as long as they like, then walks to the brass "WE THE PEOPLES" preamble in the pavers — back to the columns — and recites the seven IN ORDER, no peeking. The verifier stands at the column and checks every name against the inscription. Any wrong country, wrong order, or blank = stop, go re-study, and restart the recitation from name one. Complete on a clean seven.
candidates.where: United Nations Plaza, off Market St between Leavenworth and Hyde
candidates.failable: no (restart and re-study until the run is clean)
candidates.photo: The reciter mid-recital on the brass "WE THE PEOPLES," eyes shut, verifier at the column with a thumbs-up.
candidates.why_here: The UN's San Francisco birthplace turned into a memory recital — world order, in order, from memory.

candidates.title: Sergeant Macaulay's Playground Passport
candidates.do: At Sergeant John Macaulay Park, every teammate goes down a slide once and crosses one piece of climbing equipment without touching the ground. Finish with the whole team jumping in the air at once in front of the play structure. Complete when everyone has slid, everyone has climbed, and the jump photo is taken.
candidates.where: Sgt. John Macaulay Park, Larkin St at O'Farrell
candidates.photo: The full-team mid-air jump, playground colors behind.
candidates.why_here: A fenced pocket playground two blocks up Larkin from the banh mi counters — the Tenderloin's family backyard, and the perfect picnic spot if you pair it with The Six-Dollar Legend.

Treasure Island.intro: A flat, man-made island built from bay sand in 1936–37 to host the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition — the "Magic City" — then a Navy base, now a neighborhood-in-progress with the best free skyline panorama in San Francisco. Anchors: Streamline Moderne Building One (the old fair Administration Building, with a free museum lobby and restored 1939 fair statues out front), the western-shore seawall along Avenue of the Palms, Clipper Cove (where Pan Am's China Clipper flying boats took off — a gift of a name for this game), and Yerba Buena Island's brand-new hilltop Panorama Park with Hiroshi Sugimoto's 69-foot "Point of Infinity" spire.
Treasure Island.why_chosen: Treasure Island is a long ride out, so its three challenges are just to be there: Building One and the 1939 fair statues, the skyline from the western seawall, and Clipper Cove, all a short walk apart from the Muni 25 stop. Nothing failable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 20–30 minutes on the island. (The old games are alternates.)

candidates.title: The Magic City's Front Door
candidates.do: Go to Building One, the Streamline Moderne Administration Building of the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition, and stand among the restored statues from the fair on its lawn. Done when the whole team is there.
candidates.where: Building One, 1 Avenue of the Palms (by the Muni 25 stop).
candidates.photo: The team among the 1939 fair statues, Building One's Moderne facade behind.
candidates.why_here: The island was built from bay sand for the 1939 World's Fair; Building One and its statues are what's left of the "Magic City."

candidates.title: The Whole Skyline
candidates.do: Walk to the western seawall along Avenue of the Palms and take in San Francisco head-on across the water: the whole skyline, the Bay Bridge, and on a clear day the Golden Gate. Done when the whole team is at the seawall.
candidates.where: Western seawall along Avenue of the Palms, a short walk from Building One.
candidates.photo: The team at the seawall with the entire city skyline behind you.
candidates.why_here: The best free skyline panorama in the city is the one you can only get from outside it.

candidates.title: Clipper Cove
candidates.do: Go down to Clipper Cove, the sheltered water between Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island where Pan Am's China Clipper flying boats took off across the Pacific in the 1930s. Done when the whole team is on the beach.
candidates.where: Clipper Cove Beach, off Treasure Island Road near the causeway to Yerba Buena Island.
candidates.photo: The team on Clipper Cove's beach, boats in the cove and Yerba Buena Island behind.
candidates.why_here: The flying boats that crossed the Pacific left from here — and it's the cove this game's name winks at.

candidates.title: Touch the Sky at the Point of Infinity
candidates.do: Get to Panorama Park on Yerba Buena Island, home of the 69-foot "Point of Infinity" spire. Find the one spot on the hilltop where, in a single photo, the spire's tip appears to touch exactly the top of Salesforce Tower (or the Transamerica Pyramid's spire) across the bay — two points meeting, no gap, no overlap. Complete when the photo shows the two tips kissing. (The Muni 25 stops on Yerba Buena Island on its loop, or it's a ~12-minute uphill walk from the Treasure Island flats — an easy paved climb.)
candidates.where: Panorama Park, hilltop of Yerba Buena Island (opened 2024, free, open daily)
candidates.failable: no (keep hunting for the angle; if fog hides downtown, a Bay Bridge tower top counts as the backup target)
candidates.photo: The two tips meeting — a 69-foot needle and a 1,070-foot tower, joined.
candidates.why_here: Sugimoto engineered the sculpture to taper toward a mathematically infinite point — this is the one place in SF you can line infinity up with the skyline.

candidates.title: Skyline Roll Call
candidates.do: From the western-shore seawall walkway along Avenue of the Palms, spot and photograph (zoom is fine) 4 of these 5 landmarks: the Transamerica Pyramid, Salesforce Tower, Coit Tower, Alcatraz, and the Golden Gate Bridge. Complete when you have all four in photos taken from the seawall (one wide labeled shot or four zoomed shots both count).
candidates.where: Western shore of Treasure Island, seawall along Avenue of the Palms (any point between Building One and the Great Lawn)
candidates.failable: no (fog can slow you down, but the near landmarks always show)
candidates.photo: The full postcard panorama with the team in front — the exact view the 1939 fair was built to show off
candidates.why_here: This shoreline is the city's mirror: nowhere else do you face the entire SF skyline head-on at water level.

candidates.title: Paper Clipper Airfield
candidates.do: In the 1930s, Pan Am's China Clipper flying boats took off from Clipper Cove. Fold one paper airplane per teammate (bring paper). From a marked line at Clipper Cove's beach or lawn, each teammate throws; the challenge is complete when any plane flies at least 8 walking paces before touching down. You get 3 rounds of throws total. Retrieve every plane — leave no paper behind.
candidates.where: Clipper Cove Beach / marina shoreline, between Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island (off Treasure Island Road at the causeway)
candidates.failable: retryable (each round of team throws = one attempt; 3 rounds max)
candidates.photo: A plane mid-launch over the cove, Bay Bridge in the background
candidates.why_here: You're re-flying the China Clipper from its actual home water — and it's the cove this game's name winks at.

candidates.title: Statue Charades, Class of 1939
candidates.do: On the lawn in front of Building One stand restored statues from the 1939 fair's Pacific Unity sculpture court. Walk the lawn and study their poses. Number the statues from the left. Then one teammate, the performer, generates a random number on a phone (re-roll repeats) and freezes in that statue's exact pose; the team gets ONE guess, pointing at the statue. Right = next performer. Wrong = new statue, streak restarts. Complete at three in a row. (If the statues are fenced, play from outside the fence.)
candidates.where: Building One lawn, 1 Avenue of the Palms (just past the island's Moderne guard-tower entrance)
candidates.photo: The performer frozen beside the statue they became.
candidates.why_here: These are literal survivors of the World's Fair this island was built for — and they hold still for you to copy.

candidates.title: Find the Magic City's Receipts
candidates.do: Two finds, both at Building One: (a) photograph the bronze California Historical Landmark No. 987 plaque commemorating the island's 1936–37 construction and the Exposition; (b) step into Building One's free museum lobby (open weekends noon–7) and photograph any exhibit image or artifact showing the fair's long-gone 400-foot Tower of the Sun. Complete with both photos.
candidates.where: Building One, 39 Treasure Island Road / 1 Avenue of the Palms
candidates.photo: A teammate pointing from the plaque toward the empty spot on the island where the Tower of the Sun once stood, exhibit photo in hand
candidates.why_here: The whole island is the artifact — the plaque and lobby are where its origin story is written down.

candidates.title: TreasureFest Bounty (schedule-dependent — verify before game day)
candidates.do: TreasureFest, the island's flea-market festival running since 2011, still operates but only on select weekends and no longer publishes a fixed monthly calendar — confirm the date before including this challenge. If it's on: enter and buy any single item for $5 or less that is either gold-colored or pirate/treasure-themed. Complete on purchase.
candidates.where: TreasureFest grounds, Avenue of the Palms
candidates.cost: ~$5 (plus any gate fee — another reason to verify)
candidates.failable: no (persistence — some vendor always has a dollar trinket)
