candidates.photo: The treasure held aloft at the vendor stall
candidates.why_here: A flea market literally named for hunting treasure, on Treasure Island.

Twin Peaks.intro: Twin Peaks is the roof of the game board: two grassy ~920-foot summits — Eureka (north) and Noe (south), the Spanish called them "Los Pechos de la Chola" — with a 360° view, a famously windy saddle, and Sutro Tower's three-pronged silhouette looming one ridge over (the tower's base sits inside this neighborhood too). The eastern half of the figure-eight roadway is permanently car-free, so you can roam the loop and the summit stair-paths safely; fog isn't a bug here, it's the boss battle. (Boundary check against the official Analysis Neighborhoods dataset: both summits, Christmas Tree Point, and Sutro Tower are in; Tank Hill is in Inner Sunset and the Pemberton steps are in Castro/Upper Market, so they're off-limits for this tile.)
Twin Peaks.why_chosen: Signal a random word between the two summits with no phones, photograph three kinds of wildlife in the Mission blue butterfly's grassland, and find the one spot where Market Street runs as a single straight stripe to the bay. A signaling game, a wildlife hunt, a find; one fog-retryable, zero strangers, all $0, ≈ 35–45 minutes on foot. (Bridge or No Bridge is now an alternate.)

candidates.title: Semaphore on the Twins
candidates.do: Split your team in two. One group climbs the stair-path to the top of Eureka Peak (north), the other to Noe Peak (south) — they're only ~660 feet apart across the saddle. The Noe group picks a random word (a random-word generator on a phone is fine for that) and gets it across the gap any way they like — arms, bodies, letters, acting it out, shouting — but no phones for the signaling: no texts, no calls, no screens held up. The Eureka group writes down their answer, then everyone meets at the saddle to compare. Right word = complete. Wrong = new word, back up the peaks. Team of two: one person per peak.
candidates.where: Eureka and Noe summit paths off Twin Peaks Blvd, uphill from the Christmas Tree Point parking area.
candidates.failable: no (new word, back up the peaks)
candidates.photo: Zoomed from one summit: the other half of the team mid-signal against the sky.
candidates.why_here: It's the only neighborhood where your team can literally occupy both eponymous peaks at once — and signal across.

candidates.title: Summit Wildlife
candidates.do: The summit grasslands are protected habitat for the endangered Mission blue butterfly. Staying on trails, photograph THREE different kinds of animals that aren't people or dogs — any butterfly, bee, beetle, bird, lizard or the like. Complete with three animal photos.
candidates.where: Trailheads and paths of the Twin Peaks Natural Area, around the summit loop and Christmas Tree Point.
candidates.photo: The three finds in close-up.
candidates.why_here: These 31 acres are one of the last city strongholds of a butterfly that exists almost nowhere else on Earth.

candidates.title: The Market Street Arrow
candidates.do: From the Christmas Tree Point overlook, find the one spot where Market Street runs as a single straight line from the bottom of your frame all the way to the bay, and photograph it — the street must be readable as one continuous stripe pointing at the Ferry Building/waterfront. If the fog has eaten downtown, you may mark this failed and re-attempt any time you're back in the neighborhood.
candidates.where: Christmas Tree Point overlook railing, just below Eureka Peak.
candidates.failable: retryable (an attempt = one visit's try; fog-out = failed attempt)
candidates.photo: The classic postcard nobody frames right: Market Street as a perfect arrow from your feet to the water.
candidates.why_here: Market Street was platted to aim straight at Twin Peaks — this is the only place in SF where you can look down the barrel.

candidates.title: Blind Summit
candidates.do: At the base of the stair-path up Eureka Peak (north), one teammate closes their eyes (or ties a scarf over them). The rest guide them to the summit marker using VOICE ONLY — no touching, no holding hands. A step off the path or a hand on the blind climber = back to the base. Complete when the blind climber touches the summit marker; they open their eyes to the view. Pick a calm day and go slow.
candidates.where: Eureka Peak stair-path off Twin Peaks Blvd, uphill from the Christmas Tree Point parking area.
candidates.failable: no (back to the base and retry)
candidates.photo: The blind climber's hand on the marker, eyes just opening, city behind.
candidates.why_here: The classic Twin Peaks reveal — the whole city appearing at once — is better when you've earned it blind.

candidates.title: Bridge or No Bridge?
candidates.do: Before anyone can see north — standing in the Christmas Tree Point parking area facing the hillside — the team writes one word on a phone screen: "BRIDGE" or "NO BRIDGE," predicting whether at least one Golden Gate Bridge tower will be visible when you reach the Eureka Peak summit. Photograph the written call, then climb. You win only if reality matches your call at the moment you summit. One shot, no take-backs.
candidates.where: Christmas Tree Point lot (call), Eureka Peak summit (verdict).
candidates.photo: Two-photo proof: the pre-climb phone screen with the call, then the summit panorama toward the Golden Gate showing bridge or fog — team pointing either way.
candidates.why_here: Twin Peaks is the city's fog gauge; gambling on the marine layer is the most Twin Peaks thing you can do.

candidates.title: Lap the Car-Free Eight
candidates.do: Walk the entire permanently car-free eastern arm of the Twin Peaks Blvd figure eight — barrier to barrier, no shortcuts across the slope (stay on the roadway/promenade). Take a photo of the team touching the road-closure barrier or gate at the start, and another at the far barrier. Both photos = complete.
candidates.where: Twin Peaks Blvd, east side of the figure eight (closed to cars since 2016); gates at the north and south ends of the closed section, ~0.6 miles apart.
candidates.photo: Bookend shots — team hands on the closure gates at each end, empty cliff-edge boulevard curving away behind.
candidates.why_here: SF gave walkers an entire mountaintop boulevard to walk down the middle of; it deserves a victory lap.

Visitacion Valley.intro: SF's sunny southeastern valley, where a volunteer-built "ladder" of six themed community gardens — the Visitacion Valley Greenway — climbs the hillside block by block from Leland Avenue up to Tioga Avenue, its parcels linked by whimsical wrought-iron gates (8 by sculptor Jim Growden, 2 by Fran Martin) celebrating local plants and critters. Leland Avenue below is SF's most small-town main street: Hans Schiller Plaza's tiled columns, the 2011 branch library with bicycle gears hanging in its dome, taquerias, Chinese bakeries and cafés, and, at the Bayshore corner, a former grocery reborn as the Church of Clown. Anchors: the Greenway ladder, Leland Ave, and the neighborhood's hard-to-spell name. (On this map the old Schlage Lock office, Little Hollywood and the T's Sunnydale terminus sit just across the line in Bayview Hunters Point, and McLaren Park is its own neighborhood.)
Visitacion Valley.why_chosen: Walk the six-garden Greenway and see if two of you pick the same favorite, find a book with a teammate's name in its title at the library without saying a word, and walk the Native Plant Garden's switchbacks without touching a leaf. A mind meld, a silent hunt, a careful walk; one one-shot and one retry-style, zero strangers, $0, ≈ 35–50 minutes.

candidates.title: Climb the Garden Ladder
candidates.do: The Visitacion Valley Greenway is a ladder of six block-long gardens. Start at Hans Schiller Plaza on Leland Ave and walk all six, one garden at a time — crossing Raymond, Arleta, Teddy, Campbell and Tucker — to the Native Plant Garden at Tioga Ave; number them 1–6 from the bottom. No talking about favorites on the way. At the top, two teammates each secretly pick their favorite garden, then reveal at the same moment (fingers up for its number). Same garden = complete. Different = failed, no retry. The gardens are open sunrise to sunset except the Agricultural Garden, which you can see from the sidewalk.
candidates.where: Visitacion Valley Greenway, Leland Ave up to Tioga Ave.
candidates.photo: The two teammates revealing their fingers at the top garden, the Greenway stepping down the hill behind them.
candidates.why_here: Neighbors turned six vacant lots into a stairway of gardens — each with its own iron signature.

candidates.title: Your Name on the Shelf
candidates.do: Inside the Visitacion Valley Branch Library, find a book whose title includes the first name of someone on your team — the exact name, spelled the same, on the cover or spine. NO talking anywhere inside the library: point, gesture, nudge, whatever works, but not a word. Done when that teammate holds up the book with their name in its title. Reshelve it where you found it (or leave it on the return cart).
candidates.where: Visitacion Valley Branch Library, 201 Leland Ave (weekend hours: Sat 10–6, Sun 1–5).
candidates.photo: The teammate holding up the book with their own name in the title, in silence.
candidates.why_here: The neighborhood's library is its quietest room — the place to hunt the shelves for yourself without saying a word.

candidates.title: Hands Off the Native Plants
candidates.do: The Greenway's top garden, the Native Plant Garden, climbs about 40 feet to Tioga Ave on a paved path that zigzags back and forth for some 200 feet. Start at its bottom gate and walk the whole path up to the Tioga gate as a team without anyone touching a single plant — not a branch, not a brushing leaf, not even a fallen leaf on the path under your shoes. Anyone touches anything green, brown or growing = the whole team walks back down to the bottom gate and starts over. Done when everyone reaches the Tioga gate clean.
candidates.where: Native Plant Garden, top of the Visitacion Valley Greenway (bottom gate up to Tioga Ave)
candidates.failable: retryable (a touch means walking back to the bottom)
candidates.photo: The team at the Tioga gate, the zigzag path (and every untouched leaf) behind you.
candidates.why_here: Neighbors planted this slope with natives and built a switchback path through it — the garden's whole point is to be left alone, so you'd better not touch it.

candidates.title: The New Arrivals Wager
candidates.do: Inside the Visitacion Valley Branch Library, before anyone finds it, the team agrees on ONE guess: how many books are on the New Arrivals display shelf right now? Write it down, then find the shelf and count together in library voices. Within 3 = complete. Off? One more guess, on the hold shelf, and count that. Miss twice and the library wins — mark it failed. While you're there, look up: "Full Circle," Mark Grieve and Ilana Spector's steel hoops studded with recycled bicycle gears, hangs 20 feet up in the dome.
candidates.where: Visitacion Valley Branch Library, 201 Leland Ave (Sat 10–6, Sun 1–5)
candidates.failable: retryable (two guesses total: New Arrivals, then the hold shelf)
candidates.photo: The guess held up beneath the hoops, shelf in the background.
candidates.why_here: The 2011 library became Leland Ave's proudest building — and its New Arrivals shelf changes every day, so nobody can know the number in advance.

candidates.title: Clown School Entrance Exam
candidates.do: The corner storefront at Bayshore Blvd and Leland Ave, a grocery that sat empty for some 15 years, is now the Church of Clown, a clowning school and theater. Out front on the Leland Ave sidewalk (away from the Bayshore curb), pass a circus basic: balance a stick upright on one open palm for 10 counted seconds. It must be found or bought today and at least as long as your forearm (a fallen stick, a baguette, a rolled-up flyer). Your feet may move; your other hand may not touch it. Drop = the next teammate tries; once everyone has dropped, the whole team waits one minute before the next round. Complete when anyone makes 10.
candidates.where: Church of Clown, 2400 Bayshore Blvd at Leland Ave (Leland Ave sidewalk)
candidates.failable: retryable (each full round of drops costs a one-minute wait)
candidates.photo: The balancer mid-count, stick upright on a palm, the Church of Clown storefront behind.
candidates.why_here: A long-dead corner grocery reborn as a church for clowns is Vis Valley's most unexpected storefront, and palm-balancing is exactly the kind of silly skill it exists to celebrate.

candidates.title: Picnic at the Mosaic Columns
candidates.do: Buy any snack or drink (≤$10 total) from an open storefront on Leland Ave between Bayshore Blvd and Rutland St, then eat it sitting at Hans Schiller Plaza — on the benches under the pergola or by the low mosaic wall. Complete when the team photo shows the treat, a teammate mid-bite, and at least one of the plaza's three tiled columns.
candidates.where: Leland Ave commercial strip; Hans Schiller Plaza at Leland Ave near Rutland St
candidates.photo: Team snacking under the pergola with the whimsical mosaic columns in frame
candidates.why_here: Leland is the little main street "outsiders never visit" — being the outsiders who do, then picnicking in the plaza its neighbors tiled by hand, is pure Vis Valley.

candidates.title: Spell It Right: Visitacion
candidates.do: Half the city writes it "Visitation." Outside the Visitacion Valley Branch Library, make words from the real name instead. One teammate sets a 3-minute timer; then phones away except one used as the notepad. Write as many different English words of 4+ letters as you can using only the letters of VISITACION, each no more often than it appears (three I's; one each of V, S, T, A, C, O, N). No names, no abbreviations, no anagram apps. 15 valid words = complete. Short? Wait five minutes, then start a fresh list from zero.
candidates.where: Outside the Visitacion Valley Branch Library, 201 Leland Ave
candidates.failable: retryable (a miss costs a five-minute wait and a fresh list)
candidates.photo: The word list on screen with its count, held up in front of the library.
candidates.why_here: Friars named the valley on July 2, 1777, the Feast of the Visitation — La Visitación — and San Francisco has been misspelling it ever since.

West of Twin Peaks.intro: The leafy quarter tucked between Portola Drive and Ocean Avenue, where San Francisco pretends to be a storybook suburb: the fog-combed eucalyptus dome of Mount Davidson (928 ft — the city's highest natural point, with a 103-foot concrete cross hidden in the trees), the streetcar village of West Portal huddled around the 1918 Twin Peaks Tunnel mouth, and a cluster of grand 1910s "residence parks" — St. Francis Wood, Forest Hill, Balboa Terrace, Westwood Park, even a Sherwood Forest — each with its own ceremonial gates, fountains, and stairways. Anchors: the summit, the tunnel, the village street, the gates.
West of Twin Peaks.why_chosen: Summit Mount Davidson to the hidden cross (the trio's "the place is the game" entry), call K, L or M before the next train pops out of the Twin Peaks Tunnel (the neighborhood's one-shot), and hit exactly $5.00 of candy at Shaw's. One climb, one called shot, one math puzzle; zero strangers, ~$5, ≈ 35–45 minutes.

candidates.title: Summit the Hidden Cross
candidates.do: Enter Mount Davidson Park from Juanita Way or Dalewood Way and follow the forest trail to the summit — a gentle 10-minute walk under the eucalyptus. The 103-foot concrete cross (lit by FDR himself via telegraph in 1934, and rumored to be 3 feet taller than planned because the crew had leftover concrete) stays invisible in the fog-forest until you step into the clearing. Complete with one photo of the whole team at the cross.
candidates.where: Mount Davidson Park summit; trailheads at Juanita Way (north) or Dalewood Way (southwest).
candidates.photo: The whole team at the foot of the 103-foot cross, eucalyptus all around.
candidates.why_here: The literal top of the city, and a giant monument you can't see until you're standing under it — only on Mount Davidson.

candidates.title: Tunnel Roulette
candidates.do: Stand on the West Portal Ave sidewalk with a clear view of the ornate 1918 Twin Peaks Tunnel mouth. Three streetcar lines — K, L, and M — all pop out of that one hole. Start a video and call ONE letter out loud BEFORE the next outbound train's headlights appear in the tunnel. If the train that emerges shows your letter: done. If not: failed, forever. (A shuttle or out-of-service train doesn't count — redo the call.)
candidates.where: Twin Peaks Tunnel west portal, West Portal Ave at Ulloa St.
candidates.photo: Video freeze-frame or photo of the team pointing at the emerging train, its route letter legible — triumph or agony, both are keepers.
candidates.why_here: The neighborhood is literally named after this tunnel mouth; it's a Muni-powered coin flip with three sides.

candidates.title: Exact Change at Shaw's
candidates.do: Shaw's has sold candy on this block since 1931. As a team, choose candy whose prices add up to EXACTLY $5.00 before any tax — no more, no less. No phone calculators; mental math and paper only. Ring it up: exactly $5.00 = complete. Off? Back to the shelves, re-add on paper, and try again, as many times as it takes.
candidates.where: Shaw's, 122 West Portal Ave. (If Shaw's is closed, any West Portal sweet shop counts.)
candidates.failable: no (back to the shelves and try again)
candidates.photo: The receipt reading $5.00 held up with the candy haul, Shaw's sign behind.
candidates.why_here: A candy shop older than the Golden Gate Bridge deserves a proper arithmetic exam.

candidates.title: Coin in the Fountain of St. Francis Wood
candidates.do: Walk through the grand stone entrance gateway of St. Francis Wood (St. Francis Blvd at Portola Dr, 1913, by the architect of Berkeley's Campanile) and down the boulevard's landscaped center median to the big circular fountain. From the fountain's rim, each teammate tosses a coin into the raised center basin — the small upper bowl, not the big pool. Complete when every teammate has landed one; unlimited tries.
candidates.where: St. Francis Blvd median fountain, St. Francis Wood (public sidewalks and medians).
candidates.photo: The coin mid-air over the basin, gateway pylons up the boulevard behind.
candidates.why_here: A 1913 residence park with its own Beaux-Arts fountain — a wishing well on a boulevard median that most of SF has never seen.

candidates.title: Water Up the Grand Stairway
candidates.do: In Forest Hill, climb the grand Pacheco Street stairway starting at Magellan Ave — a formal balustraded staircase lined with giant concrete flower urns, built so this hillside residence park could have its own Spanish-palace entrance. Fill a cup to the brim with water at the bottom. Carry it to the top without spilling more than a fingertip's depth — no lids, no hands over the top. Spilled? Back to the bottom, refill. Complete when every teammate has made a clean climb.
candidates.where: Pacheco St stairway, from Magellan Ave up to the top landing, Forest Hill
candidates.photo: A brimming cup held level on the top landing, urns marching down behind.
candidates.why_here: The most palatial staircase in the city was built for a grand entrance; make yours without spilling.

candidates.title: Robin Hood's Other Forest
candidates.do: San Francisco has a neighborhood called Sherwood Forest, tucked onto Mount Davidson's flank — and yes, it has a Robinhood Drive. Find a Robinhood Dr street sign (off Lansdale Ave, a short detour from the Dalewood Way park entrance). Then, on the wooded edge of Mount Davidson Park just uphill, pick a tree trunk at least 20 paces away and hit it with a pinecone. Every teammate must hit the trunk; unlimited tries.
candidates.where: Robinhood Dr at Lansdale Ave, then the Dalewood Way edge of Mount Davidson Park
candidates.photo: The team under the Robinhood Dr sign, then the pinecone mid-flight.
candidates.why_here: A street named for the world's most famous archer, beside a forest — the only place in SF the archery contest makes sense.

candidates.title: Parked Cars on the Ghost Track
candidates.do: Urbano Drive is an oval because it sits exactly on the old Ingleside Racetrack, the last horse-racing venue in San Francisco. At the Entrada Court entrance, before anyone looks down the street, the team agrees on ONE guess: how many cars are parked along the OUTER curb of the whole oval right now? Write it down, then walk the full lap counting together. Within 10% = complete. Off? One more guess — the inner curb — and walk the lap again (about a mile). Miss twice = failed.
candidates.where: Urbano Drive oval, Ingleside Terraces; start and finish at the Entrada Court entrance (Sundial Park is inside it).
candidates.photo: The guess and the count held up at the Entrada Court gate, the curve of the old track behind.
candidates.why_here: You are literally pacing the footprint of a 19th-century racetrack; the street's shape is the proof, and its curbs never stop changing.

candidates.title: Streetcar Under the Deco Tower
candidates.do: The El Rey Theater at 1970 Ocean Ave is an Art Deco movie palace with a stepped 150-foot tower (a city landmark; the tower once carried an aircraft beacon). The K Ingleside streetcar runs right down Ocean Avenue in front of it. Capture ONE photo that contains both the full El Rey tower (top included) and a K streetcar passing. Trains come every 10–15 minutes on weekends, so scout your camera angle while you wait. Shoot from the sidewalk — never from the trackway.
candidates.where: El Rey Theater, 1970 Ocean Ave (at Fairfield Way)
candidates.photo: the shot itself — streetcar and 150-foot Deco tower in a single frame, team optional in foreground
candidates.why_here: Nowhere else in SF does a streetcar glide past a neighborhood Art Deco cinema tower like this.

candidates.title: Build a Sundial on the Sundial
candidates.do: Outside the fence of Sundial Park's giant dial, build your own: a stick or pencil stood upright in the grass or a dirt patch, a ring of pebbles for hour marks. Set it so it reads the CURRENT time within 30 minutes — no compass apps, no peeking at the big dial for the shadow angle. Check against a phone. Complete when it reads right. Fog? Build a pebble cairn instead: seven stones stacked, standing for ten counted seconds.
candidates.where: Sundial Park lawn, Entrada Court, Ingleside Terraces
candidates.failable: no (adjust the stick until it reads)
candidates.photo: Your six-inch sundial with the 33-foot one behind it, both casting shadows.
candidates.why_here: Joseph Leonard built the neighborhood's landmark sundial as a 1913 publicity stunt; a pencil and seven pebbles can do the same job.

candidates.title: Shadow Forecast at the Giant Sundial
candidates.do: Find Sundial Park at the center of Entrada Court (inside the Urbano Drive oval): a 33-foot dial with a 28-foot gnomon. If the sun is out, mark where the tip of the gnomon's shadow falls right now (a shoe, a coin). Then the team agrees on a prediction: place a second marker where the shadow tip will be in exactly TEN minutes. Wait it out (phones away). Shadow tip within one hand-width of your marker = complete. Off? Re-mark and predict the next ten. Fogged in? Instead, guess the dial's diameter in paces, then pace it — within 10%.
candidates.where: Sundial Park, Entrada Court off Urbano Drive, Ingleside Terraces
candidates.failable: no (re-predict, or take the fog option)
candidates.photo: Two markers and a shadow tip, gnomon looming behind.
candidates.why_here: A 1913 "world's biggest sundial" hidden in one of SF's foggiest neighborhoods — the joke writes itself, and the shadow moves faster than you think.

Western Addition.intro: The Western Addition (official Analysis Neighborhood) is the Fillmore District plus Cathedral Hill and Anza Vista: the "Harlem of the West," where 1940s–50s Fillmore Street clubs hosted Billie Holiday and John Coltrane before redevelopment bulldozed most of it. Today the neighborhood keeps that memory in engraved sidewalk pavers, a jazz poem etched into blue glass on the Fillmore bridge over the Geary trench, and murals on Divisadero; it still has the Fillmore Auditorium at Geary & Fillmore and SF's weirdest-roofed building, St. Mary's Cathedral, on Cathedral Hill. Boundary notes (checked against the DataSF polygon): Alamo Square is Hayes Valley, everything north of Geary's centerline (Hamilton Rec, the Boom Boom Room corner, Japan Center) is Japantown, and the Church of 8 Wheels is Hayes Valley — everything below stays south of Geary or on Cathedral Hill.
Western Addition.why_chosen: Act show names off the Fillmore marquee, sit five silent minutes under the cathedral's shimmering tiers, and cry a real tear among the blue glass panels on the bridge over the Geary trench. Charades, a pause, a performance; two at the Fillmore & Geary corner and one on Cathedral Hill (a 10-minute walk east), nothing failable, zero strangers, $0 (or an onion), ≈ 30–40 minutes. (The other four are alternates.)

candidates.title: Marquee Charades
candidates.do: Stand under the Fillmore Auditorium's corner marquee and read off the show names posted there and on the building's poster cases (if fewer than five names are up, add names from the venue's own upcoming-shows list on your phone until you have at least five written down). Number the list. One teammate is the headliner: they generate a random number on a phone (re-roll repeats), keep it secret, and act that name out, no words, no letters, no pointing at the sign. The team gets ONE guess. Right = the next teammate headlines with a fresh name. Wrong = new name, and the streak resets. Complete when the team gets three names in a row.
candidates.where: The Fillmore, 1805 Geary Blvd at Fillmore St, southwest corner (exterior only).
candidates.failable: no (streak resets until you hit three)
candidates.photo: The headliner frozen mid-act with the marquee readable above them, the rest of the team mid-shout.
candidates.why_here: This 1912 hall, run first by Fillmore legend Charles Sullivan and then Bill Graham, is where SF learned its band names; act your way onto the marquee.

candidates.title: Fourteen Tiers of Silence
candidates.do: Go inside St. Mary's Cathedral (free, open daily until 5 p.m., later on Saturdays; if a Mass is underway, sit at the back) and spend five minutes there in complete silence as a team, under the altar canopy: a one-ton curtain of thousands of aluminum rods hung on gold wire, in fourteen tiers. No talking, no whispering, phones away the whole time (one teammate can set a silent timer first, then pocket it too). Anyone makes a sound? Start the five minutes over.
candidates.where: Cathedral of St. Mary of the Assumption, 1111 Gough St at Geary Blvd, Cathedral Hill (enter from the plaza; visitors welcome outside service times).
candidates.place_name: Cathedral of Saint Mary of the Assumption
candidates.failable: no (a sound restarts the five minutes)
candidates.photo: Afterward, the team seated in the pews under the glittering canopy and the four colored window ribbons of the roof cross.
candidates.why_here: "Our Lady of Maytag" hides its best trick indoors: a shimmering fourteen-tier canopy under a soaring cross of light — five quiet minutes in the middle of the race is the point.

candidates.title: Feeling Blue
candidates.do: Walk out on the Fillmore St bridge over the Geary trench, among the 20 blue glass panels etched with a jazz poem (an installation called *Three Shades of Blue*), and make one teammate cry: a real tear, so no water or eye drops. Anything else goes: a sad song, a sad memory, a staring contest with the wind, an onion bought on the way. Any teammate can take a turn. Done when the photo shows a tear on a cheek, blue glass behind.
candidates.where: Fillmore St bridge over Geary Blvd, between the Fillmore (1805 Geary) and the north side; stay on the sidewalk side of the panels.
candidates.photo: One tear on one cheek, the blue glass panels behind, and a team trying not to laugh.
candidates.why_here: A poem about the Fillmore's jazz and blues, etched in blue glass on the bridge over the expressway that split the neighborhood — the one place in the city built for feeling blue.

candidates.title: Taboo on the Blue Bridge
candidates.do: Walk out on the Fillmore St bridge over the Geary trench and find the 20 blue glass panels etched with a jazz poem (an installation called *Three Shades of Blue*). Number the panels 1–20 in your head from the Fillmore-Auditorium end. One teammate is the describer: they secretly pick a panel, read it, and describe what it says in their own words — none of the words on the glass, no numbers, no spelling. The team reads along the bridge and points at ONE panel. Right = new describer, new panel. Wrong = same describer, new panel, streak resets. Complete at three in a row. Tip: the etching is faint; read it with the light behind you, up close.
candidates.where: Fillmore St bridge over Geary Blvd, between the Fillmore (1805 Geary) and the north side; stay on the sidewalk side of the panels.
candidates.failable: no (new panel until the streak reaches three)
candidates.photo: The describer mid-gesture with the team pointing at a blue panel, the Geary trench and the 38 buses below.
candidates.why_here: A poet laureate's poem about this exact corner, etched in blue glass on the bridge that stitches the Fillmore back to Japantown across the expressway that split them.

candidates.title: Sidewalk Time Machine
candidates.do: Walk Fillmore St from Geary Blvd south toward Turk St (check both sidewalks) and find THREE different pavers engraved with the names of jazz-era businesses or musicians. At the third one, pick a reader: eyes closed, they recite all three names in the order you found them, plus one detail from each paver (a street number, a word from the description). One slip = walk back, re-read, and start the recital over. Complete when a full, error-free recital is on video.
candidates.where: Fillmore St, Geary Blvd south to Turk St (the Fillmore Heritage Center at 1330 Fillmore & Eddy marks the historic heart).
candidates.failable: no (persistence — re-read and restart until it's clean)
candidates.photo: Three pavers, each with a teammate's shoe beside it, plus the reader mid-recital with eyes shut.
candidates.why_here: The Fillmore set its lost "Harlem of the West" clubs into the pavement; no other SF sidewalk tells this story.

candidates.title: Mural Memory on Divisadero
candidates.do: Find Mel Waters' 2014 "Harlem of the West" jazz mural on the west side of Divisadero between Eddy and Ellis. Everyone studies it for 60 seconds, then the whole team turns its back. Three fixed questions, answered as a team: (1) how many instruments are painted, (2) how many figures wear a hat, (3) how many figures have their eyes closed. Turn around and check by counting together. Three for three = complete. Any miss = a new 60 seconds and try again.
candidates.where: 1233 Divisadero St, west side, between Eddy St and Ellis St.
candidates.failable: no (new study round until three for three)
candidates.photo: The team with their backs to the mural mid-answer, then the recount.
candidates.why_here: Muralist Mel Waters painted the neighborhood's jazz royalty back onto its walls — this is the Divisadero end of the Harlem of the West, and the wall is dense enough to punish a lazy memory.

candidates.title: Call the 38
candidates.do: Climb the Webster St pedestrian bridge over the Geary Blvd trench. Before each bus appears, the team calls TWO things out loud on video: its direction (DOWNTOWN or OCEAN) and its line (38 local or 38R Rapid — the sign on the front shows which). The next 38-family bus to pass under the bridge decides it. Both parts right = complete. Wrong = make a new call for the next bus and keep going.
candidates.where: Webster St pedestrian bridge over the Geary expressway trench, Geary Blvd & Webster St (the last of the trench's footbridges; the Steiner one came down in 2020).
candidates.time: 5–15 min (Muni's busiest line; buses come constantly)
candidates.failable: no (one call per bus — keep calling until you hit)
candidates.photo: The team on the bridge celebrating, the verdict bus below with its sign readable.
candidates.why_here: The bridge is a relic of the Geary expressway that reshaped the Western Addition — and calling the 38 over its trench is peak transit-race tension.
